Final 08 Committee Paper

PRICES AND PRODUCTS SUPERSEDED, 2026-09-18, by D-0140

This is the paper the committee saw on 16 August and reviewed on 31 August, and it is not edited. It remains MFC's authoritative commercial document for its reasoning, its structure and its asks.

What has changed since. MFC goes to market with two products, not three; Essentials is retired as a sold product; measurement is not removable; the hour is banded at $600, $800 and $1,000; materials are $50 and $25; and the half-day loaded floor is $1,767.18.

Read it for the model. Take no price or product line-up from it.

Executive summary

Mental fitness is how well we navigate life's everyday moments: how we think, work with what we feel, act on what matters, and connect with ourselves and others (Source: MFC's public definition). MFC teaches people how they actually function in those moments, and trains one three-step routine so it is there when they need it. Education and training for mental fitness, for everyone, before anything is wrong. We sell that to organisations as three products.

This paper asks you to settle the product line, our staged approach, and one decision that is yours rather than ours. Three real products, published prices, and a staged twelve-month plan you can track us against at every meeting.

Three things to know before you read the rest, stated once and not repeated below.

  1. We can price and quote today. We cannot yet contract, and we cannot put a facilitator in front of a participant until the clinical safety items close. Nothing in this paper softens that, and nothing here is a measurement of our own delivery: we have run no cohorts and have no paying customer. Where a figure is arithmetic rather than something we have measured, or an estimate, or a working assumption chosen so a plan can be modelled, it says so beside it.
  2. The largest risk is that MFC is one person. Every delivery hour in every plan here is Hunter's. There is no second facilitator and no standard for choosing one (section 6).
  3. We are waiting on a first customer, not on funding. We hold about $12,000 (Source: founder-reported cash position as at 2026-08-09, not independently verified against a bank account), running costs are small, and nobody has ever been asked to buy anything from us.

What we are asking you for.

The ask Type
1 Adopt the three products at the prices in section 3 Agree
2 Adopt the statement of what MFC is and is not in section 1 Agree
3 Add the optional monthly session, offered only after a delivery Agree
4 Approve our staged approach (3, 6, 9 and 12 months, section 5.3) and the success metrics we expect at each stage Agree
5 What happens to a live monthly commitment if Hunter is unavailable Decide, yours not ours

The first year, in one line. Twenty organisations approached, ten conversations, five quotes issued, three accepted, eight organisations delivered to, five of them paying, about $9,800 of revenue of which the charity keeps about $6,130. The volumes come from our own first-year plan (Source: FINAL-07); the two money figures are that plan's arithmetic recomputed at the prices in section 3 [Source: derived]. That is a floor we can defend rather than a target we are stretching for.

What we are doing, why, how, and by when

This is MFC's product and commercial strategy. A broader organisational strategy, covering governance, administration and marketing, does not yet exist and is best written after the review date named in section 8.

1. What MFC is, and what it is not

We teach mental fitness the way physical fitness is taught (Source: MFC's product-category framework, §1.1): somebody explains how it works, then you train, on your own real situations, until you can reach the routine under pressure. The statement we are asking you to adopt:

Mental Fitness Collective delivers skills-based mental fitness education and training with measurement. What it can do is teach a practised routine people can use in real moments, and measure honestly whether they used it.

It is not clinical care or therapy. It is not a substitute for legal or work-health-and-safety advice. It is not a standalone psychosocial risk management system, and it is not a control an employer can rely on to discharge a duty.

Rationale, plainly. Workplace mental-health law is about the conditions people work in, and training removes none of them; Victoria has written that into regulation, where training "must not be the predominant measure (subject to reasonable practicability)" (SR 103/2025) (Source: research/market-psychosocial-compliance-landscape.md). Wellbeing programmes, Mental Health First Aid and therapy each do a real job well; we are not a better version of any of them, we do a different job, training a person on their own state without needing anything to be wrong.

Stated plainly
On duties Nothing an organisation buys from us changes its own legal duty, and we never say that what we sell discharges a duty, satisfies a Code obligation, or counts as consulting workers
The regulatory context What we sell belongs to the class of measure regulators have demoted (Source: research/market-psychosocial-compliance-landscape.md §3.6). Research does not separate mental fitness from resilience training as a distinct, measurable thing, so we present the category as our own way of organising the work, never as a validated discovery (Source: MFC's product-category framework, §4)
The gate on the wording No lawyer and no work-health-and-safety practitioner has read any of our positioning, and it cannot go in front of a buyer until one has. The statement above is a working boundary, not an approved one
A conflict we are not resolving here Our Framework says we do not claim to prevent mental illness; our Constitution names it as a principal activity. That needs qualified legal advice, and no legal conclusion is drawn here

We never say that we prevent or treat mental illness, that we replace therapy or crisis support, that any other provider fails, or that a single session produces lasting behaviour change.

What makes this different, stated honestly. The loop is not new: parts exist in DBT, ACT and CBT. What we have not found elsewhere in the category is one three-step procedure, cued to any moment, run identically every time, with nothing to diagnose first (Source: 13-founder-voice-v2-category-and-competitors). Not claimed as proven: zero cohorts run, and nobody in this category has funded the proactive, universal version of it. That gap is the opportunity.

2. What's in it for me

Why should a person care, why should an organisation spend money on it, and what will we be able to prove.

The human lens

Everyone has these moments, and they are not only the hard ones. The sentence said in anger, the silence when somebody needed them to speak, being somewhere else entirely at the end of a hard day. And just as much, the good ones: showing up fully for someone, connecting with intention instead of by accident. We are all human, we all have moments like this constantly, at work and everywhere else, and we expect ourselves to handle them well. Almost nobody is taught how, let alone trained and given the chance to practise. That is what we are trying to solve. The gap between knowing what to do and doing it is not a character flaw. It is a skill nobody was ever taught, and it is trainable.

What a person gets, specifically. Not another method they are simply told to do. An actual grounding in what is happening inside them in a moment: their thoughts, their feelings, what their body is doing, and what they can start to do about it. From there, a loop they can actually recall and use in the moment itself, not just understand afterwards, because knowing what to do and being able to reach it under pressure are two different gaps, and the second one is the one we see missing most. Practice at using it, in the room, on their own real situations. And afterwards, a Radar: simply a short list of moments they choose to keep practising, kept alive by a reminder tied to something already in their day, since a skill with no cue attached to real life does not stick on its own. And a way back after getting something wrong that does not turn into a verdict on who they are.

It is theirs, not their employer's. Nobody has to identify as unwell, disclose anything, or accept that something is wrong with them in order to take part. That matters, because it is the single biggest reason people do not use what workplaces already offer them.

The business lens

What an organisation is actually buying, stated as levers rather than promises:

The lever What it means in practice
A practised skill, not an awareness session People leave having used the routine on a real situation of their own, not having watched a presentation about it
Evidence for a psychosocial initiative A documented training initiative that sits alongside your own controls, with measurement attached, at a time when regulators expect organisations to show what they are doing
Data about your own people A short measurement before, immediately after, and again at day 21, reported back with the numbers underneath, including when the answer is that nothing changed
Reach across a whole team at once Everybody gets the same routine, so a team can use it with each other rather than a few individuals having a private skill
A shared Radar, not only an individual one Individual change does not hold if the environment stays the same. A team agrees its own short list of moments and norms, the same tool at group level
A cost you can size before you commit Fixed prices, published here, from $600 to $3,900 plus $95 a person (Source: 110)

The return-on-investment question, answered honestly. For a team of ten, Foundations (section 3) is $4,850 (Source: 110), which is $485 a person [Source: derived], once. What that buys is five things, and they should be seen before the number is compared to anything: a session for whoever leads the group, a half day with the team, a facilitated return three weeks later, a written report back to the organisation, and measurement taken at three points (Source: 110).

What we can honestly say is the mechanism, not a measured outcome: a person who has this skill and reaches for it, difficult moment or good one, is better placed to handle it than a person who does not. That is the actual selling point; what we have not measured is that we cause it. What we cannot honestly do is convert any of it into a payback figure. MFC cannot and will not claim improvements in engagement, retention, absenteeism, productivity or claims costs. We do not have access to an organisation's HR data, we have run no cohorts, and any such number would be invented.

So here is the exact line between what we will show you and what we will not.

We will be able to show We will not be able to show
Whether people could remember and use the routine at three weeks, with the number it was asked of That the training reduced turnover, absence or claims
What changed in people's own reported ability to use it, before and after That any change would not have happened anyway
Whether a team kept using it once we left A financial return per dollar spent
Whether clients continued, and the reasons given by those who did not Anything at all about clinical outcomes

3. The three products

Three products, plus one option offered only after a delivery. They are a ladder of depth, not a ladder of length: the first rung meets the idea, the second teaches the routine and comes back once, and the third practises it until it holds and helps the organisation build it into how it works. The extra money buys depth and adoption support, not more minutes.

Introduction Essentials Foundations
In one line A room meets the idea. One hour, with no direct further input after it — and, per below, that hour can still carry a longer reach than the room itself The routine, taught properly, with one return and a short report. The initial foundation an organisation actually buys More of the wider approach, and time to work through it properly. The only one built for adoption rather than for learning
What it is One hour, in person or online. People meet the idea and try one thing on a real situation somebody offers. No direct further input after it: no return, no measurement, no report A 45-minute session with whoever leads the group, then 90 minutes with the team, in person, where people learn the routine and use it on a real situation of their own, then a 30-minute online session about three weeks later taking the final measurement, plus a short written report A 45-minute leader session, then a half day with the team: the same routine, plus more of the wider approach and time to work through it properly. An on-site session about three weeks later, which where the team is ready turns into implementation work, then a fuller written findings report and a conversation about it
What the organisation gets afterwards No direct further input from us — it is reach, not a programme. We do not measure or claim anything beyond the room itself; the idea may land with someone who acts on it later, at their own pace, but that is not something we track or promise A short written report, one to two pages: what was run, the themes, and what to do next. It reports themes, not participant data, because our reporting floor forbids participant data on a group under 20, so it is lighter than the Foundations report and should never be described as the same thing (Source: 110 §2) A written findings report interpreting what that group's own measurement showed, and a conversation about it. Four hours of work sit behind it against one for Essentials (Source: 110 §3)
Why you would choose it You want a room to see the thing before anybody spends money You want your people to have the routine, and a half day off the floor is not possible or affordable You want it to stick in the organisation, not just land with individuals. It is the more experiential product and the one built for workplace adoption
Price $600 booked, or free as outreach up to 20 times a year (Source: 110) $1,250 for 2 to 5 people, $1,550 for 6 to 10, $1,800 for 11 to 15 (Source: 110) $3,900 plus $95 a person (Source: 110)
Where it stands today Content exists and has been run. The only one of the three already built (Source: the pricing decision, §3) Designed, never delivered, and the return has never been rehearsed (Source: the pricing decision, §3) Half-day built and current; the three-week return is designed and never rehearsed (Source: the pricing decision, §3)

The leader session is in both Essentials and Foundations, inside the price, never sold separately (founder decision, 2026-08-16) (Source: 130-ESSENTIALS); Introduction is a one-hour taster with no follow-through, so it has none. If the person who runs the team does not know what their people were asked to do, the practice dies the same week. The disclosure that travels with it is not softened: it is informed by the approach of the RESPECT trial, where the evidenced dose was four hours (Milligan-Saville et al. 2017) and ours is about one, and we claim no effect on employees.

Why Essentials has the shape it has. The 90 minutes are in person because that is where a room works out loud together, and the return is online because a second site visit would price out a thin-budget organisation. This return format is untested (as noted in the table above), so we do not yet claim it works.

3.1 The option offered after a delivery

A 30-minute guided session, monthly, same day, same group, online by default. A short form goes out beforehand, we open by telling the group what their own answers said, and we work on whatever it showed. Every third month their leader joins for the last fifteen minutes. Rationale: we tell people mental fitness is trained rather than taught, and this is the only part of what we sell whose shape matches that.
Price and term $400 a month for 8 to 15 people, $300 a month for a smaller group [Source: derived]. Three months to start, continuing as long as they want it
When it is offered Never in the first quote. We deliver what they bought, then ask
Its status An option under development, not a settled priced product, with no name until we have run it (Source: the pricing decision, §3.1)

3.2 Introduction, online

Not a new decision, an existing offer we are simply describing. Introduction already runs online at $450 (Source: 110 §4) for a team, not a solo stranger: one hour, learn the loop and start on reps, the same way a team of two would take a meeting. It scales with the group the way Essentials does, from a small team up to a larger one of 10 to 20. This is separate from, and safer than, an early individual-seat design we are not pursuing, which would have put a stranger in distress online with no employer, no host and no local support.

4. Who each product is for

What separates the three products is the size of the organisation and how much money it has.

Foundations Essentials Introduction
The organisation Has a training budget and a line for professional development Little or no training budget; buying this is a noticeable decision No budget for this, or has never bought training at all
Typically 50 to 250 staff, an HR or safety lead, a board asking what is being done; releases 6 to 20 people twice (Source: 110) A team of 2 to 15 (Source: 110): a small business, a small not-for-profit, or one team where half a day off the floor is not possible A chamber, a peak body, a conference, a club, a community group
What they pay $3,900 plus $95 a person (Source: 110) $1,250 to $1,800 (Source: 110) $600, or nothing

This is the mission point, stated plainly. Smaller organisations and thin-budget not-for-profits are barely reached in this market, because almost everything in it is priced for organisations with a training budget. Introduction and Essentials exist so a seven-person business or a volunteer committee can get something real rather than nothing, and Foundations is what makes them possible.

5. How we reach organisations, what we measure, and by when

5.1 How we get top-of-funnel: three routes to market

How we get top-of-funnel is a relationship question, not a marketing-spend question. Nothing is sold cold; every route starts with someone who has already met Hunter or been introduced.

Route What it is, and why it is one of the three
Safety consultants, brokers and peak bodies Borrowed trust, no sales function required: named consultancies, brokers and bodies approached directly, in ranked order
Warm direct sales Organisations we can already get a meeting with, sold as our first case studies. Costs nothing, and can start this week
Community talks and events A short talk or activity, 5 to 15 minutes, at an existing community event. Already run before; it reaches an organisation and grows the charity's own base of supporters at the same time

Rationale. One person who delivers everything can open a small number of doors properly, not a large number badly, so this is sequenced by trust already built. Social media is active now, not deferred: over 9,000 followers already (Source: founder-reported, 2026-08-17, not independently verified), and consistent posting is the cheapest lever we have. An ambassador with a large, genuinely connected following is a lever we are exploring for the same reason: what we teach is simple and quick to learn, which makes it easy for someone else to carry. Once we have real traction, a roving MFC community across different parts of Sydney is worth building; not before.

On an executive-network route, which we have looked at. Genuinely a good idea; we have considered partnering with an existing group over building one. Not one of the three we start with: founder hours are the constraint. If we are genuinely struggling to reach people at 3 to 6 months, this is the first thing we pick up.

5.2 What we measure, and when

We measure three times: before, immediately after, and again at day 21. The questions separate whether a person could not remember the routine from whether they could not use it, because those two failures need different fixes (Source: the measurement research). A recognised evaluation framework, Kirkpatrick, has been proposed; we have not adopted it, and it goes to our measurement advisers first (Source: founder record, 2026-08-16).

What cannot be concluded from it. We do not claim behaviour change at day 21, and a three to four month follow-up is not designed, costed or funded for standard delivery. Organisations choose their own product, so we cannot say the longer product works better, or that the monthly sessions cause anything, and we do not control the environment somebody returns to (Source: MFC's product-category framework, §1.2).

Our founding case studies add a three-month wave, checking unaided recall, still no claim the training caused anything (Source: B5c). This starts to turn a session into evidence. Using it beyond our own report needs ethics approval (HREC) before collection, so a university or research partner is a live, unstarted task, not a formality (Source: 00-hrec-and-data-strategy); data storage is designed and cleared the same way.

5.3 The plan, and what success looks like

3 months from start 6 months from start 9 months from start 12 months from start
Stage Readiness Proof Proof into repeatability Repeatability
The choice we are making Become sellable and get in front of buyers. Not new products, not a second facilitator Convert quotes and deliver Repeat what worked once Publish what we found
What must be true 20 organisations approached, 10 conversations, 5 quotes issued (Source: FINAL-07) 3 quotes accepted, first deliveries done, monthly session offered once. The measure that matters: a price quoted and accepted, not a product built First paying delivery's day-21 measurement collected 8 organisations delivered to, 5 paying, one group's day-21 numbers published (Source: FINAL-07). A client kept paying, or told us why not
Governance Clinical review commissioned, named person and date Reviewer question resolved, review under way Review substantially complete Clinical review obtained: the year's hard gate. Ending with it open means a year we could not lawfully deliver at all
What would tell us it is not working Fewer than 10 conversations out of 20 approaches No quote accepted Clinical review still not commissioned Nothing delivered, or delivered and nobody continues
Also happening Top-of-funnel outreach begins here: named consultants and peak bodies approached; commission the clinical, legal, safety and privacy reads; confirm insurance; build first modules Rehearse the monthly session unpaid; register the comparison first Hold the review date set in section 8 Settle how free delivery is funded; publish one honest finding

Delivery is not a month-three milestone: it depends on the clinical safety items closing first, so a realistic first delivery falls in months 3 to 5 [estimate, Source: FINAL-07]. The year's plan is 4 Introductions, 3 Essentials and 1 Foundations at the founding case-study rate, about 61 facilitator hours against a model built to carry 42 organisations a year, so capacity is not the limit [Source: derived, FINAL-07].

6. The risks, in the order they should worry you

# Risk The honest position What we are asking for
1 MFC is one person (executive summary, item 2). No standard exists for selecting a second one, no training requirement, no fidelity checklist and no observed certification (Source: FINAL-01 §5) Named, not defended. A one-off session that cannot be delivered is a booking moved; a monthly session that cannot be delivered is a promise to a paying client missed Item 5: a written position on what happens to a live monthly commitment if Hunter is unavailable. Not a succession plan; the client agreement needs something to point at
2 We cannot deliver to a participant yet (executive summary, item 1). Clinical and safety matters have been open since 29 July 2026 Open, not stalled. No named reviewer and no date yet exist, and every month this stays open is a month of the twelve-month plan we cannot deliver against Not an ask in this paper: who carries out the clinical review is being resolved outside it
3 Nobody has ever bought anything from us. No named prospects, no objections heard Why months 0 to 3 are selling rather than building Nothing. Ours to fix
4 The monthly session has never been run. Every timing figure is an estimate Why it goes to you as an option rather than a priced product Item 3, as an option

Three things already reduce risk 1: commitments run three months at a time, we can say a slot is not available, and the monthly session is a fixed shape opened from a form, which makes it the right first thing for a second person to learn. What is missing is any second person, and any standard for choosing one.

7. The money
What we hold About $12,000 (Source: founder-reported cash position as at 2026-08-09, not independently verified against a bank account)
Income and costs No income, and no grant income is safe to count on (Source: FINAL-05 §8). Running costs are small: website, registration, insurance (Source: Hunter, 2026-08-16, not yet itemised)
No runway date appears here Fixed costs have never been itemised; we will not give a runway figure built on anything softer
How much time we have Unknown. Sixty delivery hours a month is an assumption [assumption]
How Hunter is paid From the end of this year, per session facilitated, at $66.10 an hour (Source: the half-day pricing decision, §1) rather than a salary, so it comes out of work somebody has already bought
If it does not work Pause delivery and preserve cash, push corporate sales, or seek a bridge (Source: FINAL-05 §10). The review date we are asking you to set decides which

So we are not running out of money. We are waiting on a first customer, and the first paying work lands three to nine months out [assumption].

7.1 Our approach to grants

We are counting on services, not grants. Workshops and the three products are the plan; grants might be there and will help, but none appears in the money table above and we are not operating as if they keep us alive. The process: we hold a tracker of upcoming opportunities, and when one comes up, a working group (Rachel, Jake and Hunter) discusses whether we can genuinely tailor our approach to fit it. We only pursue an opportunity that is a real fit and genuinely beneficial, not every open window (Source: FINAL-05 §1-4). Donations become relevant once we have one measured, published cohort.

Who pays for the free work. Twenty free Introductions a year cost about $800 in cash and about 75 hours of Hunter's time [Source: derived], so what limits free work is the calendar, not the bank account.

8. What the committee is being asked for

# To agree Why, and what follows if it is not agreed
1 Adopt the three products at the prices in section 3 (Source: 110) Three genuinely different organisations, one price sheet, checked against published Australian prices (Source: the pricing research). A view has been put that $5,000 should be our floor (Source: committee correspondence relayed by the founder, 2026-08-16); Foundations reaches $5,040 at twelve people [Source: derived], and a floor across everything would delete Essentials and the free Introduction, and with them the small business and the community group
2 Adopt the statement of what MFC is and is not in section 1 Every piece of our material is built on it, and it keeps us inside what a safety adviser or lawyer would accept
3 Add the optional monthly session, offered only after a delivery, three months minimum, as an option under development The only part of what we sell whose shape matches our claim that fitness is trained rather than taught
4 Approve our staged approach and expected success metrics at 3, 6, 9 and 12 months (section 5.3) The floor we can defend, not a target we are stretching for; it lets you track us against something concrete at each meeting
# To decide, because this is not ours to take Our position
5 What happens to a live monthly commitment if Hunter is unavailable We have no position. Even a minimal one is enough; the client agreement needs something to point at

How free and reduced-price delivery is funded is our plan, not something we are asking you to decide: grants and an honest cap. This corrects our own strategy document, whose $400 per-sale contribution (Source: FINAL-01 §2) would raise about $2,400 a year [Source: derived] and does not exist in our prices today (Source: 110). A third direction, not decided today: reducing price for things valuable to us now (research participation, full measurement, a testimonial), rather than a levy or a grant. A narrow version already exists in our founding case-study rate (Source: 110); nothing broader is costed, and would come back to you with numbers attached.

And our own review date, also not something we are asking you to decide: three months after our first quote goes out, at which point either a price has been accepted or we take one of the contingencies in section 7 deliberately rather than by drift. Nothing here needs the AGM, and we are not asking you for pricing detail, session design or build and channel order, which sit with the operating side.

What makes this different, stated honestly. The loop is not new: parts exist in DBT, ACT and CBT. What we have not found elsewhere in the category is one three-step procedure, cued to any moment, run identically every time, with nothing to diagnose first (Source: 13-founder-voice-v2-category-and-competitors). Not claimed as proven: zero cohorts run, and nobody in this category has funded the proactive, universal version of it. That gap is the opportunity.

2. What's in it for me

Why should a person care, why should an organisation spend money on it, and what will we be able to prove.

The human lens

Everyone has these moments, and they are not only the hard ones. The sentence said in anger, the silence when somebody needed them to speak, being somewhere else entirely at the end of a hard day. And just as much, the good ones: showing up fully for someone, connecting with intention instead of by accident. We are all human, we all have moments like this constantly, at work and everywhere else, and we expect ourselves to handle them well. Almost nobody is taught how, let alone trained and given the chance to practise. That is what we are trying to solve. The gap between knowing what to do and doing it is not a character flaw. It is a skill nobody was ever taught, and it is trainable.

What a person gets, specifically. Not another method they are simply told to do. An actual grounding in what is happening inside them in a moment: their thoughts, their feelings, what their body is doing, and what they can start to do about it. From there, a loop they can actually recall and use in the moment itself, not just understand afterwards, because knowing what to do and being able to reach it under pressure are two different gaps, and the second one is the one we see missing most. Practice at using it, in the room, on their own real situations. And afterwards, a Radar: simply a short list of moments they choose to keep practising, kept alive by a reminder tied to something already in their day, since a skill with no cue attached to real life does not stick on its own. And a way back after getting something wrong that does not turn into a verdict on who they are.

It is theirs, not their employer's. Nobody has to identify as unwell, disclose anything, or accept that something is wrong with them in order to take part. That matters, because it is the single biggest reason people do not use what workplaces already offer them.

The business lens

What an organisation is actually buying, stated as levers rather than promises:

The lever What it means in practice
A practised skill, not an awareness session People leave having used the routine on a real situation of their own, not having watched a presentation about it
Evidence for a psychosocial initiative A documented training initiative that sits alongside your own controls, with measurement attached, at a time when regulators expect organisations to show what they are doing
Data about your own people A short measurement before, immediately after, and again at day 21, reported back with the numbers underneath, including when the answer is that nothing changed
Reach across a whole team at once Everybody gets the same routine, so a team can use it with each other rather than a few individuals having a private skill
A shared Radar, not only an individual one Individual change does not hold if the environment stays the same. A team agrees its own short list of moments and norms, the same tool at group level
A cost you can size before you commit Fixed prices, published here, from $600 to $3,900 plus $95 a person (Source: 110)

The return-on-investment question, answered honestly. For a team of ten, Foundations (section 3) is $4,850 (Source: 110), which is $485 a person [Source: derived], once. What that buys is five things, and they should be seen before the number is compared to anything: a session for whoever leads the group, a half day with the team, a facilitated return three weeks later, a written report back to the organisation, and measurement taken at three points (Source: 110).

What we can honestly say is the mechanism, not a measured outcome: a person who has this skill and reaches for it, difficult moment or good one, is better placed to handle it than a person who does not. That is the actual selling point; what we have not measured is that we cause it. What we cannot honestly do is convert any of it into a payback figure. MFC cannot and will not claim improvements in engagement, retention, absenteeism, productivity or claims costs. We do not have access to an organisation's HR data, we have run no cohorts, and any such number would be invented.

So here is the exact line between what we will show you and what we will not.

We will be able to show We will not be able to show
Whether people could remember and use the routine at three weeks, with the number it was asked of That the training reduced turnover, absence or claims
What changed in people's own reported ability to use it, before and after That any change would not have happened anyway
Whether a team kept using it once we left A financial return per dollar spent
Whether clients continued, and the reasons given by those who did not Anything at all about clinical outcomes

3. The three products

Three products, plus one option offered only after a delivery. They are a ladder of depth, not a ladder of length: the first rung meets the idea, the second teaches the routine and comes back once, and the third practises it until it holds and helps the organisation build it into how it works. The extra money buys depth and adoption support, not more minutes.

Introduction Essentials Foundations
In one line A room meets the idea. One hour, and nothing follows it The routine, taught properly, with one return and a short report. The smallest thing an organisation actually buys More of the wider approach, and time to work through it properly. The only one built for adoption rather than for learning
What it is One hour, in person or online. People meet the idea and try one thing on a real situation somebody offers. Nothing follows it: no return, no measurement, no report A 45-minute session with whoever leads the group, then 90 minutes with the team, in person, where people learn the routine and use it on a real situation of their own, then a 30-minute online session about three weeks later taking the final measurement, plus a short written report A 45-minute leader session, then a half day with the team: the same routine, plus more of the wider approach and time to work through it properly. An on-site session about three weeks later, which where the team is ready turns into implementation work, then a fuller written findings report and a conversation about it
What the organisation gets afterwards Nothing. It is reach, not a programme A short written report, one to two pages: what was run, the themes, and what to do next. It reports themes, not participant data, because our reporting floor forbids participant data on a group under 20, so it is lighter than the Foundations report and should never be described as the same thing (Source: 110 §2) A written findings report interpreting what that group's own measurement showed, and a conversation about it. Four hours of work sit behind it against one for Essentials (Source: 110 §3)
Why you would choose it You want a room to see the thing before anybody spends money You want your people to have the routine, and a half day off the floor is not possible or affordable You want it to stick in the organisation, not just land with individuals. It is the more experiential product and the one built for workplace adoption
Price $600 booked, or free as outreach up to 20 times a year (Source: 110) $1,250 for 2 to 5 people, $1,550 for 6 to 10, $1,800 for 11 to 15 (Source: 110) $3,900 plus $95 a person (Source: 110)
Where it stands today Content exists and has been run. The only one of the three already built (Source: D-0103 §3) Designed, never delivered, and the return has never been rehearsed (Source: D-0103 §3) Half-day built and current; the three-week return is designed and never rehearsed (Source: D-0103 §3)

The leader session is in both Essentials and Foundations, inside the price, never sold separately (founder decision, 2026-08-16) (Source: 130-ESSENTIALS); Introduction is a one-hour taster with no follow-through, so it has none. If the person who runs the team does not know what their people were asked to do, the practice dies the same week. The disclosure that travels with it is not softened: it is informed by the approach of the RESPECT trial, where the evidenced dose was four hours (Milligan-Saville et al. 2017) and ours is about one, and we claim no effect on employees.

Why Essentials has the shape it has. The 90 minutes are in person because that is where a room works out loud together, and the return is online because a second site visit would price out a thin-budget organisation, but no group has run a 30-minute online return, so we do not claim it works.

3.1 The option offered after a delivery

A 30-minute guided session, monthly, same day, same group, online by default. A short form goes out beforehand, we open by telling the group what their own answers said, and we work on whatever it showed. Every third month their leader joins for the last fifteen minutes. Rationale: we tell people mental fitness is trained rather than taught, and this is the only part of what we sell whose shape matches that.
Price and term $400 a month for 8 to 15 people, $300 a month for a smaller group [Source: derived]. Three months to start, continuing as long as they want it
When it is offered Never in the first quote. We deliver what they bought, then ask
Its status An option under development, not a settled priced product, with no name until we have run it (Source: D-0103 §3.1)

3.2 Introduction, online

Not a new decision, an existing offer we are simply describing. Introduction already runs online at $450 (Source: 110 §4) for a team, not a solo stranger: one hour, learn the loop and start on reps, the same way a team of two would take a meeting. It scales with the group the way Essentials does, from a small team up to a larger one of 10 to 20. This is separate from, and safer than, an early individual-seat design we are not pursuing, which would have put a stranger in distress online with no employer, no host and no local support.

4. Who each product is for

What separates the three products is the size of the organisation and how much money it has.

Foundations Essentials Introduction
The organisation Has a training budget and a line for professional development Little or no training budget; buying this is a noticeable decision No budget for this, or has never bought training at all
Typically 50 to 250 staff, an HR or safety lead, a board asking what is being done; releases 6 to 20 people twice (Source: 110) A team of 2 to 15 (Source: 110): a small business, a small not-for-profit, or one team where half a day off the floor is not possible A chamber, a peak body, a conference, a club, a community group
What they pay $3,900 plus $95 a person (Source: 110) $1,250 to $1,800 (Source: 110) $600, or nothing

This is the mission point, stated plainly. Smaller organisations and thin-budget not-for-profits are barely reached in this market, because almost everything in it is priced for organisations with a training budget. Introduction and Essentials exist so a seven-person business or a volunteer committee can get something real rather than nothing, and Foundations is what makes them possible.

5. How we reach organisations, what we measure, and by when

5.1 How we get top-of-funnel: three routes to market

How we get top-of-funnel is a relationship question, not a marketing-spend question. Nothing is sold cold; every route starts with someone who has already met Hunter or been introduced.

Route What it is, and why it is one of the three
Safety consultants, brokers and peak bodies Borrowed trust, no sales function required: named consultancies, brokers and bodies approached directly, in ranked order
Warm direct sales Organisations we can already get a meeting with, sold as our first case studies. Costs nothing, and can start this week
Community talks and events A short talk or activity, 5 to 15 minutes, at an existing community event. Already run before; it reaches an organisation and grows the charity's own base of supporters at the same time

Rationale. One person who delivers everything can open a small number of doors properly, not a large number badly, so this is sequenced by trust already built. Social media is active now, not deferred: over 9,000 followers already (Source: founder-reported, 2026-08-17, not independently verified), and consistent posting is the cheapest lever we have. An ambassador with a large, genuinely connected following is a lever we are exploring for the same reason: what we teach is simple and quick to learn, which makes it easy for someone else to carry. Once we have real traction, a roving MFC community across different parts of Sydney is worth building; not before.

On an executive-network route, which we have looked at. Genuinely a good idea; we have considered partnering with an existing group over building one. Not one of the three we start with: founder hours are the constraint. If we are genuinely struggling to reach people at 3 to 6 months, this is the first thing we pick up.

5.2 What we measure, and when

We measure three times: before, immediately after, and again at day 21. The questions separate whether a person could not remember the routine from whether they could not use it, because those two failures need different fixes (Source: R3). A recognised evaluation framework, Kirkpatrick, has been proposed; we have not adopted it, and it goes to our measurement advisers first (Source: founder record, 2026-08-16).

What cannot be concluded from it. We do not claim behaviour change at day 21, and a three to four month follow-up is not designed, costed or funded for standard delivery. Organisations choose their own product, so we cannot say the longer product works better, or that the monthly sessions cause anything, and we do not control the environment somebody returns to (Source: K-12 §1.2).

Our founding case studies add a three-month wave, checking unaided recall, still no claim the training caused anything (Source: B5c). This starts to turn a session into evidence. Using it beyond our own report needs ethics approval (HREC) before collection, so a university or research partner is a live, unstarted task, not a formality (Source: 00-hrec-and-data-strategy); data storage is designed and cleared the same way.

5.3 The plan, and what success looks like

3 months from start 6 months from start 9 months from start 12 months from start
Stage Readiness Proof Proof into repeatability Repeatability
The choice we are making Become sellable and get in front of buyers. Not new products, not a second facilitator Convert quotes and deliver Repeat what worked once Publish what we found
What must be true 20 organisations approached, 10 conversations, 5 quotes issued (Source: FINAL-07) 3 quotes accepted, first deliveries done, monthly session offered once. The measure that matters: a price quoted and accepted, not a product built First paying delivery's day-21 measurement collected 8 organisations delivered to, 5 paying, one group's day-21 numbers published (Source: FINAL-07). A client kept paying, or told us why not
Governance Clinical review commissioned, named person and date Reviewer question resolved, review under way Review substantially complete Clinical review obtained: the year's hard gate. Ending with it open means a year we could not lawfully deliver at all
What would tell us it is not working Fewer than 10 conversations out of 20 approaches No quote accepted Clinical review still not commissioned Nothing delivered, or delivered and nobody continues
Also happening Top-of-funnel outreach begins here: named consultants and peak bodies approached; commission the clinical, legal, safety and privacy reads; confirm insurance; build first modules Rehearse the monthly session unpaid; register the comparison first Hold the review date set in section 8 Settle how free delivery is funded; publish one honest finding

Delivery is not a month-three milestone: it depends on the clinical safety items closing first, so a realistic first delivery falls in months 3 to 5 [estimate, Source: FINAL-07]. The year's plan is 4 Introductions, 3 Essentials and 1 Foundations at the founding case-study rate, about 61 facilitator hours against a model built to carry 42 organisations a year, so capacity is not the limit [Source: derived, FINAL-07].

6. The risks, in the order they should worry you

# Risk The honest position What we are asking for
1 MFC is one person. Every delivery hour in every plan is Hunter's. There is no second facilitator, no standard for selecting one, no training requirement, no fidelity checklist and no observed certification (Source: FINAL-01 §5) Named, not defended. A one-off session that cannot be delivered is a booking moved; a monthly session that cannot be delivered is a promise to a paying client missed Item 5: a written position on what happens to a live monthly commitment if Hunter is unavailable. Not a succession plan; the client agreement needs something to point at
2 We cannot deliver to a participant yet. Clinical and safety matters have been open since 29 July 2026 We can price and quote; we cannot yet contract, and we cannot put a facilitator in front of a participant Not an ask in this paper: who carries out the clinical review is being resolved outside it
3 Nobody has ever bought anything from us. No named prospects, no objections heard Why months 0 to 3 are selling rather than building Nothing. Ours to fix
4 The monthly session has never been run. Every timing figure is an estimate Why it goes to you as an option rather than a priced product Item 3, as an option

Three things already reduce risk 1: commitments run three months at a time, we can say a slot is not available, and the monthly session is a fixed shape opened from a form, which makes it the right first thing for a second person to learn. What is missing is any second person, and any standard for choosing one.

7. The money
What we hold About $12,000 (Source: founder-reported cash position as at 2026-08-09, not independently verified against a bank account)
Income and costs No income, and no grant income is safe to count on (Source: FINAL-05 §8). Running costs are small: website, registration, insurance (Source: Hunter, 2026-08-16, not yet itemised)
No runway date appears here Fixed costs have never been itemised; we will not give a runway figure built on anything softer
How much time we have Unknown. Sixty delivery hours a month is an assumption [assumption]
How Hunter is paid From the end of this year, per session facilitated, at $66.10 an hour (Source: D-0096 §1) rather than a salary, so it comes out of work somebody has already bought
If it does not work Pause delivery and preserve cash, push corporate sales, or seek a bridge (Source: FINAL-05 §10). The review date we are asking you to set decides which

So we are not running out of money. We are waiting on a first customer, and the first paying work lands three to nine months out [assumption].

7.1 Our approach to grants

We are counting on services, not grants. Workshops and the three products are the plan; grants might be there and will help, but none appears in the money table above and we are not operating as if they keep us alive. The process: we hold a tracker of upcoming opportunities, and when one comes up, a working group (Rachel, Jake and Hunter) discusses whether we can genuinely tailor our approach to fit it. We only pursue an opportunity that is a real fit and genuinely beneficial, not every open window (Source: FINAL-05 §1-4). Donations become relevant once we have one measured, published cohort.

Who pays for the free work. Twenty free Introductions a year cost about $800 in cash and about 75 hours of Hunter's time [Source: derived], so what limits free work is the calendar, not the bank account.

8. What the committee is being asked for

# To agree Why, and what follows if it is not agreed
1 Adopt the three products at the prices in section 3 (Source: 110) Three genuinely different organisations, one price sheet, checked against published Australian prices (Source: R2). A view has been put that $5,000 should be our floor (Source: committee correspondence relayed by the founder, 2026-08-16); Foundations reaches $5,040 at twelve people [Source: derived], and a floor across everything would delete Essentials and the free Introduction, and with them the small business and the community group
2 Adopt the statement of what MFC is and is not in section 1 Every piece of our material is built on it, and it keeps us inside what a safety adviser or lawyer would accept
3 Add the optional monthly session, offered only after a delivery, three months minimum, as an option under development The only part of what we sell whose shape matches our claim that fitness is trained rather than taught
4 Approve our staged approach and expected success metrics at 3, 6, 9 and 12 months (section 5.3) The floor we can defend, not a target we are stretching for; it lets you track us against something concrete at each meeting
# To decide, because this is not ours to take Our position
5 What happens to a live monthly commitment if Hunter is unavailable We have no position. Even a minimal one is enough; the client agreement needs something to point at

How free and reduced-price delivery is funded is our plan, not something we are asking you to decide: grants and an honest cap. This corrects our own strategy document, whose $400 per-sale contribution (Source: FINAL-01 §2) would raise about $2,400 a year [Source: derived] and does not exist in our prices today (Source: 110). A third direction, not decided today: reducing price for things valuable to us now (research participation, full measurement, a testimonial), rather than a levy or a grant. A narrow version already exists in our founding case-study rate (Source: 110); nothing broader is costed, and would come back to you with numbers attached.

And our own review date, also not something we are asking you to decide: three months after our first quote goes out, at which point either a price has been accepted or we take one of the contingencies in section 7 deliberately rather than by drift. Nothing here needs the AGM, and we are not asking you for pricing detail, session design or build and channel order, which sit with the operating side.
