Final 13 Market Gap And Differentiator Sent 2026 08 17

The market, the gap, and what we are doing differently

Companion reading to the committee paper. Not required, and not a decision request. This is the short version of about eighteen months of market research, written so the reasoning behind our positioning is visible rather than assumed. Source markers are removed from this copy for readability; every figure is checkable, and the full citation trail is available on request.

How this document is built, in one pass. The market is real and already funded (scale, section 1). "The gap" is not one thing, it is two worth keeping separate: who can access these skills at all (section 1), and whether the sector even agrees what "mental fitness" means (section 1). What we do differently is one ordered procedure instead of a menu or a diagnosis step, argued against the named competitors (sections 2 to 3). The clearest opportunity is a validated way to measure whether a taught skill gets used, which no delivered Australian programme has adopted yet (section 5). Sections 4, 6 and 7 are the honesty layer: why the gap has stayed open, what we are and are not claiming, and what would prove us wrong.

1. The problem is not that people lack information

The scale, first. In the latest national survey, 21.5% of Australians, 4.3 million people, met criteria for a 12-month mental disorder (Source: ABS National Study of Mental Health and Wellbeing, reference period Dec 2020 to Oct 2022, released 2024). Australia already spends $14.5 billion a year on mental health services, $537 for every person in the country, not just those 4.3 million (Source: AIHW mental health expenditure, 2023-24 reference year), and that spending flows through the same clinically gated system this section is about to describe.

Australia does not have a mental-health awareness shortage. What it has is an access problem, and it is more specific than cost.

Every route we identified that an ordinary adult can take to learn structured psychological skills is gated, and it is gated one of three ways (Source: 30-cost-of-access-for-the-average-adult §Every route is gated):

The gate What it means in practice
A diagnosis The only nationally subsidised route, Better Access, requires a GP to assess a mental disorder. The skills come attached to a clinical eligibility condition
Money The ungated routes, private psychology, mindfulness-based courses, commercial coaching, are open to anyone who can pay, from $330 for a single private session up to $24,720 for a full annual coaching or mindfulness programme (Source: 30, verified against published provider prices, 2026)
Symptoms The genuinely free routes are open, but you enter them by reporting that something is wrong

No more than 4.7% of Australians saw a Medicare-subsidised psychologist in 2024-25 (Source: 30 §303, derived from published service counts against population). That is the scale of the subsidised route.

We searched for a fourth door and did not find one, including social media, checked separately. Specifically: an Australian, population-level, free, non-clinically-gated way for an adult to learn and practise these skills before anything is wrong. The obvious candidate for a fourth, informal door is social media, so we tested it on its own: the Australian charities genuinely active there (The Man Cave, R U OK?, #chatsafe) use the channel for awareness and check-in prompts, not for teaching a repeatable in-the-moment procedure; individual creators sometimes do teach a real technique for free, but that is one person's following, not a national or population-level channel a person would reliably encounter. Search terms and dates are recorded in the source file (Source: 30, searched 2026-08-06 and 2026-08-17) so the absence can be audited rather than taken on trust.

A second, more basic confusion sits underneath the access problem: the sector has not agreed what "mental fitness" is, or how it differs from mental health. Our own review of how the term is used in Australia, searched 2026-08-01 and not independently re-verified since, found six incompatible ways organisations frame it, as a capacity, a practice, a set of habits, a skill set, a performance outcome, or a score, and found that several of the highest-profile users of the term publish no definition of it at all on their programme pages (Source: 13-category-coherence). This gap is not one we are claiming to have closed by invention. An Australian, peer-reviewed, expert-consensus definition already exists, and our research found it largely uncited: Robinson, Oades and Caputi (2015, International Journal of Wellbeing), a 25-expert Delphi panel, defined mental fitness as "the modifiable capacity to utilise resources and skills to flexibly adapt to challenges... enabling thriving." Our own working definition, arrived at separately, sits close to the same sentence. We cite this as a striking parallel worth naming, not as external proof of our own definition. The panel's own sharpest line, also unadopted anywhere we found: mental fitness should describe the process, mental health the outcome, the distinction we hold to directly (Source: 13-category-coherence, Source: 00-foundations/K-05-short-distinction).

That is the gap this organisation exists to work in, on both counts. Not "mental health matters," which is settled, but: if these are life skills, why can only some people get them, and only by paying or by declaring a problem first, and why can the sector not even agree what the skill is called?

2. The landscape, stated accurately

It would be easy, and wrong, to say nobody else teaches anything usable in the moment.

Seven of nine comparators we assessed publish a named technique or framework (Source: 13-founder-voice-v2-category-and-competitors, cross-comparator pattern, revised four times under independent check).

Who What they actually have What they do not have
Smiling Mind A cued "STOP technique" for acute stress, a "Brain Break", and a five-skill mental fitness model structurally parallel to ours One ordered procedure taught as the thing you run every time
The Working Mind Four named coping strategies, including operationally specified breathing, plus a colour-coded continuum for recognising your own state A single ordered procedure to run once you have noticed. Their colour scale reads the state; it is not the routine that follows it
Gotcha4Life A named exercise library, a five-step cued exercise, and an emotion vocabulary that routes people to matching exercises A single repeated procedure rather than a menu to select from
Positive Intelligence A ten-second technique explicitly built for real-time use, and a body-based shift step A version without a diagnosis step, or one that is free

The four above are illustrative, not the full count. Of the remaining five: The Resilience Project and AIS Mental Fitness Program also publish a named framework or run a multi-session programme; Danny Frawley Centre publishes four named domains but its session-level content is genuinely not public, so it is counted as unknown rather than assumed either way; only Mental Fitness Australia and batyr, a certification business and a storytelling charity respectively, published no named in-the-moment technique at all (Source: 13-founder-voice-v2-category-and-competitors, full nine-way breakdown).

So the honest question is not whether anyone else works in the moment. They do, and we say so.

What we did not find anywhere is a single ordered procedure, cued to any moment, run identically every time, with nothing to diagnose first (Source: 13-founder-voice-v2-category-and-competitors).

The clearest illustration is Positive Intelligence, because it is the closest and the best funded. The count, stated so it can be checked, of what their own published material names: ten named "saboteurs" and five named "Sage" response modes, fifteen constructs in total across the two taxonomies (Source: 13-founder-voice-v2-category-and-competitors §Complexity). We are not claiming to know exactly how a PQ user moves through those fifteen constructs moment to moment, only that there are fifteen of them to learn, against our three identical steps, in the same order, every time, with no diagnosis step at all.

One distinction worth keeping straight, because it is easy to blur. Several of these organisations publish a way of recognising your state: a scale, a continuum, a vocabulary for what you are feeling. We have that too. What we are describing is the step after that: the routine you run once you have noticed. Recognising a state and having a procedure to follow are different things, and conflating them makes the field look more crowded than it is.

We are not claiming we invented the loop, and we will not. Parts of it already exist in established clinical models, and Positive Intelligence's own published material describes a structurally similar sequence. The difference is architecture, not novelty: one repeated procedure against a library or a curriculum. That distinction survives scrutiny. A novelty claim would not.

And it is worth naming who these organisations are. Positive Intelligence is a commercial enterprise selling into large employers, and so are several others in this space (Source: 13-founder-voice-v2-category-and-competitors). Of the charities, the strongest have moved toward children and young people: Smiling Mind has explicitly narrowed to children's mental fitness (Source: 31-deep-dive-closest-peers). We are not critical of that, and it is often where the funding is. But it leaves the ordinary working-age adult, who is not in crisis and not in a school, as a group not well served by any of the organisations we reviewed. That is the group we are built for.

3. What we actually teach, and why it is shaped this way

Three steps, in the same order, every time: Stop, Shift, Do. Notice the moment. Become workable, through the body or through your thinking. Then choose the next move.

It is taught on a structure people already carry. Stop is red, Shift is amber, Do is green (Source: 13-founder-voice-v2-explaining-mental-fitness). That is deliberate rather than decorative. The design assumption is that a person who is already under pressure will not retrieve a framework they have to think about, and that anything requiring recall, choice, or working-out is liable to fail at exactly the moment it is needed most. Borrowing a structure learned in childhood means there is nothing new to remember at the point of use. What the workshop then does is build the felt sense of each stage, so someone recognises where they are without having to analyse it.

The part we would most want understood: this is not a crisis tool. Most of what is offered in this space is entered through struggle, because without visible feedback struggle is the only reliable motivational hook (section 4). That shapes everything downstream: the language, the timing, the assumption that you come when something is wrong.

One distinction we want to be precise about, since we have just said this is not a crisis tool. Two separate claims, kept separate on purpose: first, MFC does not design, position, train for, or claim any effectiveness at crisis-level distress or self-harm risk. Second, and only about the mechanism, not its effectiveness: Stop-Shift-Do is not rebuilt as a different tool for harder moments, it is the same three-step structure throughout the everyday range this document is scoped to (the table below). We make no claim about how, or whether, it performs at severities beyond that range. It does not replace therapy, counselling, psychiatry, medication or crisis support, and where distress or risk is outside the scope of education, the right response is a referral or a crisis pathway, not this, and this document should not be read as saying otherwise.

What it looks like
In an everyday hard moment Catching yourself before the sentence you would regret; noticing an unhelpful spiral of thought and doing something other than continuing it
Proactively, in an ordinary one Stopping at the front door at the end of a hard day, shifting deliberately, and walking in actually present rather than still somewhere else
In a good moment Noticing something is going well and choosing to be in it, rather than letting it pass while you think about the next thing

That is the wider claim, and it is a claim about everyday scope rather than effectiveness at any severity. The same procedure applies in a difficult conversation, on a run, or walking through your own front door, because the underlying system, how you think, how you feel, how you act, how you connect, does not change between ordinary contexts. Only the moment does. That range is the everyday hard, ordinary, and good moments in the table above, not a claim about crisis-level distress.

Nowhere in our research did we find this taught as one ordered, universal, everyday procedure for adults (Source: 13-founder-voice-v2-category-and-competitors). Named techniques exist. State scales exist. Curricula exist. A single loop that a person runs in any moment of their own life, good or difficult, taught to people who have nothing wrong with them, is the thing we could not find.

The two gaps, and why we target the second one

Our own read of the field, stated as a position rather than something we have measured: there are two distinct gaps here, and the sector is closing one of them while leaving the other alone.

The first is literacy. Knowing what regulation is, being able to name a difficult moment, having the concept of shifting your state. A great deal of what is on offer, apps, curricula, awareness campaigns, does real work here, and we think it is genuinely improving.

The second is retrieval under pressure. Knowing what to do is not the same as being able to do it when friction is actually rising. This is precisely the enactment gap in section 5: a validated way to measure it exists, and no delivered Australian programme uses it. If the only data a programme collects is a wellbeing score or a stress-reduction score, it will never show what building this skill proactively actually looks like, because those instruments were built to measure symptoms, not use.

We are aiming squarely at the second gap, on the honest expectation that this makes us harder to fund in the near term. Government and philanthropic money in this sector still flows overwhelmingly to treatment rather than capacity-building (section 4). Positioning proactively, before anything is wrong, sits against that current rather than with it. We think that is where the field needs to go, not where the money currently is, and we are naming that as a real cost of this approach rather than pretending it is not there.

4. Why the gap has stayed open

The obvious explanation is professional gatekeeping, and we checked it. It does not hold. Teaching skills derived from clinical models by non-clinicians is increasingly normal across schools, workplaces and coaching (Source: 13-founder-voice-v2-why-the-gap-stayed-open). Ruling it out makes the four remaining explanations stronger.

The force Why it keeps the gap open
The money cannot flow there Mental health receives roughly 2% of government health budgets globally (Source: 13-...-why-the-gap-stayed-open, a global figure used here as a proxy for the pattern rather than an Australia-specific number); within it, prevention and promotion is a few cents per treatment dollar. Capacity-building did not lose an argument. There is barely a funding channel pointed at it
Mental fitness has no mirror Physical fitness supplies its own feedback: visible change, measurable load. Mental fitness supplies none. The sector defaults to entry through struggle because, without visible feedback, struggle is the only motivational hook reliably strong enough. That is not carelessness; it is the only lever available
The moment is occupied by researchers, not teachers There is an active research frontier intervening at the right moment: just-in-time adaptive interventions, ecological momentary interventions. The science agrees with our premise. But every version requires instrumentation, a device, monitoring, calibration, because that is what is fundable and publishable. The taught, human, device-free version is empty
What works is the least investable shape available The transfer evidence (Source: 13-...-why-the-gap-stayed-open): 62% of trained content applied immediately, 44% at six months, 34% at one year. The strongest predictor a designer controls is the environment after the training, not the quality of the content. The fix is a recurring human environment, which is the least scalable and least investable thing that could be built

We also asked what the clinical literature itself says, not only what the funding pattern suggests. We commissioned our own rapid, PRISMA-guided review of peer-reviewed systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomised controlled trials for interventions conceptually aligned with mental fitness: cognitive-behavioural, mindfulness-based, acceptance-based, compassion-focused, and positive-psychology approaches. This is an internal MFC review, not an independently published one, conducted by two researchers working with MFC (Source: Fidler & Prout, MFC rapid systematic review, searched via EBSCO/PsycINFO/CINAHL/Scopus/Medline, 31 July 2025). From 1,746 records, 10 studies met the inclusion criteria, with effects generally small to moderate (g ≈ 0.20 to 0.50) on distress and wellbeing, and digital delivery showing smaller effects than face to face. The finding that matters here is the conclusion, not the effect sizes: across those 10 studies, these approaches were delivered in fragmented, inconsistently conceptualised ways, with no attempt among them to integrate into one coherent, skills-based system. That is a related, evidence-side version of the same gap described above, not an identical claim: the table explains why nobody built the thing; this is whether the evidence has even been organised into something buildable.

We also looked for the graveyard, not just the gap

An empty space can mean nobody entered. It can equally mean people entered, failed, and stopped publishing, which leaves the same empty-looking space and a very different strategic conclusion. Failed organisations do not maintain websites. So we searched deliberately for what had already died rather than only for what was missing (Source: 51-the-graveyard-what-has-already-failed).

That search is the reason we are cautious rather than triumphant, and three findings matter:

  • A large, directly relevant 2024 study is cross-sectional. It cannot establish that the training caused the outcome, in either direction. We had been treating it as stronger than it is.
  • A major school-based mindfulness trial returned a null result on its primary outcome. Its own authors reported the adverse indicators as small and not clinically relevant, with no intervention-related adverse events. We state it that way rather than the more dramatic version.
  • Mental Health First Aid is the closest surviving analogue, and it demonstrates both that a taught procedure can reach national scale and where the ceiling of that model sits.

The honest conclusion: the individual-content model is not demonstrably working, and the transfer evidence points at the practice environment as the thing that matters. We do not claim more than that. Specifically, we do not claim that content without an environment fails, because no source we found supports that, and it would be the kind of overstatement this document exists to avoid.

5. The measurement gap, which is the actual opportunity

This is the strongest finding in our research, and it is the one we would want a committee member to take away.

A validated, Australian-developed way to measure how often a person actually used a taught skill in daily life already exists. The ANU Centre for Mental Health Research has published a skill-enactment line: a thirteen-item scale, alpha 0.84, asking how often someone did the thing, not whether they completed a module. A second validated instrument, the Frequency of Actions and Thoughts Scale, does something similar (Source: 24-crisis-data-and-application-gap §2.2, both primary sources cited there).

The two largest published Australian wellbeing evaluations we found do not use it. The Resilience Project's evaluation covers 40,149 students; Smiling Mind's covers 733 schools. Both report symptom and wellbeing scales. Neither reports whether a taught skill was used (Source: 24 §2.2).

The gap is not that the measure is unavailable. It is that no delivered Australian programme has adopted it.

That claim is deliberately narrow, and it is auditable: the search terms and the date are published in the source file (Source: 24, searched 2026-08-06). We state it that way rather than the broader "nobody measures this," which we could not defend.

Why this matters more than any feature comparison. The question it puts to the sector is uncomfortable and fair: if the largest published evaluations in this country do not report whether people used what they were taught, on what basis is behaviour change being claimed? We would rather be the organisation that measures it and publishes an unflattering answer than one that asserts an outcome it never looked for.

And adopting it is not research and development. It is a procurement decision. On current evidence, doing so would make MFC the first delivered Australian programme to report whether the skills it teaches actually get used (Source: 24 §2.2).

The honest caveat, stated here rather than discovered later. Being early to measure something means the first numbers will be small, imperfect and quite possibly disappointing. We have run zero cohorts. We expect our own early data to be modest, and we would publish it anyway. That is the trade, and we think it is the right one for a charity rather than a vendor.

6. What we are doing, and what we are not claiming

The workshop is the entry point. It is not the product. Our own research is blunt about this: the architecture with the weakest evidence is exactly the one-off session, and the workplace resilience evidence shows the effect fading once contact ends (Source: 38-adherence-and-behaviour-change-likelihood). The product is the practice layer that follows: the return contact, the leader involvement, the Radar, the measurement. Part of that is built and part of it is not, and we would rather say so.

Why now, with the complication included. Workplace psychosocial regulation in Australia has already tightened, not just started to. In NSW, approved codes of practice became legally binding on 1 July 2026: comply, or demonstrate an equivalent-or-higher standard. Victoria's psychological health regulations have been in operation since 1 December 2025. Both are now in force, not pending (Source: 25-whs-psychosocial-and-mfc-fit §1.7, re-verified against live legal-sector reporting 2026-08-17, both current).

But this cuts both ways and we will not present only the flattering half. The Victorian regulations make training-only unlawful as an employer's predominant control where changing the work itself is reasonably practicable, and the NSW code names reliance on mainly administrative controls as a failure (Source: 25 §239). So the regulatory window is real, and what it rewards is training positioned as reinforcing an employer's other controls, never as a substitute for them. That is exactly the boundary we have already adopted in the committee paper.

On the design, stated as reasoning rather than proof. Three steps rather than fifteen is a deliberate choice about what a person can retrieve when they are already under load. We do not have evidence that a three-step routine is retrievable where a more complex system is not. Nobody has run that comparison, including us. It is a design rationale, and it is falsifiable, which is why we are comfortable stating it plainly rather than dressing it up.

On whether people will keep practising, an honest estimate rather than a measurement. We have run zero cohorts, so this is not our own data. It is what the comparable adherence and transfer literature implies for a design like ours (Source: 38 §1.5), if we change nothing: 10 to 25% of workshop participants still doing deliberate practice at three months, and 2 to 10% at twelve months, lower again for mandated corporate cohorts. We publish that estimate because being asked for it is much worse than offering it, and because no programme we assessed publishes a comparable figure at all.

On scale, the arithmetic we cannot avoid. At around twenty workshops a year, one facilitator does not reach population scale in any meaningful timeframe (Source: 43-theory-of-change-and-the-missing-middle §1.5). Other people delivering it solves this, but train-the-trainer formats rate poorly in some of the transfer evidence, an unresolved tension (Source: 43 §2.3). The cheap next step is certifying a small number of facilitators as a measured experiment, not a rollout.

On being copied. Not a moat, by design: the method should spread, and another organisation teaching it well is the mission working, not a loss. What we would hold is the measurement, whether taught skills actually get used, which is the part no delivered Australian programme currently has (Source: 39-licensed-diffusion-and-the-mhfa-model, Source: 43 §1.6).

7. What would tell us we are wrong

A positioning document that cannot be falsified is marketing. These are the things that would tell us this analysis is wrong, written down now so they can be checked against later rather than quietly forgotten.

If this happened What it would mean
A well-resourced organisation names an ordered loop and attaches a cue to it within twelve months The architecture difference in section 2 stops being a position. Our own research names this as the falsification test, and we have no defence prepared if it happens (Source: 36-the-opportunity-and-what-has-to-happen)
Our own day-21 and three-month numbers come back at the bottom of the range, or null The practice layer is not doing what we think it does. We publish it and rework the design rather than reframing the measure
A delivered Australian programme adopts an enactment measure before we do Our clearest differentiator was a procurement decision anyone could have made, and someone made it first
Buyers consistently want the one-off session and refuse the return contact The market is telling us the entry point is the product after all, and our model does not survive contact with what people will actually buy
Certified facilitators deliver measurably worse outcomes than the founder The scale path in section 6 does not work, and the honest position becomes that this stays small

We would rather write these down than be asked for them. We will revisit this table honestly once we have our first delivered cohort's day-21 and three-month numbers, not wait to be asked.

In one paragraph. These are life skills, and only some people can reach them, because every existing door we found requires a diagnosis, a payment, or a problem. The gap has stayed open because every funding and research incentive in the sector points away from the un-instrumented, human, taught version of it. A validated way to measure whether people actually use what they learned exists, and no delivered Australian programme has adopted it. We intend to be the first, we expect the early numbers to be modest, and we would publish them either way.

Every figure in this document carries its source. The full research corpus, including the checks that corrected several of our own earlier claims, is available on request.

Subject: MFC — our thinking ahead of the committee send

Hi Onno, Hi Jake,

Thanks for Friday. Two things attached, both written to be argued with rather than approved.

1. Our thinking for the committee send. Not the paper itself — the reasoning behind it. What we've decided since the 20 July session, why, and where the thinking is weakest. It's structured against the committee's own seven gaps, because they didn't challenge the strategy, they challenged whether we'd done the work underneath it.

2. The pricing. A half-day Foundations session at $2,500 base plus $95 per participant, capped at 20 — $4,400 for a full room, which sits in the upper half of the committee's own $3,000–$5,000 steer. The document shows the full cost buildup behind it. The short version: MFC isn't selling a workshop, it's selling a workshop plus a measured answer to "did this change anything?" — and that second part is about a third of the work per engagement. Once it's properly costed, the number follows.

Two things in there I'd particularly like you to push on.

The grant finding is blunter than the committee will expect. Across eleven Australian and NSW policy areas, we found no currently open, competitive, adult/young-adult non-clinical-appropriate government funding door for MFC at our current scale. There's abundant policy language and very little accessible money. That's the real argument for the service model — but it lands partly on Rachel's workstream, and I'd rather you told me now if it's too blunt for the room.

I've named the "everything routes through Hunter" gap as unresolved rather than papered over. The fortnightly cadence and working groups help at the margin. They don't fix it. I think naming it is right, but I can see the argument that it undercuts confidence at the wrong moment.

Onno — the flexibility you asked for is in: a lower community rate, in-kind discounts for case-study and media consent, and pro bono framed as short-term investment for long-term gain rather than a default.

The two documents themselves — the consolidated paper and the sales strategy, about 14 pages together — I'll write once you've had a look at the reasoning. Happy to cut that down if 14 is still too long for what the committee asked for. No rush this week given the EOI and Wednesday's holiday; whenever you get to it, I'll turn it around within a couple of days.

The short piece on the industry, the gap and the opportunity is coming separately.

Thanks both, Hunter

Annex 2026 08 31 Product Comparison And Buyer Realism

Annex: what each one covers, and would anyone actually buy it

Not read aloud. This is what Hunter reaches for when someone asks "what's the difference" or "is that realistic".

1. The one-line answer to "what's the difference"

It is not minutes. It is what becomes possible.

  • Introduction is a room meeting the idea. Nothing follows it.
  • Essentials teaches the routine and comes back once, remotely, to practise it. Each person leaves with their own plan.
  • Foundations teaches it in depth, then comes back on site, and is the only one that can turn individual practice into something the team agrees and the leaders commit to, with dates.

The paper's own words: a ladder of depth, not a ladder of length. The extra money buys depth and adoption support, not more minutes.

2. What each one covers, and what it produces

Introduction Essentials Foundations
Time from the organisation 1 hour, once 2 hours across 3 weeks 4 hours 50 across 3 weeks
What is taught What mental fitness is; Stop, Shift, Do; the four shift routes; one guided rehearsal on a scenario given to the room The same, plus the three common misreads, the State Check, and one rehearsal on the person's own real moment All of that, plus teach it back in your own words, a breakpoint diagnosis of where your loop actually fails, troubleshooting a moment where the first move doesn't work, and two unaided recall tests rather than one
Rehearsals 1, on a scenario 2 scenarios plus 1 own moment 3 scenarios plus own moments, with variation and a second pass
Participant leaves with The Reference Card Card, plus a written if-then plan and three moments they chose to practise Card, plus three moments and a next move for each
The organisation receives Nothing. It is reach, not a programme A short written report: what was run, the themes, what to do next A written findings report interpreting that cohort's own measurement, delivered within ten working days, plus a conversation about it once they have read it
Measurement None Before, after, and at three weeks Before, in session, and at three weeks
The outcome we are aiming at They can name what this is, and one thing to try They can run the routine on their own real situation and have written down when they will use it The team has agreed two shared moments, placed them in a routine that already exists, and the leaders have said out loud what they will make true, and by when

3. The two return sessions

Why we come back at all. A skill you learn once and never revisit decays. The return is not a second lesson and not a drill. It is a check-in.

The first fifteen minutes are the same for both products.

  1. Here is what you did. We show the room its own picture from the first session and the weeks since: what came up, what people caught at the time, what people tried. Aggregate, no names. This is the moment people see that it worked for somebody in the room.
  2. The thing you asked about. At the end of session one, or by a short form a week before, everyone is asked one question: what is one more thing you would like to learn, or one thing you are finding hard. Whatever comes up most, we cover. They tell us, and we bring it. That form comes to us, never to their manager.

Then the two diverge.

Essentials Foundations
Length Up to an hour, online 75 minutes, on site
The rest of the session More understanding of what they asked about, then reps on it The same, then the collective piece
The collective piece Not included The room agrees two moments it will work on together, and places each one in a meeting or routine that already happens, with a named starter and a review date
Leaders Not present Join for the last twenty minutes and each answers one question out loud: which one of these can you make true, and by when
The team leaves with Individuals better at the thing they asked about That, plus two agreed moves and the leaders' commitments with dates

Why Essentials stops short of the collective piece. It is online, and the leaders are not in the room at the end. The commitment is the whole point of the collective piece, and there is nobody there to make it. Foundations is on site and sequences the leaders in deliberately, which is what turns two agreed moves into something with a name and a date against it.

One rule protects this, and it is not a headcount. If something is really about workload, safety, staffing or how one person behaves, it is not a shared moment. We say so in the room and put it in the what-has-to-be-true-around-us column as a category, with no names. That is what stops a team sheet becoming a complaint about the manager who is about to walk back in.

This design replaced a more complicated one on 30 August (D-0114), which sorted participants into three categories from a survey and picked modules against percentage rules. It was heavy to deliver and it treated a friendly question as though it were a risky one.

4. The 90 minutes versus the half day

The half day is not the 90 minutes stretched. It contains six things the 90 minutes does not have at all:

  1. Teach it back. Each person explains the routine in their own words on a neutral example and is corrected. Nothing predicts retention like having to produce it.
  2. A breakpoint diagnosis. Where does your loop actually break, without any of it being a score against a person.
  3. Troubleshooting. A moment where the obvious first move does not work, revealed halfway through, then alternatives.
  4. A second unaided recall test, twenty minutes from the end, from a single opening line and nothing else.
  5. A third rehearsal variation, so the routine is practised across different kinds of pressure rather than one.
  6. Two proper breaks, which is the difference between a workshop people can absorb and one they endure.

Essentials keeps the spine: the routine, the misreads, the recall drill, the State Check, the four routes, one rehearsal on their own moment, and the written plan. What it gives up is depth, variation and diagnosis.

5. Would an organisation actually say yes

Where the prices sit against what is already sold in Australia. Every comparator below is drawn from the Product and Pricing Book's market table (Source: 110-PRODUCT-AND-PRICING-BOOK.md, market-position section). MFC's own prices are founder decisions of 2026-08-16 (Source: D-0103).

Price Per person Source
MFC Foundations, 10 people $4,850 $485 Founder decision 2026-08-16 (D-0103)
MFC Foundations, 15 people $5,325 $355 Founder decision 2026-08-16 (D-0103)
MFC Essentials, 10 people $1,550 $155 Founder decision 2026-08-16 (D-0103)
Mental Health First Aid, in-house, 10 to 20 $3,500 to $7,500, two full days Source: Better Being and Wellbeing Campus, two secondary sources. Not MHFA's own rate card. Treat as an estimate
Mental Health First Aid, public seat $385 to $399 Source: Wellbeing Campus, secondary. $399 inc GST; corporate from about $350 + GST
A one-day psychosocial hazards course $715 Source: cciwa.com, vendor published. Non-member ex GST; $595 member
A comparable wellbeing workshop $1,199 to $1,399 Source: thewellnessworkshop.com.au, vendor published, incl. travel and materials

Sources, and how solid each one is. Mental Health First Aid in-house, $3,500 to $7,500 for a class of 10 to 20 (Source: Better Being and Wellbeing Campus, two independent secondary sources; neither is MHFA Australia's own rate card, so treat this as a secondary-sourced estimate, not a quoted price). MHFA public seat $399 including GST, with corporate packages from around $350 a head plus GST (Source: Wellbeing Campus, also secondary). The one-day psychosocial hazards course at $715 is CCIWA's published non-member rate excluding GST, $595 for members (Source: cciwa.com, vendor published). The $1,199 to $1,399 wellbeing workshop is The Wellness Workshop's own published page, inclusive of travel, setup and materials (Source: thewellnessworkshop.com.au, vendor published).

Foundations sits inside the band that market already pays, and below the per-seat price of the best-known comparator. Essentials sits below the cheapest comparable workshop. Neither is expensive for what the market already buys.

The real barrier is not the fee. It is the release time. Foundations asks for four hours fifty per person across three weeks, on three dates fixed at contracting. At fifteen people that is seventy-two and a half hours off the floor, worth roughly three to four thousand dollars of salary (working assumption: $45 to $60 an hour fully loaded. MFC holds no salary data for any buyer, so this is an illustrative rate, not a measured one). On that assumption the buyer's true cost is closer to nine thousand than five.

But that is exactly where we win the comparison. Two days of Mental Health First Aid for the same fifteen people is about two hundred and ten hours off the floor, worth roughly ten thousand five hundred at the same illustrative rate (derived, same working assumption; the two-day duration comes from the comparator sources above), on top of a fee in the same band. We ask for about a third of the time, for a fee in the same range. If anyone says Foundations is a lot to ask, that is the answer.

Who says yes. An organisation of fifty to two hundred and fifty staff with a training budget and someone accountable for psychosocial risk, releasing six to twenty people. Who says no, and we should expect it: anyone who cannot release people three times in three weeks, and anyone who needs the training to satisfy a legal duty, which we tell them plainly it does not.

And the objection that will actually stop the first sale is not price. It is that we have never run a cohort, have no case study, no measured result and one facilitator. That is why the first deliveries are priced as founding case studies, and it is the reason the plan is built around getting three organisations to yes rather than around a marketing budget.

6. Two things to be careful about if this comes up

First, we currently hold two definitions of our own products and they disagree. The internal definition written on 29 August describes each product as its teaching session alone, with the return, the report and the manager session listed as outside the core. Everything in this annex, and everything the committee holds, describes them as inside. Hunter's decision of 30 August (D-0113) settles it commercially: they are inside the price. The 29 August packs still need aligning, and until they are, an internal reader could quote either.

Second, the committee's copy of the paper carries a superseded line about reporting. It says the Essentials report gives themes rather than participant data because the group is under twenty. That headcount gate was withdrawn on 19 August. The correct position is that we report themes and never participant data at every group size, as a privacy rule rather than a size rule.

And the standing caveat. Nothing here has been run. The returns have never been rehearsed, no cohort has been delivered, and the design choices in the return session are marked in our own records as reasoned judgement, not evidence.

Original source: 60-projects/committee-pack-v1/ANNEX-2026-08-31-product-comparison-and-buyer-realism.md

B1 Outcome Chain

B1 — The outcome chain

What this document is. For each format, an unbroken chain: what a participant can do afterwards → what must be taught to produce that → what happens in the room to produce it, with a time → which measurement item detects it → what it does and does not license MFC to say.

Why it exists. The session content, the format difference and the measurement items were each designed separately. The 90-minute session is currently a compressed 3-hour session rather than a session designed to a bar of its own; the forms measure what seemed sensible rather than what the room is built to produce. This is the spine the session plan and the forms both attach to.

What is locked and what is open. K-07 is locked — five public skills, Stop–Shift–Do, State Check, the Radar, the Mental Rep, the staged arc, seven deep skills beneath. Nothing here changes any of it. What is open, and what this document exercises, is which of those the room actually has time to produce a behaviour from, which is a product decision, not a framework one.

The single design constraint everything else follows from. The primary outcome measure is opportunity-conditional: F-01 (how many times did your chosen moment come up) → F-02 (in how many did you run the steps) → F-03 (in how many did you finish). That ratio only works if the participant leaves with one recurring moment, named specifically enough to be counted, and frequent enough to come up inside a seven-day window. Every outcome below is written so that measure can detect it. Anything in the existing build that does not serve it has to justify itself on its own.

Format 1 — Essentials, 90 minutes

Talk-led with real practice in the room. Teams of 1–15. Also used for schools, public talks and keynotes. The bar: one moment, one full pass, one tool, counted.

E1 — Names one recurring moment from their own week, specific enough to count

Field Content
Outcome Writes down one moment that recurs in their own week, stated as a situation with a trigger and a place ("when my daughter asks for the iPad at dinner", not "stress"), and states out loud to a neighbour or the facilitator that it comes up at least twice a week.
Why it matters This is the denominator. Without a specific, recurring, countable moment there is no F-01, no ratio, and no way to tell "didn't practise" from "had no opportunity" — the exact failure the instrument was rebuilt to avoid. It is also the participant's cue, so it carries the whole transfer path (D-0008).
What must be taught The Radar prompt, verbatim ("Think about the person you are trying to become in this season of life"); one worked example of a vague moment being narrowed to a countable one; the two named stuck points ("my moment is too big", "I can't think of one") with a scripted way through each. Not the two ownership layers, not the two strands, not three moments.
The activity 10 min. 3 min facilitator narrows one vague moment to a countable one, live, on the board. 4 min private silent write on the moment slip. 3 min countability test, done in pairs and out loud, on the format only, never the content: "Does it have a place and a trigger? Would it come up twice in a week?" Nobody reads their moment out; the pair tests the shape by asking two questions and hearing yes or no.
Evidence it worked P-08 (post, existing) — "Write the one recurring moment you have chosen to work on." Scored for form only: does it name a situation, not a feeling. P-10 (NEW, post) — "How often does that moment come up in a typical week?" (a number). Without P-10, an F-01 of zero at three weeks is uninterpretable, and a participant who chose an annual event is invisible until it is too late to fix.
Claim boundary Licenses: "participants leave having chosen and written one specific recurring moment." Does not license: that they have a Radar, a practice, or a habit. One written moment is a starting condition, not a behaviour change.

E2 — Explains, without MFC vocabulary, why knowing what helps does not produce doing it

Field Content
Outcome Says in one or two sentences, to another person in the room, why someone who knows what would help still does the other thing — using none of MFC's words. If they need MFC's words, they learned the framework, not the idea.
Why it matters This is the beat whose absence Hunter identified in the existing build ("cycling through the framework"). It is also the only outcome that makes the definition land as an answer rather than an assertion, and it earns Stop later. Everything downstream is a solution to a problem the room has to actually hold first.
What must be taught A plain, causal account of ordinary experience: under load, attention narrows and the practised response arrives before the considered one; the old route is faster because it has been used more. Delivered as description a participant recognises from their own life, never as science — no brain diagrams, no amygdala, no fight-or-flight. K-08's ladder puts mechanism claims at Level 3, pending.
The activity 7 min. 4 min facilitator account, built on one of the moments already named in Recognition. 3 min explain-back: "Turn to one person. Say it back in your own words — you're not allowed to use anything I just called it." Facilitator listens to two or three, corrects nothing except a science claim.
Evidence it worked B-06 (existing, all three timepoints) — the scenario item: someone intends to pause and listen, but interrupts before realising; which explanation best fits. This item already exists in the forms draft and already measures exactly this.
Claim boundary Licenses: "participants can account for the gap between knowing and doing in their own words." Does not license any claim about mechanism, brain change, or that understanding the gap closes it. Understanding is not doing — that is the content of the outcome itself.

Authority flag. This outcome corresponds to K6 in 10-product-finalisation-v1/02-design-rationale-and-outcomes-checklist.md, which is marked "Proposed — requires Hunter's approval under D-0018" and was never approved. No decision record adopts it. The forms draft's B-06 already measures it — the instrument is ahead of the approved content. This chain assumes K6 is approved; if it is not, E2 falls and B-06 measures nothing the session teaches. See founder question 2.

E3 — Says what each of the three steps means, unprompted, without the colours

Field Content
Outcome Given "Stop, Shift, Do" and nothing else, states what each one is: catch the moment; create enough space where useful and available; make the next move with intention. Answering "red, amber, green" is a fail — that is the mnemonic retrieved, not the mechanism.
Why it matters Retrieval under load is the entire design intent. A step someone can recognise on a slide but not produce in a car park is not available in a real moment.
What must be taught K-07's locked Stop–Shift–Do wording. The traffic light named exactly once, as contrast (D-0054), then the three corrections at the point of teaching: red is catching the moment, not freezing in it; amber is making space, which is not always calming down; green is the next move with intention, not the right answer. Stop taught as the pivot — what changes when attention arrives — not as step one of three.
The activity 8 min teach (0:26–0:34) plus 8 min drill (0:40–0:48). Call-and-response, choral by default, never cold-called. Two sets, alternating, finishing on Set B: Set A the mapping, Set B the corrections drilled as standing items ("Is amber calming down?" → "No — making space."). Explanatory feedback mandatory, never correctness-only (D-0004).
Evidence it worked P-02 (post, existing) — scenario: which response shows the three steps in order. F-04 (3 weeks, existing) — did you remember the three steps during a real moment: while it was happening / afterwards / no / no relevant moment.
Claim boundary Licenses: "participants could state the three steps and what each means, and X% reported recalling them during a real moment at three weeks." Does not license that they used them well, or that recall predicts use.

E4 — Reads their own state as too much / too little / workable, for a specific moment

Field Content
Outcome Asked in the room, silently, answers for themselves; and can say why "workable" is not "calm" — that it is about what choice is available, not how pleasant it feels.
Why it matters It is the only sanctioned self-assessment language MFC has, and it is the precondition for Shift meaning anything. It is also K-08 rule 9's protection, delivered in the room rather than in a footnote.
What must be taught The three words with the anchor phrase "for this moment" used every time; the distinct-construct lock (State Check is not a fourth step); and the access idea underneath — state changes what is available to you, not only how you feel.
The activity 6 min. 4 min teach. 2 min live State Check on themselves, now: "Don't answer out loud. Right now, in this room — too much, too little, or workable for this moment?" Ten counted seconds of silence. Then: "That was a Stop." Never shared, never collected, never scored (K-08 rule 7).
Evidence it worked P-03 (post, existing) — what does a "workable" state mean. The single most misread idea MFC teaches.
Claim boundary Licenses: "participants can use MFC's state language on a real moment of their own and distinguish workable from calm." Does not license any claim about emotion regulation, physiological change, or that the check improves state.

E5 — Names one shift move in their own words that they would actually reach for

Field Content
Outcome Writes a concrete move, in their own words, that they would use in the moment they chose at E1 — "stand up and walk to the kitchen before I answer", not "Move it" and not "breathing".
Why it matters It is the difference between recognising a list and holding a tool. A category name written back is recognition; a concrete self-worded move is the only thing an in-room activity can actually produce.
What must be taught The Shift menu as a menu to pick from, not a taxonomy to learn — Move it / Zoom in or out / Ask a different question / Bring someone in, with two worked examples each. The claims boundary stated aloud: breath is one option, not the required strategy (D-0083); Move it is never taught as a breathing exercise.
The activity 6 min. 2 min menu named with examples. 2 min private write: one move, for the moment you just chose. 2 min pair exchange on "which of these do you already reach for?" — existing behaviour, not a commitment.
Evidence it worked P-05 (post, existing) — "Name one thing you could do in a moment to give yourself a bit more space" (free text, one line). F-07 (3 weeks, existing) — did you use anything to give yourself space; what was it. Naming something MFC never taught is a success at F-07, not a failure, and drift from P-05 to F-07 is ownership, not attrition.
Claim boundary Licenses: "participants left with a self-worded, retrievable move, and X% reported using something at three weeks." Does not license that any tool works, that one category beats another, or that MFC's tools were the ones used.

E6 — States what counts as a rep, including one that went badly

Field Content
Outcome Says that a rep counts when the moment was caught with intention, whatever the outcome — and gives an example of a rep that did not go well and still counted.
Why it matters Outcome-independence is the most load-bearing idea for whether anyone practises after the session. If a rep only counts when it works, most people stop. It is also what makes F-02 answerable honestly: "even partly, even badly" only works if the room has already been told that partly and badly count. This outcome is what protects the primary measure from under-reporting.
What must be taught K-07's locked definition, verbatim in written materials. The counting rule: any completed pass counts, before / during / after the moment; Shift is not required if the State Check reads workable. What does not count: a moment by itself, autopilot, reading about it. Plus the normalising beat — hands up if you've ever caught yourself scrolling and put the phone down.
The activity 6 min. 3 min definition and normalising beat. 3 min: "Think of a time this week you caught something and it still went badly. That was a rep." One or two volunteered aloud, never solicited by name.
Evidence it worked P-04 (post, existing) — which example best represents a rep. Separates intentional practice from information or accidental calm.
Claim boundary Licenses: "participants can distinguish a rep from information or an accident." Does not license any claim about practice volume, and MFC does not count reps as a performance measure.

E7 — Runs one complete pass of the three steps on their own chosen moment, in the room

Field Content
Outcome Rehearses the moment they wrote at E1: names what the Stop would look like, does the State Check, picks the shift move from E5, and states the next move out loud — all three steps, on their own material, before they leave.
Why it matters This is the only place in a 90-minute session where the participant does the thing rather than hearing about it, and it is the in-room analogue of F-02/F-03. A participant who has never completed one pass on their own moment has no basis to expect themselves to complete one in a car park. It also makes the follow-up wording honest: "even partly, even badly" refers to something they have already experienced.
What must be taught Nothing new. This beat teaches no content — it applies E1, E3, E4, E5 and E6 in sequence. That is why it can exist in 90 minutes.
The activity 8 min. 2 min facilitator models a full pass aloud on the board moment. 4 min private, silent, written: four lines — the moment / what Stop looks like here / my state read / my next move. 2 min: "Hands up if you got all the way through. Hands up if you got partway." Both hands-up are named as normal, in that order.
Evidence it worked P-09 (NEW, post) — "Today, did you run all three steps on a moment of your own? (all the way through / partly / no)". Deliberately uses F-02/F-03's exact language so the in-room pass and the three-week passes are on one scale. This is currently the largest measurement hole in the build: the session's central activity has no item.
Claim boundary Licenses: "X% of participants completed a full pass on a moment of their own before leaving the room." Does not license competence, habit, or transfer. One rehearsed pass in a supported room is not one pass in a real moment, and the two must never be reported in the same number.

Essentials — minute-by-minute, 90 minutes

Clock Min Beat Serves
0:00–0:04 4 Welcome, non-clinical scope, D-0015 six controls, D-0016 disclosure + placeholder Enabling (non-negotiable)
0:04–0:08 4 Protected form time — token cards issued, Form 1 catch-up for anyone who did not complete it ahead Measurement
0:08–0:14 6 Recognition — four ordinary moments named by the facilitator; the gap named Sets up E2
0:14–0:21 7 Why the gap exists + explain-back E2
0:21–0:26 5 What mental fitness is — definition, distinction, context-neutral framing as a named sentence (D-0005) B-03/B-04
0:26–0:34 8 Stop–Shift–Do, Stop as the pivot, the three colour corrections (D-0054) E3
0:34–0:40 6 State Check + live State Check on themselves E4
0:40–0:48 8 Retrieval drill, Sets A and B, finishing on B (D-0004) E3
0:48–0:54 6 Shift menu — four named, one written in their own words E5
0:54–1:00 6 What counts as a rep, including one that went badly E6
1:00–1:10 10 The moment — narrow, write, countability test E1
1:10–1:18 8 The full pass, on their own moment E7
1:18–1:20 2 Cue attached to something already in the week; lapse-and-return line Transfer
1:20–1:22 2 Close — threshold framing, not outcome framing —
1:22–1:30 8 Protected form time — Form 2, in the room, before anyone leaves Measurement
90 Total. Protected measurement time: 12 minutes (13.3%)

Honest note on the form budget. The forms draft allows ≈5 min for Form 1 in-session and ≈8 min for Form 2. That does not fit 90 minutes without losing an outcome. The resolution here: Form 1 is genuinely sent seven days ahead and the in-room window is a 4-minute catch-up, not a completion slot. If Form 1 cannot be sent ahead — likely for very small businesses with no email list — the session runs at 94 minutes or drops the Recognition beat. That is a booking-time decision, and the facilitator must know which version they are running before they arrive.

Format 2 — Foundations, half day (~180 min content plus a break)

Full practice, plus helping the organisation embed it. Foundations carries every Essentials outcome unchanged. What follows is only what the extra time buys.

The rule this section is held to

An outcome belongs in Foundations only if it cannot be produced in 90 minutes — because it needs a partner, a second person's material, a felt contrast, or a conversation the room has to prepare. "More content" is not a reason. Three outcomes clear that bar. Nothing else does.

F1 — Runs the three steps on another person's moment, out loud, and gets through it

Field Content
Outcome In a pair, takes both roles: as the supporter, asks the three questions ("What's going on for you right now?" / offers rather than directs a shift / "What's one next step that could help?"); as the person in the moment, is taken through their own. Then names one thing that was harder about doing it with someone than alone.
Why it matters Nearly every moment worth practising has another person in it. Running the sequence alone and running it with someone are different skills, and the second is the one that changes what a team feels like. It is also the only outcome that produces observable behaviour another person could report.
Why it cannot be done in 90 minutes It needs two turns plus a debrief — a one-turn version teaches half of it and leaves the other half rehearsed by nobody — and it needs the room to already be safe, which takes the earlier self-elicitation beat that Essentials cuts. 21 minutes minimum. There is no 8-minute version of this.
What must be taught K-07's "supporting others" table — the three moves, alone and with someone. The binding limits, delivered as content and not as a caveat: offer, never force (K-08 rule 6); this is peer support, not treatment (rule 2); knowing when to stop and bring in more support is part of the skill, not an afterthought (rule 10). Opting out of pairs is stated as normal before pairs are formed, and a solo written alternative is offered by default, not on request.
The activity 21 min. 3 min model and limits. 7 min turn one. 7 min turn two. 4 min debrief: "What was harder about doing it with someone?"
Evidence it worked P-12 (NEW, post) — "Today, did you take someone else through the three steps? (both roles / one role / no — I worked alone)". F-11 (NEW, 3 weeks) — "Since the session, did you use this with another person — either taking someone through it, or saying out loud what you were doing? (yes / no / no relevant moment) What happened?"
Claim boundary Licenses: "participants practised the sequence as peer support and X% reported using it with another person at three weeks." Does not license anything about team culture, relationships, psychological safety, or that MFC delivers support to third parties. It is peer support, and MFC teaches it as such.

F2 — Picks a shift move that fits the specific moment they chose, having felt the difference

Field Content
Outcome Beyond E5's "a move I can name": states which move fits this moment and why the other three do not — and can point to something they noticed in the room when the moment was run with the move and without it.
Why it matters Matching is where the toolkit stops being a poster. A participant who has one move for all moments will abandon it the first time it does not fit, and will read that as the method failing rather than the match.
Why it cannot be done in 90 minutes It requires two tools actually tried in the room (10 min) plus the same scenario run without the skill and then with it, plus a debrief on what was noticed (15 min). Essentials can produce a named move; it cannot produce a felt contrast, and without the contrast the matching is guesswork. 25 minutes.
What must be taught The four categories with the downshift/upshift rule (the same tool can do either); two tools practised live, chosen by the room; then the contrast run. Facilitator asks what participants noticed, never what was correct.
The activity 25 min. 10 min toolkit — two tools tried live, then "which of these do you already reach for?". 15 min contrast — the same moment run without, then with; pair debrief on "what was in the second version that wasn't in the first?". The second live State Check is folded into the debrief, unannounced, demonstrating that the answer changes.
Evidence it worked P-05 (existing, as in Essentials) plus P-05b (NEW, post) — "Why that one, for that moment?" (free text, one line). The pairing is the point: P-05 alone cannot distinguish a named tool from a matched tool. F-07 at follow-up, unchanged.
Claim boundary Licenses: "participants selected a tool for a specific moment and can say why." Does not license that the tool works, that matching improves outcomes, or anything physiological. MFC has no basis for any of that and building an item that invited the comparison would manufacture a claim.

F3 — Names the one thing around them that would make the next move easier, and who they have to ask

Field Content
Outcome Writes: the enabling condition their chosen moment depends on; whether it is inside their control or someone else's; if someone else's, the named person and the sentence they will say to them, and when. Separately: states where a problem goes if it is a workload, safety or leadership problem rather than a practice problem.
Why it matters This is the environment layer, and it is where the evidence actually points for anything beyond individual content (D-0090). It is also the safeguard: the same beat that opens the collective layer is the beat that closes the door on reframing a psychosocial hazard as a skill deficit. Those two cannot be separated — teaching the first without the second is the specific misuse K-07's binding constraint prohibits.
Why it cannot be done in 90 minutes It requires the diagnostic lens first (what is shaping access here — 8 min), then the write and the routing (15 min). Attempted in 90 minutes it becomes a slogan about environment with no named person and no route, which is worse than not raising it.
What must be taught The Human Operating System's diagnostic question — "What is shaping access in this moment?" — and the Environment component only, not all six. The enabling-conditions layer of the Radar. That an Our moment requires genuine agreement and is not a demand one person makes and labels shared. The hazard route, named concretely for that organisation, agreed with the host before the session.
The activity 23 min. 8 min diagnostic question and Environment. 15 min: private write of the enabling condition, control test, the named person and the sentence; then the hazard-routing beat delivered to the whole room. Nothing is read aloud; nothing is collected; no shared or team moment is agreed in the room.
Evidence it worked F-12 (NEW, 3 weeks) — "You wrote down one thing you would ask someone for. Did you ask? (yes / no / not yet / it stopped being relevant) What happened?" This is the only item in the whole instrument that reaches past the individual without making an organisational claim: it asks whether one person did one thing, self-reported.
Claim boundary Licenses: "participants identified an enabling condition and X% reported making the request at three weeks." Does not license anything about culture, norms, team change, absenteeism, productivity or psychosocial risk. MFC has no organisational measurement instrument and, per the Commercial Model prohibitions, may not claim one engagement changes any of the above.

Escalation flag. F3 is the honest, bounded version of the collective layer. The unbounded version — Team Pulse → Team Radar Snapshot → facilitated agreement → one shared observable practice — is exactly what D-0090 §1 recommended reopening and escalated to Hunter, undecided. F3 does not build it, does not pre-empt it, and does not substitute for it. If Team Pulse is reopened, F3 becomes its first beat rather than its replacement.

F4 — Says which of the five public skills their moment mainly asks of them (weakest outcome in the set)

Field Content
Outcome Given the five public labels in their locked wording, says which one their chosen moment mainly asks for, and why.
Why it matters Honestly: mainly so the five skills stop being vocabulary that is named once and never used. The outcomes checklist already found K3 weak — named once, never used and posed the choice directly: "Either give the five skills a job, or stop claiming participants can distinguish them." This gives them a job.
What must be taught The five in K-07's locked full-sentence wording — Notice, Shift, Choose, Focus, Connect — read once, one short line each, no elaboration. The seven deep skills stay out (Stage 3).
The activity 6 min. 3 min read and illustrate. 3 min: "Look at your moment. Which one is it mainly asking for?" Private; two or three volunteered aloud.
Evidence it worked P-11 (NEW, post) — "Which of the five does your moment mainly ask for, and why?" (select one + one line).
Claim boundary Licenses: "participants can map a real moment of their own to one of the five." Does not license that they can distinguish all five, define them, or use them. This is the weakest outcome in this document and it is included conditionally — if Hunter's answer to founder question 1 is that Essentials is Stage 1, the five skills belong here and this outcome justifies them; if the answer is that they are cut from both formats, F4 goes and nothing else in the chain moves.

Foundations — minute-by-minute, 180 minutes content + 15-minute break

Clock Min Beat Serves
0:00–0:04 4 Welcome, scope, six controls, disclosure + placeholder Enabling
0:04–0:08 4 Protected form time — token cards, Form 1 catch-up Measurement
0:08–0:22 14 Self-elicitation — private write, cards collected face-down, shuffled, transcribed unattributed, read back Room safety; sets up the reveal; precondition for F1
0:22–0:28 6 Recognition — four ordinary moments; the gap named Sets up E2
0:28–0:35 7 Why the gap exists + explain-back E2
