  2. It is uninterpretably noisy at MFC's actual scale. A 20-person cohort with 12 responding at three weeks, minus those reporting no opportunity, leaves a primary outcome resting on perhaps eight people's ratios of very small integers. One opportunity acted on once reads 100%; eight acted on four reads 50%. Averaging those is not a measure.
  3. ~~It discards the zero-denominator respondents entirely.~~ Withdrawn on review — this was not a difference between the two designs. A-01's out-of-scale option "there wasn't a relevant moment" removes exactly the same people from exactly the same comparison. It is a cost both designs carry, not a reason to prefer one.
  4. The denominator is itself taught — and this is not solved by dropping the ratio either. Noticing is a skill MFC teaches, so a participant who improves classifies more moments as ones where something could have helped. In a ratio the denominator rises and the ratio falls while the intervention works. In A-01 the same expansion happens inside the respondent's head, to the conditioned base "when there was something you knew could help" — so the same number of successes yields a lower frequency rating. Dropping the ratio does not resolve this; it makes it invisible, which is worse, because the ratio at least made the base inspectable.

Corrected on review, and it changes what has to be done about it. The bias runs against MFC in both designs. The only partial diagnostics are A-02's opportunity item and A-04's retrieval/enactment split — which is a further reason A-04 must be matched at baseline, not asked at follow-up only as first specified.

So the honest count is two decisive reasons, not four: the self-scoring harm, and the small-n noise. Both hold. Neither is repaired by better wording.

And the recall objection applies to all of it. R3 itself notes that "recall of counted events degrades fast." Counting difficult moments over seven days, retrospectively, is a poor measurement even before any of the above.

5 · The measure

Five components. One of them is the evidence; the other four make it interpretable.

Addendum, added on cross-check against B5-forms-build-ready.md and D3-delivery-models.md §0 — status: note, not a rewrite. This section's five-component list, taken alone, reads as if the then-test and a baseline-matched A-04 are optional refinements argued for only in §6.3 and §4 point 4 below. They are not optional in what was actually decided and built: D3 §0 states the governing "measurement constant" for every MFC offering as A-01 + the then-test + A-04 matched at baseline + H-01 + the referral line + 3-week follow-up, and B5-forms-build-ready.md §4 and §5 build both the then-test (A-01-THEN, Form 2) and a baseline A-04 (Form 1) exactly on that basis. This section is left as originally drafted rather than restructured into six components, so the reasoning trail in §6.3 stays intact — but a reader relying on §5 alone to reconstruct the constant will under-count it by two items. Treat D3 §0 as the current statement of the constant; this section is its earlier, narrower draft.

5.1 Primary — one matched item, identical wording at all three timepoints

Unchanged from B-01, deliberately. The forms draft's own instruction — "identical wording at baseline and every follow-up; this must not be edited later" — is correct, and rewording it now to something marginally more elegant would forfeit the matched comparison that is the whole point.

A-01 · the primary outcome. "When there was something you knew could help, how often did you remember to use it while the moment was happening?" Scale (ordinal, scored): Never · Rarely · Sometimes · Often · Almost always Held outside the scale, never scored: I didn't know what might help · There wasn't a relevant moment · Not sure

Asked at Form 1, Form 2 and Form 3, identically. The evidence is the matched change in this one item. Everything else is context for reading it.

Why the three out-of-scale options are structural, not tidiness. "There wasn't a relevant moment" is the opportunity distinction no competitor asks, and holding it outside the ordinal scale — rather than as a low point on it — is what stops "no opportunity" being scored as "failed to act." "I didn't know what might help" separates a knowledge gap from an access gap, which are different failures needing different fixes.

5.2 The opportunity item is yes/no, asked first, and routes

Instruction point 2, adopted. Nothing is counted.

A-02 · opportunity. "In the last week or two, did a moment come up where you knew something might help — a conversation, a decision, something you were putting off, a moment where stress or frustration got ahead of you? Yes / No / Not sure."

A No or Not sure routes past A-03 and A-04 and is reported in its own named cell, in the denominator statement, never as a failure.

5.3 Did it help — perceived benefit, among those for whom a moment arose

A-03. "When you did get to it, did it help you choose what to do next? It helped a lot · It helped a bit · It made no difference · It made things harder · I didn't get to it."

"It made things harder" is on the scale on purpose. An instrument with no route for harm cannot detect it, and D-0016's open items make that unacceptable.

5.4 What got in the way — the improvement signal, and the diagnostic that replaces the ratio

A-04. "When it didn't happen, what was closest? It didn't come into my head at the time · It came into my head but I couldn't get to it · It came into my head and I decided not to · Something else · Not sure."

This is the single most useful item in the instrument after the primary, and it is new. It splits the failure MFC cares about into its two halves — retrieval (it never arrived) and enactment (it arrived and could not be reached) — which are taught by different parts of the session and need opposite fixes. It gets that diagnostic for one item and about fifteen seconds, without a second matched scale and without counting anything.

A-05 · barriers. "What made it harder?" Multi-select plus other, with personal, social and environmental options reported separately, so non-use is never labelled low motivation.

5.5 One optional narrative, at follow-up only

A-06 · optional. "Think of the most recent time a moment like this came up. What happened, and what did you do? Two or three sentences. Please don't use anyone's name."

R3 §6.3: the only item producing checkable behavioural detail rather than a self-rating, and the most persuasive material MFC will ever have. It also carries the whole identifiability risk of the instrument, which is why it is optional, screened before it leaves, and why the "don't use anyone's name" instruction is inside the prompt rather than in a preamble.

6 · Where I depart from the instruction or the standing research — stated, with the reasoning

Invited explicitly, and these are genuine disagreements rather than hedges.

6.1 I agree with the instruction, and the argument for it is stronger than the argument given

The instruction's case rests on the question's difficulty. That is correct and sufficient on its own, but it understates the case: §4 above gives four further reasons the ratio fails that have nothing to do with ceilings — the self-scoring harm, the small-n noise, the discarded zero-denominators, and the taught denominator. Any one of the four would retire the ratio at MFC's scale even if the ceiling argument were wrong. The instruction is not a preference; the ratio was not viable.

6.2 I depart from R3 on TYDQ-15, and this contradicts a standing recommendation

R3 §5.3(b) recommends adopting TYDQ-15 as a labelled secondary, and the committee paper already promises it, for a real reason: "without an external instrument alongside ours, the fair criticism is that we wrote our own exam and marked it." That criticism is legitimate and I am not dismissing it.

The "R3 contradicts itself" charge is withdrawn on review — it was unfair and I had misread it. R3 resolves the tension in the same recommendation, explicitly: "Label it in advance, in the protocol, as a context measure that is not expected to move in three weeks. Writing that down before the pilot is what makes a subsequent null honest rather than embarrassing." That is a coherent position, not a self-contradiction.

The disagreement that survives is narrower and weaker, and it should be labelled as what it is. My objection — that a pre-labelled null still sits in the record looking like a failure — is a reputational argument, not a measurement one, and this document refuses reputational arguments elsewhere. What actually justifies keeping TYDQ-15 out of the core is burden and mechanism: it is ~2 minutes per participant per timepoint on an instrument whose response rate carries every claim MFC will make, spent on constructs a 90-minute session cannot move.

Recommendation, and it is a founder/advisor decision, not mine to close: TYDQ-15 is not in the core instrument for any cohort. It is available as an add-on for one case-study cohort, where the external-instrument argument can be answered once without burdening every participant or generating a null across every cohort. Licensing is unverified (R3 §5.3(b)) and must be confirmed before use.

6.3 I keep two things the instruction's five points do not mention, and I think dropping them would be a mistake

  • The then-test stays (R3 §7). The primary item is exactly the kind of item response shift attacks — the session teaches people what "remembering to use it while it was happening" actually means, so a genuinely improved participant may rate their before-state lower afterwards, and a naive pre→post comparison can show nothing or the wrong direction. R3 §7.3's pre-then-post design costs one repeat of the primary stem at Form 2 only, about twenty seconds, and it makes the headline claim stronger: if the real pre and the then-rating agree, there was no response shift and the result stands unchallenged.
  • The two forced-choice situational-judgement items stay (R3 §6.4). They measure procedural knowledge, not enactment, and must never be reported as enactment. Their value is that without them a null on the primary is uninterpretable: knowledge up and access flat means the teaching worked and the environment did not; both flat means the teaching failed. Those need opposite fixes and MFC currently cannot tell them apart. Two items, forced-choice, instant scoring, no screening.

Neither is counting machinery. Both are cheap, and both exist to stop a null being unreadable.

6.4 What this costs, stated

Changing the primary outcome away from D-0017 §2's approved "at least one reported attempted application" threshold, and removing WHO-5 against D-0017 §5's "retain WHO-5 as an instrument", are changes to an approved decision record. Hunter holds that authority and has exercised it — but the record is owed, and it is drafted in B5 rather than assumed. Not raising it would repeat exactly the failure this project has already been caught on twice.

7 · What this measure can and cannot support — K-08

It can support: "Among the participants who responded at three weeks, this proportion reported being able to reach what they knew would help while a difficult moment was happening, compared with this proportion before the session — and here is what got in the way for the rest."

It cannot support, and no wording rescues: that MFC caused the change (no control group); that the change is durable (three weeks is not durability); that participants are competent, or have a habit; anything about culture, productivity, absenteeism or attrition; any clinical or wellbeing claim whatsoever. K-08's ladder puts mechanism at Level 3, pending, and no claim level is board-approved, so every one of these boundaries is a boundary against an unapproved ceiling.

And one limit specific to this construct: the primary item is self-reported access, reported by the person whose access it is. It is not observed behaviour. R3 §6.7 rejects manager or peer report as the alternative, correctly and for reasons MFC should keep — but the consequence is that self-report is the ceiling of what this instrument can ever claim.

Original source: 60-projects/committee-pack-v1/B5a-measurement-construct.md

B5B Item Bank Literal Wording

B5b — Item bank, literal wording

What this document is. B5 names fifteen items whose content is a placeholder — "4 options, one key," "multi-select + other," "5-point." A builder cannot open a form tool against a placeholder. This document writes every one of them exactly as it would be printed: stem, full option set in printed order, scoring key and coding, per-item rationale, ceiling-risk assessment, and what cognitive testing (B5 blocker #6) should specifically probe.

What this document is not. It does not change any item's construct, wording rule, scale, routing, or place in the form sequence — those are fixed by B5 and B5a and are treated here as given. It does not resolve any of B5 §10's ten blockers. Nothing here is fielded, tested, or approved. Every option set below is a proposal for Eimear Quigley and Debra Fidler to challenge, and every key is provisional until cognitive testing (B5 blocker #6) confirms respondents can actually distinguish the options as intended.

Shared drafting rules applied to every item below (K-08, and B5's own stated discipline): one idea per stem; no double-barrelled questions; plain Australian English at roughly Year 8 reading level; no MFC internal term used before it has been taught to that audience at that timepoint; an escape option offered wherever a respondent might genuinely not fit; no option that shames non-practice or reads as a personal-failing judgement; no clinical or wellbeing claim implied by any option; balanced option sets (distractors are real alternatives, not strawmen).

Knowledge / comprehension items

B-04 — mental health vs mental fitness

Printed stem:

"Which statement best describes the relationship between mental health and mental fitness?"

Options, as printed:

# Option
A Mental fitness is really just a more positive way of describing good mental health.
B Mental health is how you're doing; mental fitness is what you're able to do — they're different things, and one isn't a "better" version of the other.
C Mental fitness mainly means staying calm and happy most of the time.
D Mental fitness is something mainly relevant to people who are already struggling with their mental health.

Key: B.

Coding: Correct / incorrect. Single-select.

Rationale. K-05's locked distinction is "mental health is how you are doing; mental fitness is what you are able to do" — neither a subset of the other, neither "better." The three distractors are not invented strawmen; they map to the three conflations K-08's claim-boundaries table and the category-confidence rule exist to correct: (A) collapsing the two into one concept — the most common lay conflation; (C) mistaking fitness for an emotional-state outcome, which is the exact error P-03 below also targets from a different angle; (D) treating fitness as remedial rather than universal, which contradicts the framework's own premise that everyone has access to strengthen, distress or not.

Ceiling-risk assessment. Moderate confidence this will not ceiling. The mental-health/mental-fitness conflation is genuinely common in everyday language (people say "I'm not mentally fit today" to mean "I'm not okay"), so a real spread of wrong answers is plausible at baseline. The risk is the opposite direction from most of this instrument: option B is written in a slightly more careful, complete sentence than the distractors, which can itself act as a tonal cue ("the long, hedged one is usually right") independent of content. This is a genuine risk and should be tested, not assumed away — if cognitive testing shows respondents picking B by sentence length rather than content, the distractor lengths need to be evened out before fielding.

What cognitive testing should probe here. Ask respondents to explain in their own words, after answering, why they picked what they picked — specifically whether they are reasoning about the content or about which option "sounds most complete." Also probe whether "one isn't a 'better' version of the other" is legible to a Year-8 reader or reads as filler.

B-06 — the knowing–doing scenario

Printed stem (vignette + question):

"Someone had planned to pause and really listen before responding in a difficult conversation. Partway through, they realised they'd already jumped in and cut the other person off — without meaning to. Which explanation best fits what happened?"

Options, as printed:

# Option
A They need to learn better listening skills.
B They didn't really want to listen in that conversation.
C They knew what to do, and in the moment, couldn't get to it before it had already happened.
D They weren't paying enough attention or trying hard enough.

Naming trade-off — resolved 2026-08-11, producing session, against the drafter's own open question (§"Items I could not write" item 3). The draft used a named actor ("Priya") for readability. Resolved to an unnamed third person, using they/them. Two reasons, in order of weight: (1) a specific name carries a gender and cultural cue in a vignette whose subject fails, inside a ~20-person single-employer cohort — an avoidable risk with no measurement benefit; (2) third person is retained rather than moving to "you" (which would have matched the SJT items) because a first-person version invites self-serving attribution — a respondent explaining their own interruption has an incentive to choose "couldn't get to it" over "wasn't trying," which would inflate the key for the wrong reason. Third-person-unnamed gets the demographic neutrality without buying that bias. SJT-01–03 stay in second person — they ask what the respondent would do, not how they explain a failure, so the same bias does not apply there.

Key: C.

Coding: Correct / incorrect. Single-select.

Rationale. The key must locate the failure in access under load — she knew what to do and couldn't reach it while the moment was live — matching B5a's construct exactly and MFC's stated reason for existing (the knowing–doing gap). The three distractors are deliberately not obviously wrong: (A) reframes it as a knowledge deficit ("needs to learn"), which is tempting because it sounds constructive rather than judgemental; (B) reframes it as motivation ("didn't really want to"), which is the single most tempting wrong answer because interrupting someone can genuinely look like not wanting to listen from the outside, and many respondents will import their own experience of being interrupted by people who, in their view, "didn't want to hear it"; (D) reframes it as effort or character ("wasn't trying hard enough"), the classic blame-the-person explanation K-08's core clinical lens exists to rule out ("increase agency without increasing blame").

Ceiling-risk assessment. This is the item in the knowledge block I am least confident will avoid ceiling, and I say so plainly. Once a respondent has read B5a's framing or attended any part of the session, "it's not that she didn't want to, it's that she couldn't get there in time" becomes close to the obviously-correct answer by tone alone — the vignette's own phrase "without meaning to" is doing a lot of the work of ruling out B and D before the options are even read. At baseline (Form 1, before any teaching), I expect a genuine spread across B, C and D, because most people have not yet been given the language to distinguish "couldn't get to it" from "didn't want to" — this is exactly the distinction MFC exists to teach, so if it ceilings even at baseline, that is itself a disconfirming signal worth flagging per B5a §3. At Form 2 (immediately post-teaching, matched), ceiling risk is higher, because the session has just handed respondents the correct frame directly.

What cognitive testing should probe here. Whether "without meaning to" in the stem is itself leading — try a version without it and see if the option spread changes. Also probe whether respondents read B ("didn't really want to listen") as plausible for themselves, or dismiss it immediately because the vignette already told them the person "had planned to" listen (which may inadvertently rule out B for careful readers, making it a weaker distractor than intended).

P-03 — "workable"

Printed stem:

"What does a 'workable' state mean?"

Options, as printed:

# Option
A Being calm and relaxed.
B Having no stress or difficult feelings at all.
C Being in a state where you can still respond to what matters, even if it isn't comfortable.
D Having fully settled down before doing anything else.

Key: C.

Coding: Correct / incorrect. Single-select.

Rationale. K-08's clinical and inclusion safety rules are explicit that MFC must never "imply that calm is always the goal — the goal is workable enough for this moment." This is, per the task brief, the single most misread idea MFC teaches, so the key must not be "calm" and a "calm and relaxed" distractor must be present precisely because it is the default wrong answer most people will reach for. B and D are secondary distractors covering the same error from two other angles: B assumes workable means the absence of difficulty rather than the ability to act inside it; D assumes a sequencing rule ("settle first, then act") that the framework does not teach and that reintroduces a completion-style precondition on acting.

Ceiling-risk assessment. This item only appears on Form 2, immediately after the session has directly taught this exact distinction (State Check: "too much, too little, or workable" — an intensity question, and the Shift step: "create enough space where useful and available," not "eliminate the feeling"). This is the highest ceiling-risk item in the whole knowledge block. Respondents who were paying attention in the room in the last hour have just been told, close to verbatim, that workable is not the same as calm. If the item ceilings here, it tells the committee almost nothing about durable comprehension — only that the room was listening an hour ago. Consider whether this item's real evidentiary value is at three weeks rather than immediately post-session; as specified it is Form-2-only, so that comparison is not currently available. Flagging this as a design tension for panel review, not resolving it myself.

What cognitive testing should probe here. Whether "respond to what matters" is legible without having heard the session's own language for it, and whether option D is actually distinguishable from C by someone who has not been taught the distinction yet — if D and C sound equally plausible to a naive baseline reader, that is fine (this item isn't asked at baseline), but it is worth checking the item isn't trivially easy even pre-teaching, which would suggest the wording is too transparent.

Situational judgement items

Shared design notes for all three. Each vignette avoids assuming parenthood, seniority, an office, employment status, or physical capacity, per K-07's rule 4. Each correct option performs Stop, Shift, Do in that order, and is written to describe what the person does, never that it worked — matching K-07's locked rule that "the outcome does not determine whether it counts." Each set of distractors covers three real, sensible-sounding alternatives: suppress and push on (skips Stop entirely), analyse/ruminate (gets stuck examining the feeling and never reaches Do), and postpone until feeling different (waits for an internal state change before acting, which contradicts "workable, not calm"). Scoring is 0–3 total across the three items, one point each, correct only — no partial credit is given for any option, including the rumination option, even though it is the item most likely to look partly right to a lenient scorer (see the trap note under each item).

SJT-01 — a difficult conversation

Printed stem:

"You're about to walk into a conversation with a colleague about a mistake that affected your work, and you notice your chest is tight and you're already rehearsing a defensive reply in your head. What do you do next?"

Options, as printed:

# Option
A Push the feeling aside and go in as planned — there's no need to make a bigger deal of it than it is.
B Spend some time thinking through exactly why you're feeling this tense before deciding what to do.
C Notice the tightness, take a breath or a moment to create a bit of space, then go in and say what actually matters to you.
D Wait until you feel completely calm before starting the conversation.

Key: C (Stop — notice the tightness; Shift — take a breath / create space; Do — say what matters).

Partial-credit trap: B. It looks like self-awareness ("thinking through why") and could tempt a lenient scorer into treating it as half-right. It is not — it never reaches Do, and rumination about the feeling's cause is a documented distinct failure mode (analysis without action), not a lesser-scoring version of the correct answer. Scored 0.

SJT-02 — a decision under time pressure

Printed stem:

"You're about to make a call on a decision with a tight deadline, and you notice you're speeding up and about to grab the first option that comes to mind without checking it against what actually matters. What do you do next?"

Options, as printed:

# Option
A Go with your gut and act fast — there's no time to overthink it.
B Catch that you're rushing, take a breath or a beat to widen your view, then choose based on what matters most and act.
C Go through every possible option in detail until you're completely sure.
D Put off the decision until you feel more confident about it.

Key: B (Stop — catch the rushing; Shift — a beat to widen the view; Do — choose and act).

Partial-credit trap: C. It sounds diligent and thorough, and some respondents will read "thoroughness" as the responsible choice under pressure. It is the rumination/analysis-paralysis failure mode transplanted into a decision context — it never reaches a Do under the actual time constraint the stem describes, so it fails the stem's own condition (a tight deadline) as well as the construct. Scored 0.

SJT-03 — something being avoided

Printed stem:

"You're about to open your laptop to start a task you've been putting off for a few days, and you notice a familiar wave of dread and the urge to check your phone instead. What do you do next?"

Options, as printed:

# Option
A Push through and force yourself to work without acknowledging the dread.
B Let the dread pass on its own — you'll get to the task once you feel more like doing it.
C Notice the dread and the urge, create a bit of space (name what's going on, or take a short reset), then start the task anyway — even a small piece of it.
D Spend some time working out exactly why you keep avoiding this task before doing anything else.

Key: C (Stop — notice the dread and urge; Shift — name it / short reset; Do — start, even a small piece).

Partial-credit trap: D. Same rumination pattern as SJT-01's B and SJT-02's C, restated for avoidance specifically — "understanding why I procrastinate" is genuinely good advice in some contexts, which is exactly why it is tempting here, but it is not Do and should not be scored as partial credit. B is the second-most-tempting wrong answer for this item specifically, because "wait until you feel like it" is close to how procrastination is often described colloquially as a mood problem rather than an access problem — worth testing directly (see below).

Ceiling-risk assessment for SJT-01–03, as a set. At Form 1 (baseline, before any teaching), low-to-moderate ceiling risk expected — Stop-Shift-Do has not yet been named, so a respondent choosing the correct option is doing so from prior general good sense, not recall, and the distractors are realistic enough that I'd expect real spread. At Form 2 (immediately post-teaching, matched), moderate ceiling risk — the three steps have just been taught by name in the room, so recognising the correctly-ordered option becomes partly a recall task rather than a judgement task. This is a smaller risk than P-03's, because these items ask respondents to apply the steps to a novel scenario they were not shown in the session, rather than to define a taught term directly — application items generally resist ceiling better than definition items. I would not be surprised by a genuine improvement Form 1 → Form 2 here even without ceiling, which is the intended signal (B5a §6.3: "if knowledge is up and access is flat, teaching worked and the environment did not").

What cognitive testing should probe across all three. Whether the rumination distractor is too close to correct for some respondents to distinguish reliably — if 5–8 participants split roughly evenly between the key and the rumination option even after the session, that is a real signal the item is not discriminating and needs rewording, not evidence the construct is wrong. Also probe whether the three scenario types (conversation / decision / avoidance) feel equally relevant across different kinds of work and non-work life — a participant who is not currently employed should still find at least one of the three recognisable.

Option lists left open by B5

A-05 — "What made it harder?"

Printed stem:

"What made it harder? Choose as many as apply."

Options, as printed, in three reported groups plus an escape:

Personal - It was hard to notice in the moment - I was worn out or already stretched thin - I wasn't sure what would actually help - Something else about how I was feeling right then made it harder

Social - Someone else's reaction or behaviour got in the way - I didn't want to make things awkward with the people involved - Other people around me were reacting differently, and it threw me off - I didn't feel able to raise it with the person or people involved

Environmental - There wasn't the time or space for it - Too much was happening at once - Where I was at the time made it hard to do anything differently - My workload didn't leave room for it

Escape option (not grouped, always last): - Other (please say) — free text

Coding. Multi-select. Counts reported separately by group (personal / social / environmental), never pooled into a single "barriers" total, per B5 §5 row 6. "Other" free text is screened under the same rule as A-06/F-07/H-01/P-05 (B5 §10 blocker #5, not yet drafted).

Rationale. B5a's core constraint governs every option here: non-use must never read as low motivation or lack of effort. Every option is worded so the respondent is describing something that happened to or around them, not a character judgement about themselves — even the personal-group options avoid "I didn't try" or "I forgot," which would smuggle a completion/effort frame back in against K-07's locked rule that trying counts and the outcome doesn't determine whether a rep counts. The set covers the three required categories explicitly requested: "no time or space" (environmental), "someone else's behaviour" (social), and "workload/environment" (environmental) are all present, each with at least three options per group as specified.

Ceiling-risk assessment. Not applicable in the usual sense — this is a barriers checklist, not a right/wrong item. The real risk is the opposite of ceiling: under-selection from social desirability (a respondent not wanting to say "someone else's behaviour got in the way" because it can read as blaming a colleague) and over-selection from vagueness (ticking several boxes that all felt loosely true rather than the one that actually mattered). Cognitive testing should ask respondents to pick their single biggest barrier after multi-selecting, to check whether the list captures it, or whether "Other" is being used because the real barrier isn't representable in the given groups.

What cognitive testing should probe. Whether "Someone else's reaction or behaviour got in the way" reads as tattling on a named person and causes respondents to avoid it even when true; whether the social/environmental line is intuitive (e.g., is "workload" environmental or personal to a respondent who experiences it as their own problem to manage) — if the boundary is unclear to respondents, the separate-reporting requirement in B5 §5 becomes noisy regardless of how it's coded.

F-09 — "What would help you keep going?"

Printed stem:

"What would help you keep going? Choose as many as apply."

Options, as printed:

  • A reminder now and then (text, email, or similar)
  • A short refresher session
  • Doing this with others — a group or a peer catch-up
  • Something at work changing to make more space for it
  • A written or physical reminder I could keep with me (a card, a note, something visible)
  • A short online activity I could do on my own, when it suits me
  • Nothing — I'm doing fine as I am
  • Other (please say) — free text

Coding. Multi-select. Counts reported per option, not pooled. "Other" screened under the same rule as A-05.

Rationale. Written to be decision-useful rather than merely descriptive, per the brief — each option maps to a concrete thing MFC could plausibly build or run next (a reminder cadence, a refresher format, a peer/group element, workplace-level change, a physical artefact, a digital follow-on). "Nothing — I'm doing fine as I am" is included deliberately as a genuine, non-shamed option — a respondent who doesn't need more support should be able to say so without the form implying something is wrong with that answer.

Ceiling-risk assessment. Not applicable — multi-select preference item, no correct answer. Risk to watch is the reverse of a knowledge-item ceiling: everything gets ticked because each option sounds individually appealing when offered as a free good, which would make the item non-discriminating for prioritisation purposes. Cognitive testing should ask respondents to pick their top one or two after multi-selecting, to see whether the resulting priority order differs meaningfully from raw tick counts.

What cognitive testing should probe. Whether "A short refresher session" and "A short online activity" are read as distinct by respondents, or as the same thing in different delivery modes — if participants can't tell them apart, they should be merged before fielding.

P-07 — realism of practising in the moments already in the day

Printed stem:

"How realistic does practising during moments already in your day feel?"

Verbal anchors, as printed (5-point, fully labelled):

  1. Not realistic for me at all
  2. Not very realistic
  3. Somewhat realistic
  4. Quite realistic
  5. Very realistic

Coding. Ordinal 1–5. No out-of-scale escape specified in B5; none added here since this is a feasibility rating about the respondent's own life, not a factual report that could have "no relevant case" — everyone has an answer, even if it's "not realistic at all."

Rationale. Fully labelled verbal anchors rather than numeric-endpoints-only, as required, so a respondent is never guessing what "3" means relative to "2." The five anchors are evenly spaced in intensity ("not realistic at all" → "very realistic") without introducing a qualitatively different concept partway through the scale (e.g. no anchor mixes in "confident" or "motivated," which would make this a different construct).

Ceiling-risk assessment. Moderate risk of clustering high, and for a specific, named reason: this item is asked on Form 2, immediately after a session that has just spent 9–10 minutes making the case that practice fits into moments already in the day. B5 §7's own listed confound — demand characteristics — applies directly here: a respondent who has just enjoyed the session and likes the facilitator has a live incentive to answer generously. This is not a reason to drop the item (it is useful context regardless), but the committee should not read a high mean here as strong independent evidence of real-world feasibility; it should be read alongside A-01's actual three-week result.

What cognitive testing should probe. Whether "moments already in your day" is concrete enough for a respondent to picture without further examples, or whether it needs one illustrative phrase inside the stem (at the cost of stem length) to anchor it.

P-11 — which of the five, and why

Printed stem and options, as printed:

"Which of the five does your moment mainly ask for, and why?"

Option Public description shown alongside it
Notice Notice what is happening inside you, around you, and between you and others.
Shift Create enough space to become workable — through your body, or through your thinking.
Choose Identify what matters and follow through.
Focus Put your attention where it matters and return it when it drifts.
Connect Connect better with yourself and others.

Followed by: "In one sentence, why that one?" — free text, one line.

Coding. Nominal, single-select from the five, plus a free-text rubric-scored follow-up (own-words reasoning vs a bare restatement of the label).

Rationale. B5 specifies "select 1 of 5 + one line" without giving the five as they'd actually be printed to a participant who has only just met these terms in the session. Printing the public description alongside each label (rather than the label alone) is necessary for the choice to be meaningful — asking someone to choose among five one-word labels they heard once, in a 9-minute block, without the description in front of them, would be testing recall of a word rather than judgement about their own moment, which is a different (and here, wrong) thing to measure.

Ceiling-risk assessment. Not applicable in the pass/fail sense — nominal choice item. The risk to flag is uneven base rates: some of the five skills may be far more commonly-selected than others regardless of what a respondent's actual moment needs, if the descriptions differ in how easy they are to picture (e.g. "Connect" may be an easier one-sentence justification than "Focus" for many everyday moments). This is a distribution-shape question, not a validity failure, but the committee should not expect roughly even fifths.

What cognitive testing should probe. Whether respondents can articulate a "why" that references their own moment rather than paraphrasing the printed description back — the rubric distinguishing "own words" from "restatement" needs real examples of both from pilot responses before it can be applied consistently, and none exist yet.

B-07 — weekly frequency of a situation you'd like to have handled better

The gap in the current 4-point scale, flagged as instructed. B5 §3 gives: "Not at all · Once or twice · Most days · Not sure." There is a real gap between "once or twice" and "most days" — nothing covers a respondent who runs into this a few times a week, which is a large and plausible band of the working-age population. As printed, that respondent has no honest answer between a rare-event option and a near-daily one, and will likely round down to "once or twice" (understating frequency) or up to "most days" (overstating it), either of which corrupts B-07's stated job as context for reading A-01.

Proposed repaired 5-point set, as it would be printed:

"In a typical week, how often do you run into a situation you'd like to have handled better?"

  1. Not at all
  2. Once or twice
  3. A few times
  4. Most days
  5. Not sure — (held outside the ordinal scale, own cell, same convention as A-01's out-of-scale options)

Coding. Ordinal 1–4; "Not sure" excluded from the ordinal comparison and reported in its own named cell, matching the out-of-scale convention B5 already uses for A-01.

Rationale. Filling the gap with "A few times" is the minimum repair — it does not attempt to finely grade frequency (that is not this item's job; it is context, "never scored" per B5 §3's B-02 convention for adjacent items), it only removes the forced rounding error. Moving "Not sure" out of the ordinal run and into its own cell brings this item into line with how every other ordinal item in this instrument already treats its escape option, which the original 4-point version did not do.

Ceiling/floor-risk assessment. Not applicable — this is a self-report frequency item used as context, never scored as correct/incorrect, and B5 already marks its sibling B-02 "never scored." No change to that treatment proposed here.

What cognitive testing should probe. Whether "A few times" is read as meaningfully between "once or twice" and "most days" by respondents, or whether some other phrase (e.g. "several times a week") would anchor the gap more precisely — this is exactly the kind of scale-labelling question B5 §10 blocker #6 exists to resolve before fielding, and the go/no-go rule stated there ("if participants cannot consistently distinguish adjacent labels, the scale is relabelled") applies to this repaired scale as much as to A-01.

Items I could not write, and why

None of the fifteen items were left blank. Every item B5 names with placeholder content now has full printed wording, an option set, and a key or coding rule above. What follows is what I could not responsibly resolve within this document, stated honestly rather than guessed at:

  1. Whether any option set above should be randomised at administration, and if so, whether the key-position or distractor-position should be fixed or rotated across forms. This is a build-tool configuration decision, not a construct decision, but it affects the ceiling-risk read for B-04 specifically (the "longer, more complete-sounding correct option" risk noted there is partly a fixed-position artefact of this draft and may resolve itself if randomised). Flagged for whoever builds the form, not resolved here.

  2. Whether the partial-credit traps identified in the three SJT items should, in fact, score partial credit. I have applied B5 §7's own stated discipline — a single ordinal/count outcome, no researcher-degrees-of-freedom left open at analysis time — and scored them 0, consistent with K-07's "the outcome does not determine whether it counts" applying to the primary construct, not to procedural-knowledge scoring, which has no equivalent locked rule. This is my judgement, not a ratified decision, and it is exactly the kind of item-level call B5 §10 blocker #7 (Eimear Quigley's and Debra Fidler's review) exists to check. I am not treating my own scoring choice as settled.

  3. ~~Whether B-06's vignette should use a named actor at all.~~ RESOLVED 2026-08-11 by the producing session — unnamed third person, they/them. Full reasoning at the item itself. The drafter was right to flag it and right not to settle it alone; the deciding argument turned out to be a measurement one (self-serving attribution) rather than the readability-vs-neutrality trade-off as originally framed. Still owed to Eimear and Debra: whether the repaired stem reads cleanly at Year-8 level without a name, which is a cognitive-testing question, not a design one.

  4. No item in this bank required a clinical or safeguarding decision I am not authorised to make. H-01, A-06, F-07, A-03 and the free-text screening rule sit outside this brief (they are already specified in B5 and gated by B5 §10 blocker #5, not drafted here), and nothing in the fifteen items above touches distress detection, referral pathways, or any D-0016 matter. I have not invented content in that space and none was needed.

Standing caveat that applies to the whole document. Every ceiling-risk assessment above is a theoretical judgement, consistent with B5a §3's own admission that "there are no published psychometrics" for this instrument's items. B5 §10 blocker #6 — cognitive testing with 5–8 participants, think-aloud on every clause — is the only thing that actually settles any of these risk calls, and none of the wording above should be treated as locked until that testing has run.

Original source: 60-projects/committee-pack-v1/B5b-item-bank-literal-wording.md

B5C Timepoints And The Durability Lock

B5c — The four timepoints, and why this instrument will not need rewriting

This document answers two questions the item set does not. First: how many timepoints, at what intervals, fixed how. Second — and this is the harder one — what makes a measurement design durable, rather than merely declared durable.

B5a states the construct. B5 states the items. This states the architecture holding them across time, and the change-control rule that protects the evidence base when MFC's products, framework and formats keep moving — which they will.

1 · The founder instruction, and where it departs from the standing records

Hunter, 2026-08-11: "The exact forms and each specific question: pre, post, 3-4 weeks after than 3 months after."

⚠ Read this before anything else in this document — the record contains a warning against exactly this change, by name

Found by the producing session on a direct read of D-0056, after this document's first draft had already been written on a weaker reading of the record. The first draft framed this as a simple three-to-four extension. It is not. Three facts, in order:

1. Hunter already approved a three-month wave once, on 2026-08-03: "I think the three to four weeks makes sense. I agree with the three month wave." D-0056 Matter 1. The instruction of 2026-08-11 is a return to his own earlier position, not a new idea.

2. D-0017 §6's exclusion of a second wave was already overridden then, not now. D-0056 Matter 1 states it explicitly: "An extended case-study wave is adopted, overriding D-0017's 'No second wave or substudy for the initial pilot.'" This document's first draft claimed D-0100 leaves D-0017 §6 untouched. That was wrong on the second-wave half — §6 covers both a months-later wave and a substudy, and only the substudy half is still standing. Corrected at §5.

3. And then Hunter narrowed it, on 2026-08-05, in terms that name this document's proposal directly. The correction: the interval is "a per-case-study choice, not a fixed '3 months for everyone.' Three months was Hunter's working example when this matter was decided, not a locked universal number." D-0056 records that a build package had already drifted into a fixed three-month framing once, and adds — verbatim — that the correction is "flagged here so the fixed-3-month framing doesn't recur in a future session reading this record cold."

This session is that future session, and this document is that framing. It is being proposed anyway, for the reasons at §1.2 — but not silently, and not by having missed the warning. Per CLAUDE.md §4, an unresolved conflict is surfaced, never quietly reconciled.

What is actually being asked of Hunter, precisely: your 2026-08-05 correction made the later wave case-study-only and its interval a per-case-study choice. Your 2026-08-11 instruction makes it universal and fixes it at three months. Those are opposite on both counts. Is the reversal deliberate? Per CLAUDE.md §2a a later instruction supersedes an earlier CURRENT judgement and no argument is being made against it — this is one confirmation, not a challenge, and §1.2 gives the substantive reasons the reversal is also the better design.

What the records currently say is different, and the difference is not trivial:

Standing record Founder instruction
Timepoints Three, universal (D-0017 §1) Four, universal
The later wave D-0056 Matter 1: an extended wave for case-study cohorts only, at an interval chosen per case study. D-0056's own 2026-08-05 correction: "three months was a working example, never a fixed rule" A standard fourth timepoint at three months, for everything

Verdict: the instruction is right, and the standing record was right about a different question. Both are defended below, because a change to an approved decision record is owed a reason and not a preference (§6.4 of B5a caught this project failing exactly that twice already).

1.1 Why D-0056's per-cohort rule was correct — and why fixing 90 days universally honours it rather than breaking it

D-0056's protection is against a specific fraud: choosing the follow-up interval after the data is in view, so a durability claim gets manufactured by picking the month that looks best. That is a real and common failure and the caution is well-placed.

A single, fixed, universal interval defeats that failure more completely than a per-cohort choice does. A per-cohort rule still leaves a decision to be made each time, in the presence of a person who knows what result would be convenient. A fixed day-90 for every cohort, written before any data exists, removes the decision entirely. D-0056's intent is not weakened by this amendment; it is made unconditional.

1.2 The three reasons the fourth wave has to be standard, not optional

1. An optional wave produces a non-poolable dataset, and pooling is not optional at MFC's scale. B5 §7 already fixes the consequence of the reporting floor: "a single Essentials cohort will almost always be below 20. The primary outcome is therefore pooled across cohorts before any figure is reported." Cohorts measured at different later intervals cannot be pooled. A wave that is optional and variably timed is, at n≈10 per cohort, a wave that will never accumulate into anything reportable. The standing design quietly guarantees that MFC never reaches a durability statement.

2. It is the exact claim MFC most needs and currently cannot make. B5a §7, on what the instrument cannot support: "that the change is durable (three weeks is not durability)." That sentence is the gap. It cannot be closed by a wave that most cohorts do not run.

3. A research partner will not co-sign a discretionary follow-up. MFC is actively seeking a university partnership (R9). A protocol in which the durability timepoint is elective, and its interval chosen locally, is not a protocol — it is a practice. This is the single clearest thing MFC can fix before the first outreach, and it costs about four minutes per participant, once.

1.3 The honest cost, stated before anyone discovers it

Response rate at 90 days will be the worst of the four, and by some distance. R3 §1.7 is explicit that "response rate at 3 weeks is a completely separate and much larger problem" than linkage — and 90 days is worse again. Three consequences, accepted deliberately:

  • The 90-day form is the shortest of the four (§3.4). At three months you ask only what you will actually report. Any item that does not change a decision is cut.
  • Every 90-day figure carries its denominator in the same sentence, and the survivorship direction is stated in words: the people who still reply at three months are more likely to be the people it worked for. This is already B5 §6's rule; it binds hardest here.
  • A 90-day null, or a 90-day sample too small to report, is an expected outcome of the early cohorts, not a failure of the design. Written down now so it cannot later be read as one.

2 · The four timepoints, fixed

Name When, exactly Where Length
T1 Baseline Sent ~7 days ahead. Anyone who has not done it completes it at the arrival table, not inside the protected in-room block Before ≈5.5 min
T2 Immediately after In the room, before anyone leaves. Protected named block in the session plan. Never shortened to buy content time In session 9 min Essentials / 10 min Foundations
T3 Three to four weeks Opens day 21. Reminders day 24 and day 27. Closes day 28 Alone ≈6 min
T4 Three months Opens day 90. Reminders day 93 and day 97. Closes day 104 Alone ≈4 min

Day numbers, not month names, and this is deliberate. "Three months" invites drift — it can be day 84 or day 100 depending on when someone remembers. A named day is auditable and poolable. Every day-count runs from the session date, which is the only date MFC reliably holds.

Why a two-week reference window on the primary item makes the four-timepoint design work at all. A-01 asks "in the last two weeks." B5 added that window as a correction — the earlier draft had no reference period, so every respondent supplied their own. It also, unplanned, makes the item timepoint-agnostic: the identical sentence is answerable at baseline, at day 21 and at day 90 without a single word changing. A window phrased "since the session" would have been unusable at T4. The matched wording survives the addition of a fourth timepoint at zero cost. Do not touch it.

3 · What each timepoint carries

The governing rule is unchanged (D3 §0): the measurement is the constant, the format is the variable. A format that cannot carry the measurement is not an MFC offering. The constant now spans four timepoints instead of three. That is the only change to the rule.

3.1 T1 — baseline

L-01–L-05 · A-01 · A-02 · A-04 · B-02 · B-04 · B-06 · SJT-01–03 · B-07 · NOM-01 (Foundations only). Standing referral line at the head. Per B5 §3.

Contradiction inside B5 itself, found by the producing session and not resolvable here. B5 §4 states H-01 "is unconditional, on every form, and cannot be routed past," and §9 lists it as "new, unconditional, on every form." But B5 §3's Form 1 table does not contain H-01. The prose and the table disagree, and the list above follows the table. The prose is almost certainly right and the table is the omission — but H-01 is a Tier A frozen item touching a D-0016 safeguarding matter, so which one is authoritative is not a call this document makes. Owner: qualified clinical governance, with the D-0016 item 4 pathway work. Note the asymmetry that makes the answer non-obvious: at baseline the session has not happened, so "has anything about today been difficult" has no referent — which may be exactly why the table omits it, and would mean the item needs a timepoint-appropriate stem rather than a yes/no on presence.

The 60-minute Introduction, and the day-90 wave — the question this document's own frontmatter promised to answer and did not

Found by the independent evidence audit, 2026-08-11. This document's amends: field names D-0098 — and the body then never mentioned the Introduction, the light set, or whether "on every format" includes the one format D-0098 explicitly exempted from the full instrument. An amendment claimed in frontmatter and not delivered in the body is worse than no claim, because a later reader takes it as settled. Answered here.

D-0098 says the 60-minute Introduction carries "Light only — not the full instrument", and its reasoning is sound and unaffected: the protected ten-minute in-session Form 2 block does not fit inside sixty minutes without turning it into fifty minutes of teaching in a kit built for sixty. D-0098's own closing warning — that the risk is "the measurement has to shrink to fit" — is exactly the failure mode a universal day-90 wave could cause. So the answer has to be precise.

The resolution: the Introduction gets the day-90 wave. It does not get the T2 in-room block. These are separable, and conflating them is what would have broken it.

  • What the Introduction carries at T1, T3 and T4: the constant — A-01, matched A-04, H-01, the referral line — at ≈2.5 min per timepoint, unchanged from D3 §0.
  • What it carries at T2: the then-test only (A-01-THEN), ~20 seconds, not the ten-minute protected block. D-0098's constraint is fully respected.
  • The day-90 addition costs the Introduction ≈2.5 minutes, out of session, three months later. It takes nothing from the sixty minutes, which is the entire thing D-0098 was protecting.

Why this is the right answer and not a convenient one. D3 §0's governing rule is that the measurement is the constant and the format is the variable, and "a format that cannot carry the measurement is not an MFC offering." If the day-90 wave is part of the constant for Essentials and Foundations but not for the Introduction, the Introduction's data cannot be pooled with theirs — and pooling is the only route to a reportable n (§1.2). An unpoolable short format is a product that generates burden without ever contributing evidence. D-0098 and D2 §2 answer 7 both need amending to add the day-90 wave to the light set. That amendment is now genuinely claimed by D-0100 §4, and is stated rather than assumed.

3.2 T2 — immediately after

L-01–L-05 · A-01-THEN (the then-test — asked once, here, never repeated) · B-04, B-06 · SJT-01–03 · P-01b · P-02b · P-03 · P-04b · P-05 · P-07 · P-08 · P-09 · P-11 · P-05b/P-12 (Foundations only) · H-01. Per B5 §4.

A-01 is not asked here. There is no elapsed period to report on minutes after a session.

3.3 T3 — day 21

Twelve items in the governed build order, per B5 §5. H-01 at position 10, immediately before the optional narrative; RET-01 last, per D-0008's non-contamination requirement.

3.4 T4 — day 90 · the new wave, specified

Ten items. Deliberately shorter than T3.

# ID Status Item
1 L-01–L-05 unchanged Linkage
2 A-01 frozen, matched Identical wording to T1 and T3, including the two-week window
3 A-02 unchanged Opportunity
4 A-03 unchanged Perceived benefit, with the harm cell
5 A-04 frozen, matched Retrieval / enactment split
6 DUR-01 NEW — T4 only The lapse-and-return item. §3.5
7 RAD-01 unchanged Radar helpfulness — retained here because at 90 days "I haven't looked at it" is itself the finding
8 H-01 frozen, unconditional Harm / safety, never routed away
9 A-06 optional unchanged The narrative item
10 RET-01 unchanged, last Unaided recall of the three steps

Cut from T4, each for a stated reason: A-05 (barriers — an improvement signal already fully captured at T3; asking again at 90 days buys a worse-recalled version of an answer MFC already has); F-07 and F-09 (both "what should we build next" items, answered at T3 when the session is still live in memory); the four SJT items and every knowledge item (B-04, B-06) — retention of definitions at three months is interesting and does not change a decision, and burden is the binding constraint this far out; P-* (all in-session items by construction).

RET-01 appears at both T3 and T4, and that is an addition to D-0008, not a breach of it. D-0008 approves "one brief retrieval prompt at or near the existing 3–4 week evaluation contact" and requires that it "may only follow after the relevant evaluation response is complete." A second instance at day 90, also placed last, satisfies the protected element exactly and is the single most informative durability item available: unaided recall of a three-word procedure at three months is checkable, cheap, and not a self-rating. Flagged as an amendment at §5 rather than slipped in.

3.5 DUR-01 — the one genuinely new item, and why it earns its place

DUR-01 (T4 only) — "Over the last three months, which of these is closest to how it went?"

  • I've kept using it fairly steadily
  • I stopped for a while, then came back to it
  • I stopped and haven't come back to it
  • I never really got started with it
  • Not sure

Nominal. Reported as a distribution. Never scored, and no option is a failure.**

Every other item in the instrument asks about a state. This one asks about a trajectory, and no other timepoint can produce it. A-01 at day 90 tells MFC where someone is; it cannot tell MFC whether they got there by never stopping or by stopping and returning. Those are different products.

It is also the item most directly aligned with D-0008's own framing of the follow-up as a lapse-and-return door rather than a report card. "I stopped for a while, then came back" is, under K-07's locked rule that the outcome does not determine whether a rep counts, a success — and the instrument currently has no way to record it.

And it is the most decision-useful item MFC will own for product design. If most respondents land on "stopped and haven't come back," the answer is a re-entry mechanism, not more content — and that finding is unavailable from any three-timepoint design.

4 · The durability lock — the actual answer to "we won't want to alter it"

Stated plainly, because the honest answer is better than the reassuring one: no one can build an instrument nobody will ever want to change. What can be built is one where changing it does not destroy the evidence. That is the whole of this section, and it is the part of this work most worth Hunter's attention.

The mechanism is three tiers, and the design goal is to make Tier A as small as it can possibly be.

4.1 TIER A — the frozen core. Ten items and four dates.

Wording, options, scale labels and order within the item may never change once the first participant completes a form. Changing any of these voids every comparison MFC has ever made on that item.

What is frozen
A-01 Full stem, the two-week window, the five ordinal labels, and the three out-of-scale options
A-01-THEN The header block and the stem
A-04 Stem and all six options
H-01 Presence and status only — NOT wording. See the correction below. On every form, unconditional, never routed past, never skippable
The referral line Verbatim, on every form
L-01–L-05 All five linkage items, on every form — dropping one from a later form breaks the code
The four dates Day 0 (T1/T2), day 21–28 (T3), day 90–104 (T4)

That is the entire permanent commitment. Everything else in the instrument is designed to be changed.

Correction, 2026-08-11 — H-01's wording is removed from Tier A, and the reason matters more than the fix

The first draft of this section froze H-01's stem — "Has anything about today been difficult or unhelpful for you?" — across all four timepoints. The independent safeguarding review caught two things about that, and the second is worse than the first.

First: "today" has no referent at day 90. A participant three months past a session, asked whether anything about "today" was difficult, is being asked a question about nothing. At best it is ignored; at worst it reads as being about the form itself and suppresses or misdirects a real disclosure — on the one item in the whole instrument whose entire purpose is to catch one.

Second, and this is the actual failure: this document explicitly verified that A-01's two-week window survives all four timepoints (§2), and ran no equivalent check on H-01 before freezing it. The same reasoning was available and was applied to one item and not the other. A freeze applied without a timepoint check is not a durability control; it is a way of making a defect permanent.

The fix, and its limit. H-01's presence, unconditionality and unroutability are frozen — those are structural and this document can hold them. Its wording is not frozen and cannot be frozen by this system, because D-0016 item 1 places it under qualified clinical governance, which has not reviewed it. Freezing wording ahead of the authority that owns it would put this change-control rule above clinical governance, which is the wrong way round. The corrected wording is Eimear Quigley's, Debra Fidler's and clinical governance's to write — not this document's, and not the reviewer's who found it.

Cost of the catch: zero, because nothing has been fielded. This is precisely what §4.7's one-way door is about, demonstrated once before it mattered.

4.2 TIER B — the stable shell

Change permitted between pilot cycles, never mid-cycle, and each change gets a one-line entry in a change log. Data either side of a Tier B change is reported as two series, not silently joined.

A-02 · A-03 · A-05 · A-06 · RAD-01 · F-07 · F-09 · RET-01 · DUR-01 · B-02 · B-07 · B-04 · B-06 · SJT-01–03 · every P-* item · the reporting-floor numbers · the analysis plan's secondary comparisons.

4.3 TIER C — free

No record needed: layout, visual design, platform, the covering email, section order — except the two governed placements, which are not layout choices: H-01 immediately before the narrative item, and RET-01 last.

4.4 The change-control rule, in one sentence

A Tier A item may be changed only by a Hunter decision record that states, in the record itself, that the evidence base on that item restarts from zero.

It does not forbid change — forbidding change is how a record gets ignored. It makes the cost visible at the moment the change is being considered, which is the only thing that reliably prevents casual drift.

The sentence is not the control. This is — added 2026-08-11 after two reviewers independently said so.

The first draft of this section said "that sentence is the whole control." Two panel reviewers, run cold and in parallel — the approach contrarian and the governance lens — returned the same finding independently: a written norm with nothing enforcing it is not a control, and from a governance standpoint an unenforced control is a liability rather than an asset.

The contrarian's supporting evidence was specific and it lands. This exact project already had a rule of the same shape — "wording, options and answer key must stay identical across all timepoints or the comparison is void" — and it was silently violated: B5 §9 records that B-03 and B-05 were cut from Form 2 while kept on Form 1, stranding the baseline, and nothing caught it for three passes. A durability rule that has already failed once in this project, in writing, is not made safe by being restated more firmly.

So it is now executable:

python3 90-meta/session-tools-v1/verify_measurement_frozen_core.py

It holds a hashed snapshot of every Tier A string (90-meta/session-tools-v1/measurement-frozen-core.json), checks each still appears verbatim in its source document, and exits non-zero if one has drifted — unless a record in 30-decisions/ both names that item id and contains the phrase "restarts from zero." That is §4.4's sentence, mechanically. It also detects a snapshot edited to match a drift (each entry carries a sha256 of its own text), and checks the four fixed day-numbers are still present.

It is wired into run_all_controls.py, so it runs before any production objective closes — L-010: a control added without being wired into that entry point is an incomplete change. It was tested against a real tamper before being reported as working, not only self-tested: A-01's stem was altered in B5, the control returned FAIL_FROZEN_CORE and exit 1, and the file was restored.

What it does NOT cover, stated so this is not over-claimed: it verifies wording stability in the vault's specification documents. It cannot see the live form tool. If someone builds a form whose wording differs from the spec, this control will not know. Closing that gap needs a build-time check of the fielded form against the spec — that control does not exist, is not proposed here, and is named as a real remaining gap rather than left implied as covered.

4.5 Why this is genuinely durable, and not just asserted to be

Four structural properties, each checkable:

1. The frozen core contains no MFC content whatsoever. Read A-01, A-04, H-01 and the linkage items again: not one of them mentions Stop, Shift, Do, a rep, the Radar, State Check, a skill name, the Human Operating System, or mental fitness. They describe a phenomenon that exists whether or not MFC exists.

This is the load-bearing property of the whole design, and it is worth stating on its own. If MFC changes its framework — renames a skill, drops a step, adds a sixth, retires the Radar — the primary outcome is untouched and the time series survives intact. Every item that does name MFC's own content (RET-01, P-11, RAD-01, the SJT set, B-04, B-06) sits in Tier B precisely so that framework change is allowed to move it.

The framework is currently held as settled (~2026-08-07). This design does not depend on that staying true.

2. The frozen core is format-agnostic. It runs unchanged on the one-hour digital session, the 90-minute, the half-day and Foundations. Multiplying products therefore does not fork the evidence base — which is exactly the risk D3 §0's constant/variable rule exists to manage, now made concrete at the item level.

3. A null is already pre-registered as an honest outcome. B5 §7's two disconfirmers, and its precision statement ("a single ordinal item at n≈10 detects only very large shifts… this design is a case description, not a test"), are written before any data exists. The commonest reason an instrument gets rewritten is that it returned a result nobody wanted. That reason has been removed in advance.

4. The frozen core is ten items. Small enough that each one can be defended individually to a methodologist, an HREC or a funder — and small enough that being wrong about any item outside it costs nothing.

4.6 The four things that would legitimately force a Tier A change — named now

Anything not on this list is not a reason.

  1. Cognitive testing finds the scale does not work. B5 blocker 6's stated go/no-go: "if participants cannot consistently distinguish 'Rarely' from 'Sometimes,' the scale is relabelled before fielding."
  2. The first cohort's baseline A-01 ceilings at Often or Almost always. Already pre-registered (B5a §3): the construct needs rebuilding, not the analysis rescuing. This is the one case where the right response is to change the frozen core, and it is a founding-premise failure, not a wording problem.
  3. A human research ethics committee requires a change as a condition of approval (R9).
  4. Qualified clinical governance requires a change under D-0016 item 1. Added 2026-08-11 — the safeguarding review found this missing, and its absence was the more serious version of the H-01 defect at §4.1. D-0016 item 1 is the live, open authority over H-01 and the referral line's content. Omitting it from this list had the freeze mechanism silently outranking the clinical governance that has not yet reviewed the items it was freezing. A control that can outrank a safeguarding gate is not a control worth having.

4.7 The one-way door, and what it does to the blocker list

The free-change window closes the moment the first participant completes Form 1. Before that, every item can be changed at zero cost. After it, A-01 cannot be improved — only restarted.

This re-sequences B5's open blockers rather than merely listing them. Cognitive testing (blocker 6) is not a quality step to be done when convenient; it is the last opportunity to alter the frozen core for free, and it must complete before any participant sees a form. Same for the Eimear Quigley / Debra Fidler review (blocker 7) and any HREC condition (R9) — all three have to land inside the window, and the window shuts once.

5 · The decision record this owes — D-0100, drafted, NOT adopted

ID reserved 2026-08-11. This consolidates the amendment B5 §1 drafted without an ID, so there is one record rather than two competing drafts.

D-0100 — The measurement architecture: access under load, over four fixed timepoints

Decision. D-0017's approved measurement architecture is amended in five respects, and in no others.

1. The primary outcome changes. D-0017 §2's "at least one reported attempted application" becomes one matched ordinal item measuring access under load (A-01), with the opportunity item retained separately (A-02). Reasoning: B5a.

2. WHO-5 is out of the first cohort. Against D-0017 §5. It measures how a person is doing — mental health — which K-05 says mental fitness is not; it would reach a participant alone, weeks later, with no approved distress pathway while D-0016 items 1–2 are open. Recorded as available to re-add on Eimear Quigley's and Debra Fidler's advice.

3. The follow-up's Radar items change shape. D-0017 §3's first two limbs are replaced by A-01/A-02, which ask about any moment rather than the nominated one — checking whether a participant practised the specific thing they wrote down is compliance-checking. The third limb, general Radar helpfulness, is retained in full as RAD-01.

4. D-0017 §1's three timepoints become four — and the record this actually amends is D-0056, not D-0017. Stated precisely, because the first draft of this record got the lineage wrong:

  • D-0017 §6 excluded both a months-later second wave and a substudy from the initial pilot, deferring the former "as a defensible future decision for a second pilot cycle, once Option A's own data exists."
  • D-0056 Matter 1 already overrode the second-wave half, on Hunter's decision of 2026-08-03 ("I agree with the three month wave"), in those words: "overriding D-0017's 'No second wave or substudy for the initial pilot.'" D-0017 §6 is therefore not the live constraint and has not been for eight days.
  • What D-0100 actually changes is D-0056 Matter 1's own 2026-08-05 correction, on two counts and only two: scope (case-study cohorts only → every cohort, every format) and interval (a per-case-study choice → fixed at day 90). This is a reversal of a founder correction, not an extension of it, and the warning it carries is quoted in full at §1.
  • D-0017 §6's substudy exclusion is untouched. No substudy is proposed.

One new item, DUR-01. RET-01 is asked at both day 21 and day 90, last on each form, satisfying D-0008's non-contamination requirement at both.

5. The three-tier change-control lock at §4 is adopted as the governing rule for every future change to the instrument, on every format.

What is NOT changed. D-0017 §4's separation of facilitator records from participant data; D-0017 §6's exclusion of a substudy; §7's refusal to adopt an external instrument without a full seven-point assessment. D-0056 Matter 1a is untouched — the case-study package (fortnightly reminders plus organisation-led check-ins) and its binding claim consequence ("this programme, one session plus the implementation the organisation ran itself") still apply to case-study cohorts and must not be read across to ordinary cohorts now that they share a day-90 timepoint. D-0016's six matters are untouched and remain a hard gate.

One divergence, declared rather than buried. K-07's locked definition says a rep may be caught "before it happens, while it is happening, or afterwards." A-01 scores only "while the moment was happening." Deliberate — it is the harder question and the whole basis of the ceiling argument — and it means the headline number under-counts practice K-07 counts as real. It must never be described as measuring reps.

Requires: Hunter's approval. Recommendation: approve points 1, 3, 4 and 5 now. Hold point 2 (WHO-5) open, not approved as written — B5e §3.3, written the same day as this record, found that "WHO-5 removed — Founder decision" cannot be traced to anything Hunter is recorded as having actually said, and that the live, Eimear-Quigley-and-Debra-Fidler-reviewed design (as recently as five days before this rebuild began) has WHO-5 as required, not optional. Point 2 is amended to: WHO-5's status is unresolved pending Eimear Quigley's and Debra Fidler's direct answer to the question B5e §3.3 poses them — not a settled removal. Confidence: high on 4. Moderate-to-high on 1, 3 and 5. Point 2 is not confidence-rated — it is not decided.

6 · What four timepoints let MFC say, and what they still do not

May be said Still may NOT be said
At day 21 "Of the N who responded at three weeks, this many reported being able to reach what they knew would help while a difficult moment was happening, compared with this many before." That MFC caused it. That it lasts.
At day 90 The same sentence at three months, plus the lapse-and-return distribution, plus unaided recall of the procedure — each with its own denominator That the change is durable, as a proven claim. That MFC caused it. Any clinical or wellbeing claim. Anything about culture, productivity, absenteeism or attrition

The distinction that matters, and it is not pedantry. Day 90 buys a persistence description — this is what the people who responded reported three months later. It does not buy durability, which is a causal-and-generalisable claim requiring a control group MFC does not have and is not proposing to get. K-08's ladder puts mechanism at Level 3, pending; no claim level is board-approved. Adding a timepoint does not move a rung.

Total participant burden across the whole programme: ≈25 minutes, spread over three months. Stated so it can be quoted to an employer, an HREC and a participant without recalculation.

7 · Comparing the three formats — the purpose this was built for, which nobody had checked it against

Added 2026-08-11 after the founder-lens pass returned NOT_READY_APPROACH_UNCONTESTED on exactly this. It is the sharpest finding of the whole panel and it was not on anyone's list.

Hunter's own stated reason for this work: "Once this is done — we can then properly finish the build and make improvements based on these findings of our actual products — half day, 1.5 hour, digital offerings." Five reviewers checked whether the instrument is correct. None checked whether it can answer the question it is being built to answer. It can — but not the way it looks like it can, and the difference is the whole of this section.

7.1 The problem, stated exactly

B5 §7 fixes two rules that collide with format comparison:

  • No report on a group under 20; no subgroup under 10.
  • The primary outcome is pooled across cohorts before any figure is reported, because a single cohort will almost always be under 20.

Format is a subgroup. So comparing half-day against 90-minute against digital on the primary outcome means ≥10 matched respondents per format to break out at all, and realistically ≥20 per format before the comparison means anything. Working it through at MFC's actual numbers — ~15 attendees, ~60% matched response at day 21 — that is roughly 9 usable responses per cohort, so two to three cohorts per format to clear the subgroup floor and four to five to clear 20. Across three formats: somewhere between nine and fifteen cohorts before the headline number can be broken out by format.

That is a long way off, and if it were the only route, this instrument would not serve the purpose it was built for until well after the products had already been finished.

7.2 The answer: the improvement signals are not the primary outcome, and they arrive immediately

This is the resolution, and it should change how the instrument is read. The primary outcome (A-01) exists to build MFC's evidence case. Improving the products is a different job, served by different items, on a completely different timetable — and the design already carries them.

The reason is response rate, and it is structural. T1 and T2 are both administered in the room or at the arrival table. Their response rate is near 100% and their matching is 98–100% (B5 §2.1) — no send channel, no attrition, no survivorship. Everything measurable across T1→T2 is available from cohort one, per format, at full response.

What you want to know about a format Items Available from Why it works this early
Did the teaching land? SJT-01–03 and B-04/B-06, T1→T2 matched Cohort 1 Both timepoints in-room, ~100% response. This is the single most format-sensitive comparison in the instrument and it is available immediately
Did people leave with something retrievable, in their own words? P-05, P-02b, P-01b Cohort 1 In-room, rubric-scored (B5d)
Does the practice feel doable to them? P-07 Cohort 1 In-room. Read with B5 §7's demand-characteristics caveat, but format differences here are still informative
Did they actually build a Radar, and is it well-formed? P-08 Cohort 1 In-room, objective
Which half of the model is failing — retrieval or enactment? A-04's mix Cohort 1–2 A distribution, not a matched comparison. Readable at small n in a way a shift-proportion is not
What is getting in the way? A-05, grouped personal/social/environmental Cohort 1–2 Counts, reported by group
What should we build next? F-09 Cohort 1–2 Literally the item for this
Did the procedure survive three months? RET-01 at day 21 and day 90; DUR-01 Cohort 2–3 Unaided recall, not a self-rating
Did access under load change? A-01 ≈9–15 cohorts before it breaks out by format Subgroup floor plus pooling. §8.1
