So the honest statement, which nobody had made: MFC can start improving the half-day, the 90-minute and the digital offering from the first cohort of each — using the in-room learning and feasibility items, at near-full response. What it cannot do for a year or more is claim that one format changes access under load more than another. Those are different claims with different evidence requirements, and conflating them is how a product decision gets made on a number that cannot support it.

7.3 The rule this creates, fixed now rather than when the data is in view

Same discipline as §1.1's fixed interval, and for the same reason.

  1. Format-level differences on A-01 are not reported, internally or externally, until that format has ≥20 matched respondents pooled across its own cohorts. Below that the number is noise and will be read as signal.
  2. Format-level differences on the in-room items (SJT, B-04, B-06, P-05, P-07, P-08) may be used for product decisions from the first cohort of each format, and must be described as what they are — whether the teaching landed, never whether the format works.
  3. A product change made on in-room evidence is recorded with the reason, because it changes the thing being measured. Under §4.2 the SJT set is Tier B: changing the session invalidates the SJT series across that boundary, and it is reported as two series, not one. This is the cost of improving the product while measuring it, and it is real — but it is a cost worth paying, because the alternative is freezing three products for a year to protect a comparison that is not available anyway.

7.4 The consequence for the digital offering specifically, which is the awkward one

The 60-minute digital Introduction has no protected in-room block (D-0098, and §3.1's resolution above). So most of the fast improvement signals in §8.2's table are exactly the ones it does not carry. It gets A-01, A-01-THEN, matched A-04, H-01 and the referral line — and none of the SJT, P-05, P-07 or P-08 items that make cohort-one product improvement possible for the other two.

Stated plainly rather than buried: the digital offering is the format MFC will be slowest to be able to improve on evidence, and that follows directly from the decision to protect its sixty minutes. That decision (D-0098) is sound and is not reopened here.

Decided, 2026-08-11 — Hunter: add the one question. P-07 — "How realistic does practising during moments already in your day feel?", ~15 seconds — is added to the 60-minute Introduction's T2 (immediately-after) form. This is the single cheapest, highest-value addition available: it gives the Introduction its own in-room feasibility signal from cohort one, without touching the protected sixty minutes or adding a second item. The Introduction's T2 set (§3.1) is amended from "the then-test only" to "the then-test, plus P-07." No other in-room item is added — SJT, P-05 and P-08 remain out, since each carries real teaching-time cost D-0098 was built to avoid, and P-07 alone does not.

8 · What this document does not resolve

  • Nothing here is built, approved, sent, or participant-facing. D-0016's six matters remain a hard gate and none are closed.
  • D-0100 is drafted, not adopted. It needs Hunter's approval.

8.1 BLOCKER — the day-90 form has no delivery channel, and a harm disclosure on it has no reader

Upgraded from a footnote to a named blocker, 2026-08-11, after the safeguarding review and the governance review independently reached the same place from opposite directions. This document's first draft listed it as an open item. Three findings converged on it, which is the signal to treat it as blocking rather than noting it.

The mechanism, traced concretely. B5 §2.3 removed email from the instrument and specified two routes for Form 3: a host-circulated generic link, and an optional opt-in slip deleted at day 28. A day-90 wave therefore has no MFC-held channel at all. And H-01 — the unconditional harm item — is on that form. So the sequence is: a participant three months on, alone, discloses distress via an untraceable generic link, to no defined reader, with no defined turnaround, and no MFC-initiated follow-up beyond a printed phone number. That is not a residual risk to be accepted; it is a pathway with a hole in it, and B5 blocker 4 (clinical governance on the distress pathway) is already open for the day-21 version of exactly this.

H-01 makes this more urgent, not less, because the item invites the disclosure. Adding a fourth timepoint adds a fourth invitation. A wave that cannot be delivered, and whose harm item cannot be answered, is not a wave — and this is the one finding that could sink the day-90 proposal on its own merits.

The two options, with what each actually costs, so this is a choice and not a discovery:

A — host-circulated link only B — extend the opt-in slip to day 104
How T4 reaches people The host emails the same generic link to everyone who attended MFC emails the opt-in list directly, as at day 21
What the host learns That a three-month follow-up went to the group. Not who responded, not what anyone said Nothing new
What MFC holds Nothing A contact list, for 104 days instead of 28 — a 3.7× longer retention of the one identifying artefact in the whole design
Response rate Worse — a forwarded generic link at three months is the weakest possible prompt Better
Consent implication None beyond B5 §2.3's existing disclosure The collection notice must say day 104, before collection, not after. A retention period disclosed as one thing and used as another is the failure, not the length itself
Harm-disclosure path Still unsolved. No route back to the discloser under either option Still unsolved — an opt-in list is separate from responses by design and must never be joined

Neither option solves the harm-disclosure path, and that is the point. The channel question and the distress-pathway question look like one problem and are two. Owner: qualified clinical governance, under D-0016 items 1 and 4 — not this document, and not the committee. The harm-disclosure path remains open regardless of which channel option is chosen, and needs clinical governance's sign-off before anything is fielded.

Channel decided, 2026-08-11 — Hunter: "MFC keeps the contact list longer, and the host is notified." A third option, not originally offered, combining B's retention with A's transparency:

C — adopted: MFC retains the list to day 104, host is told
How T4 reaches people MFC emails the opt-in list directly, as at day 21 (Option B's mechanism)
What the host learns That MFC is running a day-90 follow-up and retaining contact details for it — told proactively, not left to infer (closes Option B's one-sided gap, where the host learned nothing new while MFC's retention grew)
What MFC holds A contact list for 104 days instead of 28 — unchanged from Option B
Response rate Better — MFC-sent, not a forwarded generic link
Consent implication The collection notice must state day 104 before collection, and now must also state that the host organisation is informed a day-90 wave is running (not that the host sees responses — only that the wave exists)

Why telling the host is the right addition, not a compromise. R3 §4.3's whole assurance strategy rests on the participant being able to verify what the employer knows and doesn't. A host that is quietly kept in the dark about a longer retention period, while participants are told about it, creates exactly the asymmetry that assurance strategy exists to prevent. Telling the host "MFC is running a day-90 check-in and holding contact details for it" costs nothing and closes that gap — it does not tell the host who responded or what anyone said, which remains the actual boundary.

8.2 Everything else this document does not resolve

  • Whether a 90-day wave changes MFC's health-service-provider exposure under Privacy Act s.6FB (R3 §3.8) is not assessed here. Longer retention of a longitudinal dataset is a fact a lawyer should have when answering that question.

Original source: 60-projects/committee-pack-v1/B5c-timepoints-and-the-durability-lock.md

B5D Free Text Scoring Rubrics

B5d — Scoring rubrics for the free-text and rubric-coded items

What this document is. B5 §§3–5 name nine free-text or rubric-scored items with a stem and a one-line coding note — "rubric: names the gap without mechanism language," "own words vs menu label" — and no rubric a scorer could actually apply. This document writes the rubric: the exact scoring categories, the decision rule for each, worked examples, a hard edge case, and what a scorer must not do. It also covers the three items that are not scored at all but screened and categorised (A-05/F-09 "Other," H-01's "Yes" text).

What this document is not. It does not change any item's wording, placement, or routing — those are fixed by B5. It does not resolve B5 §10 blocker 5, the written free-text screening rule for safeguarding content in A-06, F-07, H-01, P-05, and the two "Other" fields — that blocker is explicitly out of scope here and is not attempted below. It does not invent a rubric that scores outcome. Where a rubric genuinely cannot be finalised without pilot examples, that is stated, not papered over.

Governing constraints, restated because every rubric below is checked against them:

  • K-07 locked: "A mental rep is catching a moment and choosing your next move, on purpose, toward what matters... The outcome does not determine whether it counts." No rubric below may score, penalise, or treat differently a response describing an attempt that did not go well versus one that did.
  • K-08: claims and language boundaries — specifically the prohibition on brain/neuroscience mechanism claims ("rewiring," "neural pathways," dopamine/cortisol talk, etc.) appearing as if MFC teaches or validates them, and the instruction to increase agency without increasing blame.
  • B5 §8: nothing scored here is ever reported back to the participant, individually or by name. Scoring exists for MFC's own aggregate reporting only.
  • One scorer. R3 §4.2 treats two-person inter-rater checking as normal practice for rubric-coded qualitative items. MFC has one person doing this work. Every rubric below is designed to be usable by one person applying it consistently to themselves over time, not to approximate two-rater reliability that does not exist. The cost of this is stated per item and again at the end.

1 · P-01b — "In one sentence: why does someone who knows what would help still do the other

thing?"

Serves K-E2 — whether the session landed the knowing–doing gap, the reason MFC exists.

Categories and decision rules

Category Rule
Pass The response names that knowing and doing are separate — that a person can know what would help and still not do it — without attributing this to a mechanism (brain, stress chemistry, willpower-as-trait, "the amygdala," "fight or flight," "habit is hardwired," etc.). It may name a plain-language, non-mechanism reason (the moment moves fast, it's hard in the moment, you forget in the moment, emotions take over, it's easier said than done) as long as the reason stays at the level of everyday experience rather than claiming a physiological or clinical explanation.
Partial The response gestures at the gap (implies knowing ≠ doing) but is too vague, circular, or generic to demonstrate the respondent actually grasped it as a distinct idea — e.g., restates the question, or gives an answer that would fit almost any behaviour-change topic with no reference to the in-the-moment nature of the gap.
Fail — mechanism language The response explains the gap using brain, neuroscience, or clinical-mechanism language, whether or not the content is otherwise correct. This is a fail regardless of how well-written or plausible the sentence is.
Fail — no gap named The response does not identify a knowing–doing split at all — e.g., answers a different question ("because they don't really know what would help"), denies the premise, or is a non-answer.

What counts as "naming the gap"

The minimum bar is: the sentence has to be about the space between knowing and doing, not about knowledge itself. A sentence that explains why someone might not know the right thing (e.g., "they were never taught it") answers a different question and fails under "no gap named," even though it sounds related.

What "mechanism language" is, and why it fails (per K-08)

K-08's claim boundaries table lists as "Avoid saying": "Mental reps guarantee brain rewiring or guaranteed outcomes" and reserves neuroscience/mechanism framing for the seven deep skills used "directly by clinical advisors," never for public or participant-facing claims. K-08's clinical and inclusion safety rules also prohibit implying a difficulty is a personal failure rooted in a fixed trait. Two failure modes both count as "mechanism language" here:

  1. Neuro/physiological explanation — "the brain defaults to old pathways under stress," "cortisol takes over," "it's the amygdala hijacking you," "muscle memory." These import a scientific claim the framework does not make in this context and the participant has not been taught to make either.
  2. Trait-fixing explanation — "some people just have more willpower," "it's a habit that's wired in." These are not neuroscience but they do the same work K-08 prohibits: turning a moment-level, universal gap into a fixed personal or biological limitation, increasing blame rather than agency.

Note the rubric's own asymmetry, stated on purpose: a response can use plain language that happens to gesture loosely at biology ("it's just instinct," "you're on autopilot") without this being disqualifying only if it does not read as an explanatory claim of mechanism — "autopilot" as an everyday figure of speech for "I wasn't paying attention" is fine; "your brain goes on autopilot and you can't stop it" claims a mechanism and fails. The test is whether the sentence is doing explanatory work with a claimed cause, or just describing the experience in ordinary words.

Worked examples

Pass - "Because in the moment it's hard to remember or actually do the thing you know would help." — Names the gap (knowing vs. doing, specifically "in the moment"), no mechanism claim. - "You know what to do, but when it's actually happening things move too fast to catch it." — Same: gap named, plain-language reason ("moves too fast"), no claimed mechanism.

Partial - "Because change is hard." — Generic; could answer almost any behaviour-change question; does not clearly show the respondent distinguishes knowing from doing specifically, as opposed to change being effortful in general. - "Habits are hard to break." — Gestures at a related idea (habit vs. intention) but doesn't name the knowing–doing split itself; ambiguous whether the respondent has the gap or a different concept in mind. Score partial, not fail, because it is plausibly adjacent rather than off-topic.

Fail — mechanism language - "Because their brain defaults to old neural pathways when stress hits." — Explicit neuroscience mechanism claim. Fails even though it correctly implies a knowing–doing gap exists. - "Some people just don't have the willpower to follow through." — Trait-fixing; increases blame, the exact thing K-08's "increase agency without increasing blame" line exists to prevent.

Fail — no gap named - "Because they weren't paying attention in the session." — Answers "why don't they know," not "why don't they do what they know." - "They probably didn't understand it properly." — Denies the premise that they knew what would help in the first place; answers a knowledge question, not the knowing–doing gap the item asks about.

Hard edge case

"Because in the heat of the moment your body takes over before your mind catches up." This uses body/mind language that sounds mechanism-adjacent but is a common, plain-language way non-experts describe the felt experience of a fast-moving moment, not a claimed physiological mechanism (it does not name cortisol, the brain, hardwiring, or any specific causal system). Resolution: score Pass. The distinguishing test is whether a specific biological or clinical system is named or implied as the cause (fail) versus whether the sentence is a lay description of the experience of the gap using body-mind vocabulary that any non-expert would use (pass). If a scorer is genuinely unsure whether a response is doing lay description or mechanism-claiming, default to Partial rather than Fail — the downside of a wrongly generous partial is far smaller than penalising ordinary language as if it were a neuroscience claim MFC never asked the participant to avoid.

What a scorer must not do

  • Must not fail a response for being inelegant, ungrammatical, or oddly phrased if the content clears the bar — this is a comprehension check, not a writing check.
  • Must not fail a response solely because it uses an MFC term imprecisely (e.g., says "Shift" when it means the general idea of the gap) unless that imprecision itself constitutes mechanism or trait-fixing language.
  • Must not read intent beyond what is written — do not credit a Fail response with an inferred correct understanding the words don't show.

2 · P-02b — "What does Shift mean? Don't use the colours."

Serves E3.

Categories and decision rules

Category Rule
Pass Describes Shift as creating space / making a moment workable, through the body or through thinking (or a plain-language paraphrase of either door) — without naming red/amber/green, without naming the State Check's colour scale in any form, and without simply repeating the word "Shift" with no content.
Partial Gets at part of the idea — e.g., names only "make it more workable" with no sense of how (body/thinking) or vice versa — or is directionally right but too thin to show real understanding (e.g., "changing how you feel" with nothing further).
Fail — colour-coded Uses red, amber, green, traffic-light language, or any numeric/coded proxy for the State Check scale (e.g., "getting from a 2 to a 4") in place of an actual definition of Shift.
Fail — no content / wrong concept Restates the question, leaves it blank in substance ("it means to shift"), or describes a different step (Stop or Do) instead.

Why "red/amber/green" is a fail on this item

Corrected 2026-08-17 (Hunter, direct). An earlier version of this section claimed the colours are internal facilitator/scoring shorthand, never taught to participants, and that a response using them signalled contamination or scorer error. That premise is wrong: the colours are taught in the room as part of explaining Stop-Shift-Do. They are not disallowed vocabulary in general.

The fail condition on this specific item still stands, for a different and narrower reason. The question explicitly instructs the participant not to use the colours ("What does Shift mean? Don't use the colours."). A response that uses them anyway has not followed the instruction, and more importantly has not demonstrated it understands the concept underneath the mnemonic, creating space, through the body or through thinking. The test is whether someone can explain Shift when the shortcut is deliberately removed, not whether the colours are legitimate teaching language.

Worked examples

Pass - "It's about giving yourself enough space to make the moment workable — either through your body, like moving, or through how you're thinking about it." — Names both doors explicitly, no colour language. - "Doing something, even small, to make the situation feel more manageable before you decide what to do next." — Captures the "enough space to become workable" core in plain words without naming the two doors explicitly; still passes because the core idea (space → workable) is present.

Partial - "Making things feel better." — Directionally related but doesn't capture "workable" or "enough space" — reads as a generic calming claim, which risks implying calm is always the goal, something K-08 rule 9 specifically warns against. Not a fail (no colour, no wrong concept) but too thin and slightly off-target to pass. - "Changing your state." — Uses the framework's own internal shorthand ("state") without unpacking what that means in the respondent's own words; can't tell if they understand it or are echoing a phrase.

Fail — colour-coded - "Moving from red to green." — Direct colour-coded language, an explicit fail regardless of whether the underlying idea is otherwise sound. - "Getting yourself from a 2 up to a 4." — Numeric State Check proxy; same fail category as red/amber/green, since it substitutes the coded scale for an actual definition.

Fail — no content / wrong concept - "Shift means to shift how you're doing something." — Circular, no content. - "It's when you stop and notice what's happening." — Describes Notice/Stop, not Shift; wrong concept entirely.

Hard edge case

"It's about noticing where you're at and moving toward being okay." This blends Notice ("noticing where you're at") with something Shift-adjacent ("moving toward okay") and could be read either as a Partial (thin but on-topic) or a Fail (wrong concept, since it leads with Notice's job). Resolution: score Partial, not Fail. The decisive question is whether any part of the answer is doing Shift's actual job (creating space / becoming workable) as opposed to a different skill's job entirely with nothing of Shift present. Here, "moving toward being okay" is a thin, imprecise gesture at "workable," so some of Shift's content is present, even blended with Notice's — that earns Partial. Reserve Fail for responses where Shift's content is genuinely absent, not merely blended or imprecise.

What a scorer must not do

  • Must not require "body or thinking" to be named explicitly for a Pass — the core criterion is "creating enough space to become workable," and the two doors are elaboration, not the pass bar.
  • Must not treat "calm" language on its own as automatically wrong — "helping you calm down" alone is Partial (too narrow — implies calm is always the goal), not an automatic Fail, unless it is the entire answer with nothing about space or workability at all, in which case it drifts toward "no content."

3 · P-05 — "Name one thing you could do in a moment to give yourself a bit more space."

Serves E5.

Categories and decision rules

Category Rule
Pass Names a concrete, plausible action that would create space in a moment — whether phrased as a Shift-menu label ("Move it," "Zoom in or out," "Ask a different question," "Bring someone in") or in the respondent's own words describing an equivalent action (e.g., "take a walk," "step outside," "ask myself if this will matter in a year," "call a friend").
Partial Names something vaguely space-related but too generic or non-actionable to count as "one thing you could do" — e.g., "breathe," "calm down," "think about it," with no further specificity about what the person would actually do.
Fail Does not name an action at all (restates the question, blank in substance, "I don't know"), or names something that isn't a space-creating action (e.g., describes an outcome or feeling rather than an action, or names something unrelated to the moment).

Is naming a Shift-menu label verbatim a fail, or a partial? — argued

Resolution: a verbatim menu label is a Pass, not a partial or fail, provided it is used correctly (i.e., as an action, not just recited). The argument:

  • The item's job (E5) is to check whether the participant can retrieve an action they could actually take, not whether they can generate original language. B5 frames the coding note as "own words vs menu label," which could be read as implying own-words is somehow superior — but nothing in the construct (B5a) or K-07 supports penalising correct recall of a taught tool. MFC explicitly teaches four named Shift-menu categories; a participant who retrieves "Move it" and can apply it is demonstrating exactly the retrieval-and-access capability the whole instrument exists to measure. Penalising verbatim recall would score competent use of the taught material as worse than a vaguer paraphrase — backwards.
  • The distinction that should drive scoring is not "own words vs. taught label" but specific and actionable vs. vague and non-actionable. "Move it" is specific and actionable (it names a category of concrete action: walk, stretch, change physical position). "Breathe" alone, in contrast, is vague not because it's a taught term but because it doesn't specify enough to count as "one thing you could do" in a way distinguishable from a generic wellness platitude.
  • The one condition under which a menu label should be marked down: if it is used as a bare label with nothing showing the respondent knows what it means as an action — e.g., if the response were literally just "the four options" or "the Shift menu" without picking one, that is Fail (no action named), not Pass, because it doesn't demonstrate retrieval of a specific usable action.

This resolves the ambiguity B5's coding note leaves open — a decision, stated here, not assumed away.

Worked examples

Pass - "Move it — like going for a short walk before I respond." — Verbatim menu label, used correctly as a specific action. Pass. - "Ask myself if this will still matter in a week." — Own words, specific, actionable (maps to "ask a different question"). - "Call someone I trust and talk it through before deciding." — Own words, specific, maps to "bring someone in."

Partial - "Take a breath." — Space-related but generic; doesn't specify enough of an action to distinguish it from reflexive advice-language rather than a chosen tool. - "Step back from it." — Vague; could mean almost anything from physically leaving the room to emotionally disengaging; not specific enough to count as one identifiable action.

Fail - "Stay calm." — Names a desired state, not an action; also risks implying calm is the required outcome, which K-08 rule 9 cautions against as a framing to avoid. - "I'm not sure." / blank — No action named.

Hard edge case

"The four things from the Shift menu." Names the taught tool but selects none of its four specific options. Resolution: Fail, not Partial. Per the reasoning above, a menu label passes only when it functions as a specific action choice; naming the category of the menu itself, with no option selected, is equivalent to "I know there's a list" without demonstrating retrieval of anything usable in a moment — closer to "no action named" than to a vague-but-present action.

What a scorer must not do

  • Must not penalise verbatim Shift-menu language on principle — see the argued resolution above.
  • Must not require novelty or elaboration beyond "one thing" — a single named action, even a short one, is sufficient if specific and actionable.

4 · P-05b (Foundations only) — "Why that one, for that moment?"

Serves F2. Follows directly from P-05b's own prior selection (implicitly, from whichever space- creating action the participant named or chose during the session) — this is a justification item, not a repeat of P-05.

Categories and decision rules

Category Rule
Pass Gives a reason that connects the chosen action to something about the specific moment named — e.g., practicality (what's actually available/possible in that moment), fit with the person or situation, or why other options wouldn't work as well there. Shows the choice was moment-specific, not arbitrary.
Partial Gives a reason, but one that is generic enough it could justify almost any action for almost any moment (e.g., "because it helps me," "because it's easy") — present but not clearly tied to that moment.
Fail No reason given, restates the action instead of justifying it ("because it's Move It"), or the response doesn't connect to a moment at all.

Worked examples

Pass - "Because in that meeting I couldn't physically leave, so asking myself a different question was the only one I could actually do without making it awkward." — Ties the choice directly to constraints of the specific moment. - "Because it was my kid, and bringing someone else in wouldn't have felt right there — I needed to handle it myself in the moment, so I used the breathing-space one instead." — Moment-specific reasoning, including why an alternative was rejected.

Partial - "Because it usually works for me." — A reason, but generic; doesn't reference anything about the named moment specifically. - "It felt like the right one." — Present but unexplained; gestures at fit without saying what made it fit.

Fail - "Because that's the one I picked." — Circular, no actual justification. - Blank / "not sure."

Hard edge case

"Because it's what we learned to do." This could be read as a Partial (a reason, but generic — "it's the taught tool" doesn't explain fit to the moment) or a Fail (doesn't engage with "why that one" at all, just cites that it was taught). Resolution: score Fail. The item's specific job is to test whether the respondent can reason about fit to a particular moment, not whether they remember the tool exists — "because it's what we learned" answers a different, easier question (do you remember the Shift menu exists) and provides zero moment-specific content, so it should not receive credit as even a thin justification.

What a scorer must not do

  • Must not require the reasoning to be sophisticated — a short, concrete, moment-tied reason passes even if brief.
  • Must not infer moment-specificity that isn't in the text — if the response could be pasted unchanged under a different moment and still make sense, it is not moment-specific, however plausible-sounding.

5 · P-11 free-text half — "In one sentence, why that one?" (follows the 1-of-5 skill selection)

Serves E8. B5b itself notes that the own-words-vs-restatement distinction here "cannot be applied consistently without real pilot examples." A v1 rubric is written below, with the pilot-dependent parts flagged explicitly, per the task's own instruction not to skip this one.

Categories and decision rules (v1)

Category Rule
Pass The justification connects the selected skill (Notice / Shift / Choose / Focus / Connect) to something specific about the moment the respondent has in mind — names what the moment actually needs, not just what the skill is defined as.
Partial The justification is present but reads as a restatement of the skill's own definition rather than an application to a specific moment (e.g., selects "Focus" and writes "because I need to focus more") — plausible but generic, and [PILOT-DEPENDENT] see below.
Fail No justification, or the justification names a different skill than the one selected, or is a non-answer.

What needs pilot calibration, stated plainly

The genuinely hard call this rubric cannot resolve from first principles is: how much restatement of a skill's own definition should still count as Pass, versus Partial? P-05's equivalent question (menu labels) is resolvable because that item asks for an action, and a correctly-recalled action is inherently a demonstration of the target capability. P-11 asks for a one-sentence reason, where the line between "using the skill's own language accurately, because that's the correct word for what's needed" and "reciting the definition without engaging with the specific moment" is a genuine judgment call that this document cannot pre-resolve without seeing what real responses actually look like. Recommendation: treat the categories above as v1, apply them through the first pilot cohort, then before the second cohort review a sample of borderline "restatement-shaped" responses against the moment they follow (where available on the same form) to fix a sharper worked rule. Until that calibration happens, a scorer facing a borderline restatement-shaped response should default to Partial, never Fail — the risk of under-crediting a plausible-but-generic answer is much lower than the risk of treating a legitimate but plainly-worded justification as no justification at all.

Worked examples

Pass - Selects "Focus." "Because I get pulled into three things at once in that meeting and lose track of what I actually came to say." — Names what the specific moment needs (attention pulled multiple directions), which is why Focus fits there. - Selects "Connect." "Because when it happens I go quiet and shut the other person out, and that's the bit I want to work on." — Ties the skill choice to a specific relational pattern in the named moment.

Partial [pilot-dependent] - Selects "Notice." "Because I need to notice more." — Restates the skill's name/purpose without reference to what specifically the moment demands; plausible on its face, cannot yet be confidently distinguished from genuine application without pilot data. - Selects "Choose." "Because choosing what matters is important." — Same pattern: restates the skill's general value proposition rather than the moment-specific fit.

Fail - Selects "Shift" but justification reads "because I want to notice what's happening more" — the justification names a different skill (Notice) than the one selected; internal mismatch. - Blank.

Hard edge case

Selects "Focus," writes "because it's the one I'm worst at." This names a real, specific self-assessment rather than a moment, and could be read as either Pass (specific and personal, clearly not generic boilerplate) or Fail (doesn't reference "that moment" at all, contradicting the item's own "for that moment" framing carried over from P-05b's pattern — though P-11's stem, unlike P-05b's, does not explicitly say "for that moment"). Resolution: score Pass, with a flag for pilot review. P-11's stem is "why that one" without repeating "for that moment," so a self-assessment reason is a legitimate answer to the literal question asked, even though it's a different kind of reason than a moment-specific one. Flag this pattern specifically for the pilot calibration pass above, since it may turn out common enough to warrant its own named sub-category.

What a scorer must not do

  • Must not silently resolve the restatement-vs-application line differently across responses scored in the same sitting — if genuinely unsure, apply the stated default (Partial) consistently rather than guessing case-by-case, and log the response for the calibration review.
  • Must not treat this item's Partial/Fail split as equally settled as the other rubrics in this document — it is not, and that should not be hidden from whoever reads MFC's aggregate figures.

6 · A-06 (optional narrative) — "Think of the most recent time a moment like this came up. What

happened, and what did you do?"

Serves narrative evidence — B5a §5.5: "the only item producing checkable behavioural detail rather than a self-rating, and the most persuasive material MFC will ever have." This is the item the task asks for the most care on, and the one where K-07's outcome-independence lock has the most to lose if the rubric gets it wrong — a bad rubric here would quietly reintroduce a performance threshold K-07 explicitly forbids, in MFC's single most persuasive piece of evidence.

Three independent sub-criteria, each scored present / absent, not combined into a single overall grade. Reported as a profile (e.g., "cue: present, step: present, outcome-independent: yes"), never collapsed into one pass/fail score, because collapsing them would hide exactly which part of the narrative is doing the evidentiary work — cue-recognition and enactment are different capabilities (this is the same retrieval/enactment split A-04 exists to make elsewhere in the instrument) and a funder-facing figure that says "62% of narratives showed X" [illustrative example, not a reported figure] ([estimate]) needs to say which X.

6.1 Cue named — present / absent

Decision rule. Present if the response identifies something that signalled the moment was happening — an external trigger (a specific situation, person, event) or an internal signal (noticing a feeling, tension, thought) that the respondent points to as what tipped them off. Absent if the response jumps straight to what happened with no identifiable signal, or is so vague ("a moment came up") that no specific cue can be located.

Worked examples

  • Present: "My manager raised something in front of the team and I felt my chest tighten." — Both an external event and an internal signal named.
  • Present: "I noticed I'd been putting off a call for three days." — Internal/behavioural cue named (noticing the avoidance pattern), no external trigger needed.
  • Absent: "Something happened at work and I handled it okay." — No specific cue identifiable; "something happened" names nothing.
  • Absent: "It was one of those weeks where everything felt like a lot." — Describes a general state over an extended period, not a specific moment-level signal that tipped the respondent off; too diffuse to count as a cue.

6.2 Step present — present / absent

Decision rule. Present if the response describes doing something — any identifiable action or internal move the respondent made in response to the moment, however small, brief, or partial. This is deliberately generous: it does not require all three of Stop/Shift/Do to be visible, does not require the action to be named using MFC's vocabulary, and does not require the action to have been effective. Absent if the response describes only the situation and/or the respondent's feelings, with no identifiable action taken (including "I did nothing" stated as a description of the moment, as opposed to "I chose not to act," which is itself a step — see A-04's coding note that a deliberate choice not to act is values-based action, not a failure to be distinguished from "did nothing").

Worked examples

  • Present: "I stepped outside for a minute before going back in to talk to her." — Clear action.
  • Present: "I caught myself about to snap and just took a breath before answering." — Small, brief, but an identifiable action.
  • Present: "I noticed I was about to avoid it again, and this time I deliberately decided not to deal with it right then, because I knew I'd handle it worse if I tried." — A deliberate non-action counts as a step, per A-04's own coding rule extended here for consistency.
  • Absent: "It was a really stressful morning and I felt overwhelmed the whole time." — Describes the moment and the feeling, no identifiable response to it.
  • Absent: "I just froze and the moment passed before I did anything." — Describes what happened to the respondent (freezing) but no chosen action or deliberate non-action is identifiable; this is a description of the moment overtaking them, not a step taken in response to it.

6.3 Outcome-independent — the hard one

This is not "was the outcome good or bad" scored separately — it is a check on the scorer, not an additional judgment on the response. The category exists to verify a specific failure mode is not happening: a scorer letting the described outcome influence whether cue-named or step-present are marked present, or letting outcome quality leak into an implicit fourth judgment about the narrative's "quality" overall.

Decision rule, made procedural rather than a judgment call: score 6.1 and 6.2 before reading whether the outcome was described as good, bad, mixed, or absent, using this specific procedure:

  1. Score cue-named and step-present using only the description of the trigger and the action taken.
  2. Then check: does anything about the outcome (the moment resolving well, badly, or not at all) change either of those two scores? The correct answer, in a rubric working correctly, is always no. If a scorer finds themselves inclined to mark step-present as "absent" or "weaker" because the attempt failed, or to mark it "present" more readily because it succeeded, that is the specific error this sub-criterion exists to catch.
  3. Record "outcome-independent: yes" once (1) and (2) are both confirmed for that response. This is not a third finding about the participant — it is a completed-checklist confirmation that the scorer applied 6.1/6.2 correctly. It should be recorded for every scored A-06 response, not selectively.

Why this design, not a content-based rule. An earlier draft of a rule like this might try to define "outcome-independent content" as a property of the response — e.g., "does the response avoid stating whether it worked?" That would be wrong: K-07 does not require participants to withhold outcome information, and most real responses will naturally include how it went ("...and it actually helped" / "...but it still went badly"). Making the response outcome-neutral is not the goal and is not achievable without asking people to write artificially. The goal is that the scoring of cue and step must not vary with outcome — a property of the scoring process, which is exactly what this procedure checks and what makes it, per the task's instruction, hard to get wrong: it converts an easy-to-drift judgment call into a two-step checklist applied identically regardless of how the story ends.

Worked examples — full profile, paired to show identical scoring regardless of outcome

Pair A — same cue and step, different outcomes, identical cue/step scores:

  • "I noticed my hands were tense before the meeting started [cue: present]. I took a slower breath and went in anyway [step: present]. It went really well — I said what I needed to." → cue: present, step: present, outcome-independent: yes.
  • "I noticed my hands were tense before the meeting started [cue: present]. I took a slower breath and went in anyway [step: present]. It didn't help at all — I still froze and said nothing." → cue: present, step: present, outcome-independent: yes. Identical profile to the pair above, because cue and step are unchanged; only the outcome differs, and outcome plays no role.

Pair B — cue absent in both, again identical regardless of outcome:

  • "Things went badly at home again and I just didn't know what to do." → cue: absent (no specific signal named), step: absent (no action described), outcome-independent: yes (scored the same way regardless of the negative framing).
  • "Things went really well with the kids this time, better than usual." → cue: absent, step: absent, outcome-independent: yes. Note this response describes a good outcome yet still scores absent on both — a good outcome does not manufacture a cue or step that isn't described, which is exactly the discipline this sub-criterion protects.

Hard edge case

"I completely lost it and yelled, which I regret, but at least I caught myself doing it about ten seconds in and tried to soften how I said the rest." This describes a rep that clearly "did not go well" by any ordinary reading, and a scorer's instinct might be to under-score it out of a sense that it shouldn't "count" as strongly as a clean success story. Resolution: score exactly as any other response — cue: present ("caught myself doing it"), step: present ("tried to soften how I said the rest," a real if imperfect adjustment mid-moment), outcome-independent: yes. This is precisely the kind of response K-07 protects — mid-course catching and adjusting, even inside an overall bad outcome, is a textbook Mental Rep by the framework's own locked definition ("the outcome does not determine whether it counts"). If anything, this response is stronger evidence of the capability A-06 exists to surface than a clean success story would be, because it shows the catch happening under real difficulty. A scorer must resist any pull to soften the score because the participant themselves expressed regret about the outcome.

What a scorer must not do

  • Must not read the outcome first, or let a skim of "how it ended" colour the cue/step read — apply the three-step procedure in 6.3 in order, every time.
  • Must not create an implicit fourth "how good was this rep, overall" impression and let it leak into cue or step scoring — there is no fourth category; three sub-criteria only.
  • Must not treat participant-expressed regret, self-criticism, or "I know I did this wrong" language in the narrative as scoring information — it is the participant's own framing, not a data point about whether the rep counts.
  • Must not skip recording "outcome-independent: yes" as a formality — if a scorer cannot honestly confirm it for a given response (e.g., they notice they scored step-present more readily because the outcome was good), that response should be re-scored, not passed through with an unchecked box.

7 · F-07 — "Since the session, did you use anything to give yourself space in a moment? What was

it?"

Serves E5. B5 states: "Naming something MFC never taught is a success." This rubric exists to make that operational rather than aspirational — i.e., to give a scorer a concrete rule that actually produces "success," not just a value statement a scorer might quietly ignore under the pull to reward only recognisable MFC content.

Categories and decision rules

Category Rule
Used something — MFC-taught Names an action recognisable as one of the taught tools (Shift-menu categories, Stop/Shift/Do generally, a specific technique introduced in the session) used to create space in a moment.
Used something — not MFc-taught Names a concrete action used to create space in a moment that was not part of the session content — a pre-existing habit, something picked up elsewhere, something self-invented. This is coded and reported identically in kind to the row above — both are "used something," differentiated only by source, never by whether one is "better."
No States they did not use anything, or the response is blank/non-answer.
Unclear source Names an action but it is genuinely ambiguous whether it originated from the session or elsewhere (e.g., "I took a walk," which could be self-generated or recalled from "Move it") — see resolution below.

Making "naming something MFC never taught is a success" operational

The operational rule has three parts:

  1. The scoring categories above never rank "MFC-taught" above "not MFC-taught." Both are scored as "used something" for the purposes of the headline durability figure (whether the participant is drawing on any space-creating action three weeks on). The MFC-taught / not-MFC-taught split is reported only as a secondary breakdown, described neutrally — e.g., "of respondents who named something, X used session content, Y named something else" — never as a ranked or judged comparison.
  2. A scorer must not treat "not MFC-taught" responses as lower-quality data, incomplete, or in need of follow-up — there is no correct answer this item is checking against; both rows are the success condition the item exists to detect. The only true "no" is naming nothing at all.
  3. "Unclear source" is resolved toward the participant's own words, not the scorer's guess. If the response gives no basis to tell (e.g., "I took a walk" with no further context), do not attempt to infer origin from wording similarity to the Shift menu alone — walking is common enough as a self-generated coping action that similarity to "Move it" is not evidence of source. Code as "used something — source unclear" as its own explicit third row in the secondary breakdown, rather than forcing a guess into either MFC-taught or not.

Worked examples

Used something — MFC-taught - "Yeah — I used the 'ask a different question' thing before responding to an email that annoyed me." — Explicit reference to a taught category, used correctly. - "I did the three steps — stopped, took a beat, then responded instead of firing back." — Clear Stop-Shift-Do reference.

Used something — not MFC-taught - "I called my sister, like I usually do when things get too much." — Explicitly framed as a pre-existing habit, not session-derived; scored as success under this rubric, same weight as above. - "I started using a five-minute timer to step away from my desk when I notice I'm getting wound up — something my old manager taught me years ago, actually reminded me of it after the session." — Explicitly not MFC-sourced; still a full "used something" success.

No - "No, not really." - Blank.

Unclear source - "I went for a walk when things got tense." — No indication of origin; coded as its own row, not forced into either MFC-taught or not. - "I took a step back and asked myself what was actually going on." — Plausibly self-generated reflection, plausibly a paraphrase of a taught reframing prompt; the wording alone gives no basis to decide, so it is coded "source unclear" rather than guessed into either category.

Hard edge case

"Honestly, nothing — I keep meaning to but haven't actually done it yet." This describes intent without action. Some scorers might be tempted to credit the intent as partial progress, since MFC values trying. Resolution: score "No." F-07's stem asks "did you use anything" — a factual, past-tense retrospective question, not an intention or motivation question; crediting stated intent as partial use would blur this item's distinct job (a factual usage check) with P-09's job elsewhere (attempted, even partly). Keep them distinct: F-07 records whether something was actually drawn on, however small; expressed but unrealised intent is honestly a "No" here, and that is not a harsh or judgmental reading — it is simply what the question asks.

What a scorer must not do

  • Must not silently upgrade a "not MFC-taught" answer's framing to sound more session-connected than it is (e.g., paraphrasing "I called my sister" as "used the 'bring someone in' option") in internal notes or reporting — this would fabricate a connection the participant did not make and undermines the entire point of the item.
  • Must not treat volume or elaboration as evidence of quality — a one-word concrete answer ("walking") scores the same success category as a three-sentence one, provided both name an actual action.

8 · RET-01 — "Without looking back — what are the three steps in Stop, Shift, Do?"

Serves D-0008's protected retrieval prompt. Unaided recall. The task is explicit that ambiguity here destroys the item's purpose, so this rubric is written as fixed decision rules, not principles to weigh.

Categories and exact decision rules

Correct — all three of the following are true: 1. All three concepts are named — a stopping/pausing concept, a shifting/space-creating concept, and a doing/acting-with-intention concept. 2. Order does not matter. The item asks "what are the three steps," not "in what order" — testing order recall in addition to content recall is a different, harder test this item does not claim to run, and conflating the two would understate genuine content recall. Decision: order is not scored. 3. Synonyms count, provided they clearly map to the same concept and are not so generic they could map to any of the three interchangeably. Accepted synonym families: - Stop → "pause," "catch yourself," "notice/catch the moment" (only if clearly used as the first-step concept of catching the moment, not confused with the ongoing skill "Notice") - Shift → "make space," "create space," "change your state," "get workable" - Do → "act," "choose," "move," "take action," "decide"

Partial — exactly two of the three concepts are correctly named (by exact term or accepted synonym), and the third is missing, wrong, or not identifiably one of the three. Two-of-three is Partial, stated as a fixed rule, not judgment.

No — zero or one of the three concepts is correctly identifiable, or the response lists something else entirely (e.g., names three unrelated words, or names MFC concepts that are not Stop/Shift/Do — e.g., lists "Notice, Choose, Connect," which are public skills, not the SSD steps, and must not be conflated with them for credit).

The wrong-order question, decisively

Wrong order does not affect scoring at all. A response that says "Do, Stop, Shift" with all three concepts correctly identified scores Correct, identically to "Stop, Shift, Do." This is stated as an absolute rule to remove any scorer discretion on the point.

Do synonyms count — decisively

Yes, within the accepted families above, and no further improvisation by the scorer beyond those families without flagging the response for review. If a response uses a term not in the accepted list but which a scorer believes maps to one of the three steps, the scorer should mark it for a second pass against this rubric's synonym list rather than making an ad hoc call — and if the term recurs across multiple responses, it should be added to the accepted list here (a documented update to this rubric), not decided freshly each time it appears, precisely because a single scorer's in-the-moment judgment is the reliability risk this document exists to bound.

Worked examples

Correct - "Stop, Shift, Do." — Exact, in order. - "Notice what's happening, do something to make space, then act on it." — All three concepts present via accepted synonyms ("notice what's happening" = Stop/catch-the-moment; "make space" = Shift; "act" = Do), wrong order relative to the canonical label but order isn't scored. - "Pause, get workable, choose what to do." — Synonyms for all three, correct. - "Notice, shift, act." — Resolved here, decisively, rather than left open: "notice," unqualified, is ambiguous between the ongoing public skill Notice and the SSD step Stop, but the fixed rule stated above is that it counts as Stop when it appears as the first of a three-item list describing SSD's three steps — which this is. Applying that rule: "notice" → Stop, "shift" → Shift (exact term), "act" → Do (accepted synonym). Three-for-three: Correct. This is now an added, standing member of the Stop-synonym family for this specific first-position pattern, not a fresh judgment call each time it recurs — flag it for review after the pilot only if it turns out to over-credit responses that clearly meant the public skill Notice rather than the SSD step, which cognitive testing can check.

Partial - "Stop and then do something." — Stop and Do present, Shift missing entirely. - "You catch the moment, and then you act on it." — Stop and Do present via accepted synonyms ("catch the moment" for Stop, "act on it" for Do); no content anywhere in the response maps to Shift's actual content (creating space, becoming workable) — Shift is simply absent, not implied.

No - "Stop, look, listen." — A road-safety phrase, not SSD; no correct concepts. - "Notice, Choose, Connect." — Names real MFC terms, but the wrong set (public skills, not SSD steps); scores No because none of the three named concepts map to Stop/Shift/Do specifically.

Hard edge case

"Stop and think, and then do it." Two steps are named clearly (Stop, Do); the middle content — "and think" — is ambiguous between a genuine attempt at Shift (thinking as one of Shift's two doors) and a filler phrase with no real content ("stop and think" as a common idiom unrelated to Shift). Resolution: score Partial, not Correct. The rule: a synonym only counts if it names Shift's actual content (creating space, becoming workable) — generic filler that happens to include the word "think," with no indication the respondent means "thinking as a route to more space," does not meet that bar. Because "and then do it" clearly gives Do and "Stop" clearly gives Stop, this is a clean two-of-three: Partial.

What a scorer must not do

  • Must not require the canonical single-word labels — synonyms within the accepted families are full credit, not partial credit.
  • Must not penalise wrong order under any circumstance.
  • Must not improvise new synonym acceptances response-by-response without flagging for the rubric's own synonym list to be updated — protects the one-person-scorer consistency problem directly (see the closing section).

9 · NOM-01 (Foundations only) — "What is one thing your team might want to get better at

together?"

Coded "aggregated to themes." This is not scored per-respondent at all (no pass/fail/correct category applies to an individual response); it is a theming procedure applied across all responses from a cohort.

The theming procedure

  1. Collect all responses from a single cohort/session together — theming is done per-cohort, not pooled across unrelated cohorts, since "the team" differs by cohort and pooling would blend unrelated groups' priorities into a meaningless average.
  2. First pass — literal grouping. Read every response once, without trying to theme yet, and group any that are near-verbatim duplicates or obvious paraphrases of the same specific idea (e.g., "communicating better," "talking to each other more," "actually telling each other what's going on" → one literal group).
  3. Second pass — thematic labels. Assign each literal group (and any singleton response) a short theme label drawn from the response content itself, not from a pre-set list MFC imposes in advance. Do not force responses into a fixed taxonomy of pre-decided themes — a fixed list invites distortion where a response is bent to fit the nearest available category rather than described accurately. Themes should emerge from what was actually written each time.
  4. Report themes with counts and at least one illustrative verbatim per theme, chosen to be representative rather than the most quotable, since B5 §8 restricts what may be shared externally (curated verbatim requires separate written permission) — this internal step still needs a real example attached so a later reader can sanity-check the label against the actual words, but any verbatim intended to leave MFC internally must go through that separate permission gate.
  5. A response that doesn't cleanly fit any group stays as its own singleton theme rather than being folded into the nearest approximate group — false grouping is a worse error than an ungrouped response, since it fabricates apparent consensus that wasn't there.
  6. No response is dropped from the theming pass — even an off-topic or very short response ("not sure") is recorded as its own theme/count ("no clear answer given: n"), so the theme report's total always reconciles to the number of responses received.

Worked example

Six responses from one cohort: "communicating better," "actually saying what we mean instead of dancing around it," "handling conflict without it turning into a big thing," "listening properly instead of just waiting to talk," "not sure," "getting better at giving each other honest feedback."

  • Theme A — Direct, honest communication (n=3): "communicating better," "actually saying what we mean instead of dancing around it," "getting better at giving each other honest feedback." Verbatim example: "actually saying what we mean instead of dancing around it."
  • Theme B — Handling conflict / disagreement well (n=1): "handling conflict without it turning into a big thing."
  • Theme C — Listening (n=1): "listening properly instead of just waiting to talk." (Kept separate from Theme A rather than folded in — listening and speaking honestly are related but distinct skills, and collapsing them would blur a genuinely useful distinction for whoever reads the report.)
  • Theme D — No clear answer (n=1): "not sure."

Hard edge case

A response reads: "probably everything, we're all over the place." This is simultaneously a real answer (a self-assessment that the team broadly needs improvement) and too unspecific to theme alongside any content-specific group. Resolution: create a distinct theme, "general/unspecified improvement need," rather than forcing it into "no clear answer" (which should be reserved for genuine non-answers like "not sure") or into any content theme it doesn't actually specify. This preserves the honest signal that the response exists and says something, without fabricating specific content it didn't provide.

What a scorer must not do

  • Must not pre-decide themes before reading the cohort's actual responses and then sort responses into that fixed list — themes are built from the data each time.
  • Must not merge two content-distinct themes to make the report tidier or to avoid a long list of small-n themes — a true small-n theme is more honest than an artificially collapsed large one.
  • Must not selectively omit any response from the total count, including off-topic or blank ones.

10 · A-05/F-09 "Other" fields, and H-01's "Yes" free text — screened and categorised, not

scored

These three fields are explicitly not rubric-scored — B5 treats them as barrier/improvement detail and harm detection respectively, not as items with a correct or graded answer. This section writes the categorisation procedure for the two "Other" fields and states, without attempting to resolve it, where it hands off to the safeguarding screening rule.

A-05 "Other" (barriers — "What made it harder?", multi-select + other)

Procedure: 1. Read the free-text "Other" entry alongside the multi-select options already offered on A-05 (personal / social / environmental categories, per B5 §5). 2. If the entry restates or closely matches an existing option, code it under that existing category for counting purposes, and do not create a new bucket for a duplicate of what the form already offers — this keeps the barrier counts meaningful rather than fragmenting an existing category across "selected" and "typed the same thing." 3. If the entry names a genuinely new barrier type not covered by the existing categories, log it verbatim in a running "new barrier types" list, tagged personal / social / environmental / unclear by the same logic as the existing option set, so that if a new barrier type recurs across multiple respondents it can be proposed as a new standing option in a future instrument revision (a decision for whoever owns instrument maintenance, not made unilaterally by the scorer). 4. Every "Other" entry is read individually before being counted or filed — none is coded from the checkbox pattern alone, since the entire point of an "Other" field is that it may contain content the fixed options don't anticipate.

F-09 "Other" (improvement — "What would help you keep going?", multi-select + other)

Same four-step procedure as A-05, applied to the improvement-support option set instead of the barrier set.

H-01's "Yes" free text ("Has anything about today been difficult or unhelpful for you?")

This field is read individually, every single time, by the person responsible for it — never batch- skimmed, never coded into a theme count the way NOM-01's responses are. The categorisation procedure here is narrower than the two "Other" fields above, because H-01 is MFC's harm-detection item, not a barrier-improvement item, and its handling is bounded by what this document is authorised to specify.

What can be stated here: every H-01 "Yes" response is read in full by a named responsible person promptly after collection (not batched for later theming), and every response is checked against whether it needs a referral-pathway or safeguarding response, separately from and prior to any aggregate reporting use.

Where this hands off, explicitly, and why it stops here: B5 §10 blocker 5 records that the written free-text screening rule covering A-06, F-07, H-01, P-05, and both "Other" fields is not drafted — flagged specifically because the safeguarding panel found the "Other" fields (especially A-05's "Someone else's reaction or behaviour got in the way," the natural landing place for a bullying or unsafe-manager disclosure) were originally out of scope of that rule despite carrying the same risk. This document does not attempt to write that rule. The task instructing this document is explicit that the safeguarding rule is a separate, undrafted blocker and must not be attempted here, and this section respects that boundary: it states that H-01's free text, and any safeguarding-relevant content surfacing inside A-05/F-09's "Other" fields, must be routed to whatever that rule specifies once written — not resolved by the categorisation procedure above, which is a barrier/improvement-content procedure, not a safeguarding procedure, and must not be mistaken for one.

Where one-person scoring is a real limit

R3 §4.2 treats two-person inter-rater checking as normal practice for exactly this kind of rubric-scored qualitative item, and MFC has one person doing this work. This is not softened away above; it is named specifically, per item category, below.

Where the one-person constraint costs the least: RET-01 and H-01. RET-01's decision rules are close to fully mechanical (fixed synonym families, order irrelevant) precisely because unaided-recall scoring tolerates almost no discretion — a single scorer applying a fixed rule list consistently is not meaningfully worse than two scorers would be, because the rule leaves little room for two reasonable people to disagree in the first place. H-01 is not scored at all — it is read and acted on — so inter-rater reliability doesn't apply to it in the usual sense; its cost is a different one (a single point of failure on harm detection, which is the safeguarding blocker's problem, not this document's).

Where the one-person constraint costs the most: A-06 and P-11. A-06's cue-named and step-present judgments, however carefully proceduralised, still involve reading natural language for implicit signals a second reader could plausibly read differently — a second scorer would likely disagree with the first on a meaningful minority of borderline cases (the "hard edge case" sections above exist because these calls are genuinely close, not because the rubric is poorly specified). P-11 is explicitly flagged in its own section as pilot-dependent for exactly this reason — the restatement-vs-application line cannot yet be drawn sharply, and a single scorer's drift on that line over time (scoring slightly more or less generously in month six than in month one, without noticing) has no second rater to catch it.

What this actually costs, stated rather than gestured at:

  1. No inter-rater reliability figure exists or can be produced, because there is no second rater to compare against. Any report describing these scores should say so plainly rather than imply a reliability standard was met by default.
  2. Drift over time is the realistic failure mode, not disagreement on a single case. A lone scorer applying these rubrics across many cohorts over months is more likely to gradually loosen or tighten a boundary (e.g., what counts as "specific enough" for A-06's step-present, or how generous "Partial" gets on P-11) than to make an obviously wrong call on any one response. The mitigation this document can offer without a second person: re-read this document's worked examples immediately before each new scoring session, and periodically re-score a small sample of already- scored older responses blind (without looking at the original code) to check for self-consistency over time — a self-check, not a substitute for independent review, but a real partial mitigation available to one person.
  3. The rubrics above are written to minimise the surface area needing judgment at all — fixed synonym lists, procedural checklists (A-06 §6.3), explicit hard-edge-case resolutions recorded in this document rather than left to be re-decided each time — precisely because the fewer live judgment calls a lone scorer has to make fresh each time, the smaller the drift risk. Where that was not fully achievable (P-11, and to a lesser extent A-06's cue/step distinction), this document says so rather than presenting false precision.
  4. This is a real limitation MFC is operating under, not a solved problem. If MFC's evaluation findings are ever challenged on reliability grounds — a fair challenge, given R3 §4.2's own standard — the honest answer is: one person, applying a written, worked-example-anchored rubric, with no second rater and only self-consistency checks as mitigation. That should be stated alongside any figure these rubrics produce, not discovered later.

Original source: 60-projects/committee-pack-v1/B5d-free-text-scoring-rubrics.md

B5E Reconciliation Against The Live Advisor Reviewed Design

B5e — What the vault missed, and what it means

Hunter's own words, this session: "I just want to reiterate that our measurement forms we have a google doc that Eimear and Debra and myself were working from — and we made a html on the workshops and had measurement questions and the case study form all there — i want us to ensure that we know of it and have taken it into consideration."

He was right to ask, and it was not fully taken into consideration before now. This document is the catch, written the same session it was found, per CLAUDE.md §9a.

1 · What was found, and where

Three Google Drive documents plus one published artifact, none previously read in full by the session that built B5/B5a/B5b/B5c/B5d:

Document Date Status
MFC Measurement & Forms — Advisor Review Pack 13 July 2026 Sent for Eimear/Debra approval. Fuller item set (EDU-01–04, APP-01–03).
MFC Measurement Blueprint (spreadsheet: construct map, cross-timepoint matrix, data dictionary, evaluation logic, stage gates, claims/privacy rules) v0.2 → v0.3, 13–15 July 2026 Its own decision log calls it "the source of truth for advisor review" and states review packs are "temporary surfaces… decisions must be resolved into the Blueprint and Workshop Forms."
MFC Workshop Forms (the actual live operational forms — Form 1, 2, 3, Host Debrief) v0.10, 23 July 2026 The canonical, most-recent wording. Leaner than the July 13 pack.
MFC Workshop Package — 3-Hour and 1-Hour (published artifact, the HTML Hunter linked directly) Re-cut 2026-08-03, corrected 2026-08-05 Renders the same Form 1/2/3 verbatim from the live doc, explicitly labelled "Eimear Quigley and Debra Fidler's advisor-review draft," plus an audit layer with named proposed fixes.

None of these were read before B5a was written. B5a cites "the Drive Measurement Blueprint's PRE-02" once, in passing — meaning some earlier pass knew the Blueprint existed and named-checked one item from it, but never opened the Workshop Forms doc, the Advisor Review Pack, or the published HTML. That is exactly the shape of failure L-013 and L-044 already named in this vault: partial awareness treated as sufficient reconciliation.

Also confirmed, and this matters for how alarmed to be: the terminology in B5's own §9 diff table (F-01, F-02, F-03, F-05…) uses the exact item-ID scheme from this same document lineage. The 10 August rebuild was not built in ignorance of this material — it inherited its vocabulary from it. What it did not do is go back and check the rebuild against the live, advisor-engaged version before finalising. This is a partial miss, not a total one, and that distinction matters for what follows.

2 · The good news first: most of what changed was deliberate, and defensible

B5a §1 states plainly that its whole exercise began "after a founder instruction to stop building counting machinery and rebuild the construct from the gap." Read against the live documents, three things hold up as genuine, reasoned evolution rather than oversight:

  • Dropping the counted opportunity/attempt ratio (F-01/F-02/F-03). The live Workshop Forms doc still carries this. B5a §4 gives four independent reasons to retire it — self-scoring harm, small-n noise, and (with correction) the taught-denominator problem. These reasons are sound on their own terms and were reached by direct analysis, not by ignorance that the counted version existed.
  • The A-01 two-week-window fix. B5 correctly caught that an earlier internal draft (the 10 August forms draft) had dropped the reference window the live doc's Q3/Q4 always had. This is a real bug-fix, not a regression against the live design.
  • The general direction — fewer, harder-to-ceiling items, more discipline about what counts as a matched comparison. The live documents share this instinct (see the Blueprint's own "ONE QUESTION → ONE CONSTRUCT → ONE DECISION" rule) even where the specific execution differs.

What follows are the differences that were not reasoned through against the live material, and need to be now.

3 · Three genuine forks — none of these are settled, all need your call

3.1 The primary construct: one global item, or the five-situation matrix?

Live design (Workshop Forms v0.10, Form 1 Q3/Q4, repeated at Form 3): asks the SAME knowledge/access question separately across five named everyday situations — overthinking, stress/strong emotion, distraction/follow-through, difficult conversations, and struggling to be present — each on a 4-point knowledge scale and a 6-point access-frequency scale. Reported and compared per situation, never collapsed into one score. This is more granular than anything in B5.

What B5/B5a built: one global item (A-01) — "when there was something you knew could help, how often did you remember to use it while the moment was happening" — with no situation breakdown.

This is not a small stylistic difference. The five-situation matrix is already advisor-engaged, already has a wording history, and directly answers a criticism a single global item cannot: it lets MFC say which kinds of moments the workshop moves and which it doesn't, rather than one number that hides that entirely. B5a never engages with this design at all — its own single-item redesign was reasoned against the old counted-ratio problem, never against the matrix as the actual live alternative.

Genuinely open, not decided here. Arguments for keeping A-01 as a single item: shorter (the matrix costs roughly 4× the respondent time of one item, at every timepoint), and a single matched item is what a small-n cohort can actually power a comparison on. Arguments for the matrix: it is the version Eimear and Debra have already been reviewing, and it produces genuinely more useful, situation-specific findings for exactly the "improve the three products" purpose you named this work for.

Recommendation: keep A-01 as the primary matched outcome (the reasoning in B5a for avoiding a ceiling and self-scoring harm still holds), but add the five situations as the A-02-equivalent context layer, replacing the current single opportunity item — this recovers most of the matrix's diagnostic value at a fraction of its cost, and it is closer to what Eimear and Debra have actually seen. This is a recommendation, not a decision already made.

3.2 Linkage: an email, or an anonymous token+code?

Live design: Form 1 collects an actual email address, converted to a hashed ID, key stored separately from the answer dataset — the exact "email → hash to ID → store key separately" approach R3 §2 explicitly evaluated and rejected.

What R3/B5 built: no email at all — a shuffled pre-printed token card plus a self-generated identification code (SGIC), specifically to avoid MFC ever holding an identifier.

This was a reasoned, evidence-based replacement, not an oversight — R3 §2's whole table compares the two designs directly and gives real reasons (participant trust, privacy exposure, one-person admin burden, legal characterisation) for preferring token+SGIC. But this reasoning was never put in front of Eimear or Debra, who reviewed and (implicitly, by not objecting in the document) accepted the email-based design. Changing MFC's actual data-collection mechanism away from something advisors have already reviewed, without telling them why, is exactly the kind of silent supersession CLAUDE.md §4 says must be surfaced, not resolved quietly.

Recommendation: keep the token+SGIC design — R3's reasoning is more rigorous than what's currently live, and the privacy case is strong. But this needs to go back to Eimear and Debra explicitly, with R3's reasoning, as a proposed change to something they already reviewed — not presented to them as already-settled.

3.3 WHO-5: required everywhere, or removed — and this is the one that actually worries me

Live design, every document, without exception: WHO-5 is required — "WHO-5 is a required part of Workshop 1 across every delivery pathway" (Workshop Forms v0.10), carried through the published HTML as "Required · matched" in every pathway, as recently as the 2026-08-05 correction pass.

What B5 states: "WHO-5 removed — Founder decision; K-05."

I cannot find anything this attributes to. Per L-026 (a claim attributed to the founder must trace to something Hunter actually said), I looked for the actual instruction and could not find it in anything read this session. B5's own §1 gives the reasoning for removal (K-05's distinction; no approved distress pathway for it while D-0016 items 1–2 are open; "three contradictory statuses") but reasoning is not the same claim as a founder decision, and the most recent live, advisor-facing record — five days before your own instruction to stop building counting machinery — still has it as required.

This is the fork I would flag hardest. Not because removing WHO-5 is necessarily wrong — the reasoning given (D-0016's open distress-pathway gate, the definitional clash with K-05) is real and worth taking seriously. But it is currently recorded as a settled founder decision when I cannot verify it was ever actually decided by you, and it reverses something Eimear and Debra were actively reviewing as recently as five days before this rebuild started.

Recommendation: do not treat this as settled. State plainly to Eimear and Debra: "we are proposing to drop WHO-5 from the core instrument, for these reasons — do you agree, and if you don't, what's the alternative?" That is a real, bounded question for the people who were already reviewing it, not a unilateral removal.

4 · What this means for the four-timepoint architecture specifically

None of the live documents mention a fourth timepoint. All three Google Drive documents and the published HTML describe exactly three forms, consistently, across every version from 13 July to 5 August. The only later-wave concept in any of them is the case-study-only check-in named in the HTML's own "Case study" tab — which is D-0056, already fully reconciled in B5c §1's warning box.

This does not change the recommendation to field four timepoints (per §1.2 of B5c and your own instruction this session to field the whole design) — it confirms that doing so is a genuine extension beyond anything advisor-reviewed yet, not a return to something already settled. It strengthens the case for putting the day-90 wave in front of Eimear and Debra explicitly, the same way §3.1–3.3 above need to go to them — it is new to all three of them, not just to this document.

5 · What does NOT need to go back to advisors

To be precise about scope, since not everything found here is a fork:

  • The token+SGIC linkage mechanism's technical design (the exact code items, the matcher) — sound engineering regardless of which linkage method is chosen.
  • H-01, the harm item, and the referral line — genuinely new, additive, uncontroversial safety improvements the live documents did not have at all.
  • RET-01's placement rule (D-0008 non-contamination) — a compliance requirement, not a construct choice.
  • The durability lock and its executable control — infrastructure, not content.
  • The university partnership strategy (R9) — entirely independent of this reconciliation.

6 · The honest cost of this catch

Nothing was fielded, so nothing is unrecoverable — this is exactly why it matters that it was caught now rather than after the first cohort. But it means:

  1. D-0100 (the decision record drafted at B5c §5) is not ready for adoption as written — it would lock in the WHO-5-removal and linkage-method choices without the review §3.2–3.3 above say they still need.
  2. Blocker 7 in B5 §10 ("Review of constructs, wording, burden and claim boundaries — Eimear Quigley, Debra Fidler — Not started") was stated as not started because it genuinely has not started on this rebuilt version.
