It has, however, already happened once, on an earlier version that this rebuild diverged from without telling them. That distinction should be made explicit when this goes to them, so it reads as "here's what changed and why, does it still hold up" rather than a fresh cold review of something they've never seen.
  3. This is the actual, complete content of what B5 §10 blocker 7 requires — not a formality to discharge, but a real conversation that needs to happen given what §3 above found.

Backlog Rationale And Future Products

Purpose

Hunter has been generating strategy rationale, product ideas and open questions faster than any single deliverable can absorb them, and has explicitly asked that none of it be lost: "I'm hoping that you're able to remember these things, put this in our system, and go, cool, yes, this will be the next thing we'll get to. We're gonna structure this project of the completion of all these rationale and thinking. It will take time."

This file is that holding place. Nothing here is authorised to build yet — it is a queue, checked and worked through deliberately, not a backlog that quietly becomes the plan. Each item states what it is, why it matters, and what it still needs before it could be built or tested.

Open items

1. Physical/visual Radar product — "the board, not the form"

Raised: 2026-08-10 (committee-pack-v1 session, alongside the delivery-model rebuild).

The idea, in Hunter's words: "How do we make the radar a visual thing teams can pay to have? It's not just a piece of paper. It's a board, and they can write their moments on for the week... That's now a visual thing. That could be a product." Sits in the office or at home; makes the practice ambient rather than something retrieved from a drawer; something MFC could recommend at the end of a one-hour session ("we recommend getting this thing, put it in your team, in your office") as the bridge from a single session into daily use.

Why it matters — three separate arguments, not yet reconciled: - Revenue — a sellable, repeatable, low-marginal-cost product with margin, sold to teams and individuals/households — a second income line distinct from workshop delivery. - Retention/environment design — MFC's own framework says a Rep is easiest to do when the environment prompts it. A physical object in a shared space is a designed environmental cue, not a random branded item ("not just — hey, buy this shirt randomly"). This is the strongest version of the argument and ties directly to the framework, not just merchandising. - Upsell path — natural recommendation from the one-hour/short formats, which strengthens the case for those formats existing at all (see the delivery-model rebuild running in this session).

What it still needs before this is a plan, not an idea: 1. Hunter's own test, which he named himself: "is this something organisations would be open to?" — no market signal yet, only the founder logic above. 2. A design — literal object, format, what goes on it, how "moments" get written down, whether it's consumable (replaceable cards/sheets) or durable (whiteboard-style), physical cost and margin. 3. Whether it's a paid product, a bundled inclusion with the half-day, or both at different price points. 4. Reconciliation against the existing Radar instrument in R3-measurement-research.md / B5a-measurement-construct.md — is this the same Radar (an alternate physical form of the measurement instrument) or a separate consumer product that happens to share a name? This matters because if it's the same artefact, it has measurement-validity implications (self-report on a shared wall is a different data-quality problem than a private form); if it's separate, it needs its own name to avoid confusing the two in the committee paper.

Status: idea stage, not costed, not evidence-tested. Queued, not scheduled.

Standing instruction this file exists to satisfy

Hunter, 2026-08-10: everything discussed in this strategic process should eventually reach the committee paper as visible rationale — "I'm eventually gonna want to be able to have on the committee paper... this needs to be this... all the rationale and the thinking behind it." This file is the tracked queue toward that, worked through as capacity allows, not blocking the 17 August committee deadline.

Original source: 60-projects/committee-pack-v1/BACKLOG-rationale-and-future-products.md

C1 Challenge Commercial

C1 — Commercial and numbers challenge

Position up front: I would not approve this paper as written. It is the best paper this organisation has produced and it is still not approvable, for one reason above all others — it asks the committee to approve a price for a product that the organisation's own decision record forbids it from delivering, and it does not put that in the decision section. Everything below is secondary to that.

The paper is also, repeatedly, more confident than the research sitting underneath it. In several places the underlying file says "not achievable," "not demonstrated," "unverified," or "if this fails reopen the other option" — and the paper carries forward the conclusion without the qualifier. I have listed each instance with the quote from both sides. That pattern, not any individual number, is my main concern about the paper as a governance document.

0. The thing that should have been decision 1

§7 of the paper, as a bullet, fourth in a list:

"Nothing is participant-facing yet. Safeguarding matters remain open and no session may be delivered until they close."

D-0016 is status: "decided-partial — mandatory pre-pilot gate remains unresolved". Six matters remain open. Items 1–2 need qualified clinical-governance input, item 4 needs qualified legal input, item 6 needs insurer confirmation. None of that can be produced by the founder, by this committee, or by any amount of work inside MFC. It requires paying external professionals or persuading them to act pro bono, and the paper contains no date, no cost, no owner and no route for any of it.

So the paper asks us to approve a $4,200 price and a 21-session-a-year model for a service that cannot lawfully be sold to a participant-facing buyer on any date the paper is willing to name.

What I would demand instead. Decision 1 becomes: "the committee notes that no revenue is available until D-0016 items 1–6 close, and approves/does not approve a named budget and owner for obtaining the clinical, legal and insurance input required." Pricing becomes decision 4. If that sequencing is wrong, tell me why in one paragraph — but do not put it fourth in a risk list.

1. The demand engine — I do not accept route 1

1.1 There is no commercial reason for a WHS consultant to refer

The paper ranks first:

"WHS consultants, EAPs and insurance brokers as referral partners" … "They are already in the room when the psychosocial code is discussed, and they cannot supply the review evidence it requires. We can."

I have read R1 §3.3, Route 1 and Part 7 in full. I searched the entire research pack for the words commission, referral fee, rebate, reciprocity, finder's fee and kickback. There are zero hits. Not one. The channel this paper ranks first has no economic mechanism in it at all.

So answer these directly:

  1. What does the consultant get? A consultant billing $200–400/hour has just written an improvement-notice response. They do not have a gap — they have a follow-on engagement. Is MFC proposing a referral commission, a white-label arrangement where the consultant marks MFC up and keeps the client, reciprocal referral of MFC's own clients (of which there are none), or nothing? Nothing is currently the answer, and "nothing" is not a channel.
  2. Why would they attach their name to us? R1 Part 8 makes this argument better than I can, and the paper omits it entirely:

"MFC's own honest position … is that individual-level content delivered without a supporting environment lacks demonstrated durable effect, and the code puts training near the bottom of the hierarchy. A competent WHS consultant knows this. When MFC arrives offering a half-day workshop, the sophisticated partner's first question is: why would I attach my name to a lower-order control for a client I have just told to redesign the work? MFC has an answer — the measurement layer — but it is a subtle answer, and referral partnerships are built on simple ones. Channels that require a two-step explanation tend not to fire."

The paper reduces this to one risk bullet about consultants "bringing it in-house." That is the weaker half of the objection. The stronger half — that a competent adviser has a professional reason not to refer us at all — is not in the paper in any form. 3. What is the recognition substitute? We are a charity with an ABN active since 2025, zero delivered sessions, zero case studies, one unaccredited facilitator, and no published track record. A consultant referring us is lending us their credibility for free. Referring a name the client recognises costs them nothing and carries no downside. What is the offsetting benefit, in one sentence, that a consultant would repeat to their own client?

What I would demand. Either (a) a stated partner economics model — commission rate, white-label margin, or a named non-cash exchange — written into §4 before this route is ranked anywhere, or (b) route 1 demoted and re-described as "a hypothesis about a channel, with no tested economic mechanism, being tested in the twelve-week window." The paper's own falsification test is also softer than the research's: R1 says "if three or more partners engage warmly and none refers within 12 weeks, the insourcing hypothesis is confirmed and MFC should stop, not persist." Put that stopping rule in the paper.

1.2 The demand premise itself is unproven and the paper does not say so

§1 opens:

"Six weeks ago the law in New South Wales changed in a way that creates a buyer for the one thing MFC does that nobody else does."

R1 §1.3, in full:

"HONEST ANSWER: not established." … "Whether it generates training spend is not demonstrated, and the regulatory guidance actively discourages treating training as the answer."

And R1 §5.3: "It is a strong hypothesis, not a proven motivator."

The paper does concede this — in §7, in a two-column risk table, in the right-hand column, at position two. A committee reads paragraph one. The confidence gradient across this document runs downhill, and the honest statement is at the bottom of the hill. I would demand the §7 hedge appear in §1, in the same sentence as the claim: "the legal change creates an obligation; whether it creates training spend is not demonstrated and is what the twelve-week test is for."

1.3 Peak bodies at rank 2 — what makes them say yes, and when

The paper:

"One relationship reaches many employers, and the peak body carries the credibility we lack."

That sentence describes the benefit to us. It does not describe the benefit to them, and it does not survive the obvious question: ACWA/CCWT is an RTO (#90494) that already sells short courses and in-house training to this exact audience. We would be asking a training business to put a competitor's product on its own calendar. R1 Route 2 names this precisely as the reason it is not ranked 1:

"it is the route most likely to be gatekept by a training manager protecting their own function."

The paper drops that sentence.

Timeline. The paper gives none. R1 does: "Conversation within 2 weeks. Placement on a training calendar 3–9 months." Nine months is beyond the runway on any reading. NDS's partner-offers page did not render on fetch and requires direct enquiry — i.e. we do not actually know the partner programme's terms. NCOSS's evidence is that it has promoted third-party training, which is not the same as contracting an unproven one.

What I would demand. The 3–9 month calendar-placement lead time stated in the paper; membership costs, which R1 flags as "unverified, confirm before quoting"; and one sentence saying what the peak body gets — revenue share, member benefit, co-branded evidence, or a gap they have publicly admitted to.

1.4 Two routes the research recommended, missing from the paper without explanation

  • SafeWork NSW free events and Regional Roadshow (R1 Route 5). R1: "Free. Attended by exactly the employers who have just realised they have a problem. Highest signal-to-cost ratio of any event found." Lead time: "Immediate; conversations same day." Cost ~$0. It is not in the paper's ranked table at all. The one route with same-day buyer contact at zero cost has been dropped without a reason.
  • Approach Black Dog and Transitioning Well as delivery partners (R1 Route 6). Cost ~$0, four to six hours. Also absent. Given §5 below, converting the free competitor into a channel is worth one letter and the paper does not mention it.

Two omissions in the same direction: the cheapest and fastest route, and the one that addresses our largest competitive threat. Why?

2. The Run Club answer — no, I would not accept this

I proposed the Executive Run Club. R0 records what happened to it:

"on the 3 August Jake call, the Executive Run Club was recorded as 'dead, not parked — good money mechanic, not worth the effort or the saturation'" … "That judgement was made on effort and assumed saturation, not on evidence, and the board was never given a reasoned answer."

The paper now says "the mechanism is right and the venue is wrong" and substitutes Vistage. Three problems.

2.1 The Vistage substitution is presented as available; the research says it may not be

Paper:

"Vistage … operates an open speaker pathway. A pro bono three-hour session places the founder in a room of verified decision-makers with budget authority — the exact mechanism the committee proposed, without building the venue."

R1 §9.7, under the heading "The strongest argument against my own verdict here":

"I am ranking Vistage above the run club partly on an assumption — that Vistage will accept a speaker from a charity with zero delivered corporate clients and no published track record. Their stated bar is 'considered an expert in the field' and 'knows the C-suite.' Hunter may simply not clear that bar in 2026, in which case the Vistage route evaporates and the run club — slow, unqualified and demanding as it is — becomes one of the few remaining ways to get in front of executives at all. If the Vistage application is rejected, the run club question should genuinely be reopened rather than treated as settled by this document.*"

That paragraph is not in the paper. The paper presents as an available pathway something its own research explicitly flags as an unverified assumption with a named fallback — and the fallback is the proposal I made. This is the second time my proposal has been closed without the condition attached to closing it being disclosed to me. That is the specific thing I objected to in July, repeated.

2.2 "Open pathway" overstates what was verified

R1: "if there is demand for the programme, Vistage connects the speaker with a Chair." Conditional. And: "Vistage is explicitly not a leads group — it is coaching and peer advisory, 'not swapping of leads, customers, and referrals.' Speakers are there to teach, not sell." The paper does not mention this constraint anywhere. A board member evaluating "does a pro bono three-hour session produce a sale" needs to know the host organisation's stated rule is that it should not.

2.3 The paper answers on one of the two groups I named

R0 records the committee named two: the 440 Run Club and "When No One's Watching." R1:

"'When No One's Watching.' NOT FOUND."

The paper discusses the 440 and is silent on the second. If the name was recorded imprecisely, say so and ask us for the correct one — R1 explicitly recommends this. Silence reads as the proposal being dealt with rather than answered.

2.4 The hours argument is applied selectively, and this is my sharpest objection

The paper's stated reason for declining the run club:

"building our own would take four to six non-delegable founder hours every week for nine to eighteen months before a first lead. That, not market saturation, is the real objection."

I accept that arithmetic. Now apply it consistently. §6 of the same paper:

"the $20,000-plus the founder has raised through two endurance events [is] the most under-weighted asset in our strategy — it is the channel that demonstrably works at our scale, and we have been treating it as history rather than capability."

Two ultra-endurance fundraising events are vastly more founder-hour-intensive, and vastly less delegable, than turning up to a run at 5am on a Saturday. The paper costs the run club's hours to four decimal places and costs the endurance-fundraising channel's hours at zero. It cannot be both. Give me the founder-hour cost of raising the next $20,000 by the method that "demonstrably works," and put it in the same table as the run club's 4–6 hours a week.

What I would demand on the run club, in total. (a) The Vistage caveat and its fallback, verbatim, in the paper. (b) A stated decision rule: if the Vistage application is declined by [date], the Executive Run Club and the embed-in-existing-groups variant return to the committee with data. (c) The bounded, near-zero-cost test R1 actually recommended and the paper omits — twelve weeks of attendance at existing groups, success defined as three or more substantive conversations with budget-holders. R1: "That is a cheap, honest test, and it is the one management never ran before calling it dead."

3. Pricing — $4,200 is defensible, but not on the evidence the paper shows

I am not against $4,200. I am against how it is argued, and against three specific errors.

3.1 The comparator table is edited in our favour

Paper: "Three are directly comparable — flat half-day in-house fees for a group of about twenty" — and then prints four rows, the fourth being Lifeline Tasmania at $385/person, which is a public per-person course and sits in R2 §1b, explicitly outside the directly-comparable set (§1a). Sloppy at best; at worst it inflates the apparent ceiling.

More seriously, the paper omits R2's summary of that same set:

"the flat half-day in-house fee for a ~20-person group in Australia, where published, runs from AU$1,300 (charity, NFP rate) to AU$4,600 ex GST … The midpoint of the published half-day set is roughly AU$2,400–2,600."

Neither the floor nor the midpoint appears in the paper. The board is shown a $3,500–$5,500 "defensible range" without being told the published market midpoint is $2,500 and that $4,200 sits above every verified comparator except one — Preferred Training Networks' top-of-range, which is for a smaller group (under 15) and carries +$30/head materials the paper does not mention when comparing.

3.2 Yes — 68% above the nearest like-for-like, with nothing to show for it

McMillan: half day, up to 20, flat, $2,500 + GST, identical format, established provider. $4,200 ÷ $2,500 = 1.68. We are proposing to price 68% above the single closest comparator with zero delivered sessions.

R2's justification is real and the paper should use it properly: the premium is bought by the measurement and written findings report, priced against Lifeline Tasmania's published $1,870 half-day customisation line ($2,500 + $1,870 ≈ $4,370, "discounted for bundling" to $4,200). That is a defensible construction and the paper does not show it. Instead it shows a range and asserts a point inside it.

But R2 also says, and the paper drops:

"Pricing at the top of a market you have never sold into once is a positioning error even when the market supports the number."

and

"AU$5,500 is the upper bound only for a well-credentialled seller. MFC has zero customers, no case studies, and an unaccredited single facilitator."

What I would demand. The $2,500 + $1,870 build shown explicitly in §3; the market floor ($1,300) and midpoint ($2,400–2,600) disclosed; and the measurement component itemised on the quote at a stated included value — R2 cross-cutting recommendation 4, adopted nowhere: "This is the differentiator and it is currently invisible." If we cannot show the buyer what the extra $1,700 buys, we are not charging a premium, we are just charging more.

3.3 "Price is not the variable to optimise" — half sound, and used to dodge

The reasoning is genuinely good and it is R2's, not the paper's: the buyer commits ~$3,844 of irrecoverable staff time regardless, so a $500 fee move is ~6% of their total outlay and will not decide the sale. I accept that.

Where it becomes a dodge. R2 states the same fact cuts the other way and the paper prints only our half:

"(3) It also raises the bar on the offer itself. At AU$8,244 all-in for 20 people, the buyer is spending AU$412 per head of real money and time. That is the number the offer has to be worth — not AU$220."

Also dropped: "The standard sales use of this figure is 'our fee is only half your real cost, so it's good value.' That argument is weak, because it is equally available to every competitor and it raises the buyer's perceived risk rather than lowering it." The paper then makes exactly that argument, in a highlighted box, as a headline statistic.

And the logic is symmetric in a way the paper never acknowledges: if $500 does not decide the sale, $500 does not decide it downward either. The same reasoning that licenses $4,200 licenses $2,500 — and $2,500 is what the closest comparator charges and what a first-time seller with no track record would rationally charge to buy its first three case studies. The paper never engages with that.

What I would demand. Either an explicit statement that we are deliberately foregoing volume for price at zero track record and accept slower first sales, or a launch price with a stated, evidence-triggered escalator (R2 gives one: move up after the first genuine case study). Pick one and own it.

3.4 Three pricing numbers that do not trace

Paper Research Problem
"$4,200 … 3.4× direct cost" (§3 table) Paper's own §3: "Direct cost $877. With overhead, $1,228." $4,200 ÷ $877 = 4.79×. $4,200 ÷ $1,228 = 3.42×. The table says "direct" and means "fully loaded." Mislabelled in the decision table the committee is being asked to approve.
"$2,400" community/NFP tier R2 §9d recommends $2,800 small organisation and $1,800 community/NFP as two separate tiers $2,400 appears nowhere in the research. It is a split-the-difference number with no stated basis, in a decision the committee is asked to approve.
"Covers cost with a thin margin" (of the $2,400 tier) Fully loaded cost $1,228 $2,400 − $1,228 = $1,172 contribution — 95% above fully loaded cost. That is not a thin margin. R2's $1,800 tier leaves ~$570, which is. The descriptor was carried over from a different number.
"$400 minimum [Introduction], below which it loses money" strategic-consolidation-v1/05: 1-hour direct cost 2.0 × $66.10 = $132.20, loaded ~$185 At $400 we do not lose money; we make ~$215. The floor may be right for other reasons (travel, sales time) but "below which it loses money" is false as stated.

3.5 Four of R2's five cross-cutting recommendations were dropped, and one of them contradicts decision 2

R2 §9d cross-cutting recommendations: (1) flat fee — adopted; (2) overflow as a band, e.g. 21–30 = +$800 — dropped; (3) state GST on every quote — adopted; (4) itemise the measurement and report at a stated included value — dropped; (5) recover travel separately beyond a stated radius — dropped.

On (5), R2's exact words:

"MFC currently absorbs it, which silently destroys the margin on any regional booking."

The paper asks the committee, in decision 2, to commit MFC to regional and rural NSW delivery — at a flat $4,200 with travel absorbed, which its own pricing research says destroys the margin on exactly those bookings. A regional session with flights and a night's accommodation could consume $800–1,500 of a $2,972 contribution, and the community tier at $2,400 would run close to break-even or below. Nobody has modelled a single regional session. I would not vote on decision 2 without that model and a travel-recovery clause in the price card.

4. The economics — 21 sessions, and the assumption nobody stated

4.1 The paper upgraded its own source's confidence

Paper §3: "Twenty-one sessions a year reaches $60,000; twenty-seven reaches $80,000. That is a real target for a one-person organisation but it is not reachable from our current position."

R2 §5c, on the same arithmetic:

"the sustainability finding is: AU$60,000–80,000 of earned revenue requires ~19–30 sessions a year, which is at or beyond one person's realistic capacity once sales is counted."

and

"That is not achievable for one person."

"At or beyond one person's realistic capacity" became "a real target for a one-person organisation." That is a direct confidence upgrade over the source, in the sentence that carries the financial model. It is the single clearest instance of the pattern I flagged at the top.

4.2 The founder hours, worked out

Delivery side, at the paper's own 11 hours: 21 × 11 = 231 hours.

What the price allows for everything else: the 40% overhead is $350.84 a session — 5.3 hours at $66.10 — to cover, per strategic-consolidation-v1/05, "sales and product development and governance and admin, for the whole organisation, per session." Across 21 sessions that is 111 hours a year for the entire non-delivery business.

What the paper's own §9 plan actually requires, from R1's hour estimates:

Activity Source Hours/year
Route 1 — build + 2 hrs/week maintenance R1 Route 1 96–112
Route 2 — build + 2–3 hrs/week R1 Route 2 130–160
Route 3 — StateCover/LGNSW R1 Route 3 6–8
Vistage: application, prep, two 3-hour pro bono sessions R1 §9.6 ~30
Fortnightly email, 3–4 hrs × 26 R1 Route 7 78–104
Grants: Camden, Parramatta, FRRR, Perpetual R4 §"priorities" 42–54
Governance, ACNC, committee, D-0016 closure, measurement build, facilitator manual not costed anywhere 150+ (my estimate)
Non-delivery total ~530–620
Delivery paper §3 231
Total ~760–850

The price allows 111 hours for work that requires 530–620. The model under-provisions the non-delivery half of this business by roughly five times.

I want to be fair: 760–850 hours is not, by itself, more than one full-time person can work. Raw hours are not what makes 21 unachievable. Two other things do.

4.3 The load-bearing assumption the paper never states

R2's conversion assumption — "1 sale per 5–8 qualified conversations" (labelled as an assumption, not a finding). Twenty-one separate sales therefore need 105–168 qualified conversations a year — two to three and a half a week, every week, from a standing start, while delivering 231 hours. That is the fantasy version, and R2 says so.

But the paper has an answer it never actually deploys. §2: "A 120-person organisation is six sessions: one relationship, sold once." On that model, 21 sessions is roughly four clients, and four closes needs 20–32 qualified conversations a year. That is achievable.

So the whole financial model rests on selling in series of ~6, and the paper never says so. It never states the implied client count. Nowhere does it say "21 sessions means landing four organisations of 100+ staff a year." And that unstated assumption then collides with the rest of the paper: our named channels (peak bodies for community-welfare and disability providers, small NSW councils, community-tier pricing at $2,400) point at organisations that are mostly too small to generate six cohorts, and organisations over 200 staff are exactly where our credibility is thinnest and procurement is slowest.

What I would demand. A single line in §3: "21 sessions assumes N client organisations averaging M cohorts each." Then defend N and M. If N is 21, the model fails on R2's own conversion arithmetic. If N is 4, say which four kinds of organisation and how a four-month-old charity closes them.

4.4 The $60,000 is not a salary, and the paper lets us think it might be

The $66.10/hour in the cost base is, per strategic-consolidation-v1/05, "the casual-loaded national minimum ($26.44 base → $33.05 casual with 25% loading) doubled." Two consequences the committee should have in front of it:

  1. We are already paying the founder inside the cost line — for 231 of ~800 hours. 231 × $66.10 = $15,267. The remaining ~570 hours are paid nothing. So "contribution of $60,000" sits on top of $15,267 of costed labour and ~570 hours of uncosted labour. Is $60,000 the salary, is it $75,267, or is it neither because the $66.10 is imputed rather than cash? The paper does not say, and a runway calculation cannot be done until it does.
  2. The rate is below the vault's own benchmark. strategic-consolidation-v1/09 records: "the vault holds 'day rates $900–$1,800' for the closest analogue; $66.10 × 8 = $528.80/day sits below it. A cheap external check existed and this programme did not run it." If the facilitator line were costed at even $900/day, direct cost per session rises from $877 toward ~$1,500, loaded cost toward ~$2,100, and contribution falls from $2,972 to roughly $2,100 — at which point $60,000 needs 29 sessions, not 21, and $80,000 needs 39. The headline number is materially sensitive to a rate assumption that the organisation's own review says was never checked.

4.5 The real ceiling for one facilitator

R2 searched for an Australian benchmark and found none: "NOT FOUND (Australian): any Australian benchmark for realistic annual delivery volume for a solo workshop facilitator," with only non-primary material suggesting 50–70% billable utilisation. So nobody knows.

My own view, stated as a board member and not as a finding: the ceiling is not the number of sessions, it is the number of concurrent client relationships one person can originate, deliver, measure, analyse, report and debrief without the measurement — our entire differentiator — degrading. Each session carries a three-week follow-up wave, a cohort analysis and a client debrief. Twenty-one of those, overlapping, is a data operation, not a workshop schedule.

And year one cannot be 21 under any assumption, because D-0016 blocks delivery from today with no end date. The paper models a steady state and presents it as a target. I would demand a three-year ramp — year 1, year 2, year 3, with the D-0016 closure date as the start of the clock — and the runway date the paper admits it does not have, before any financial model is approved.

5. Black Dog — the distinction is real; the buyer will not make it unaided

The paper:

"Their two programmes train leaders and managers … We do a different job — we teach staff a specific procedure for their own difficult moments and then measure whether they used it."

The distinction is real. I checked R6 against the source description and it holds: Leading a Mentally Healthy Workplace (employers/executives) and Managing for Team Wellbeing (managers and supervisors) are both manager-layer and environment-layer. MFC's offer is staff-layer procedure plus enactment measurement. That is genuinely a different product.

And it will not survive the buyer's version of the question, which is not "are these the same product" but "I have a $0 option from a national institution for workplace mental health; justify $4,200." R6 itself concedes the segment problem in terms the paper softens:

"'Small-to-medium NSW workplaces' is a weaker beachhead than assumed, and the segment logic should be revisited. The buyer most able to say yes cheaply is also the buyer with the strongest free alternative."

R6's actual recommendation is to move to segments Black Dog does not reach: over 200 employees, non-private employers, outside NSW, and grant-funded settings. R2 §10 says the same: "it argues for MFC concentrating on the 200+ segment."

The paper does not make that segment change. It keeps the SME framing, prices a community tier at $2,400 aimed squarely at small organisations, and answers Black Dog with a product distinction rather than a targeting change. That is the rationalisation risk in this paper's clearest form: a true distinction used in place of a decision.

Pushing until it breaks or holds, here is where I land — it holds as a claim and fails as a strategy:

  • It holds because a small NSW employer who takes the free Black Dog manager programme still has no staff-level practised skill and no evidence of enactment. Those are genuinely unserved.
  • It fails as a strategy because that employer does not know they have that gap, and $4,200 is what it costs to find out. The buyer's mental model is a category — "workplace mental health training" — with a free option in it. We are asking a small business owner to perform a hierarchy-of-controls analysis in order to see why our product is not the free one. Almost none of them will.
  • The exception that saves it: the free offer stops at 200 employees. Above that line, Black Dog's offer is not available and the distinction does not need to be made by the buyer at all.

What I would demand. State the primary buyer as NSW employers over 200 staff, non-private employers, and grant-funded community settings, and say plainly that under-200 private NSW SMEs are a secondary segment where we expect to lose on price and do not intend to compete. Also: take R1's Route 6 and write to Black Dog. If they will not partner, we have lost a letter.

6. Numbers that do not trace, are stale, or are more confident than the source

6.1 Arithmetic errors

# Paper Correct Note
1 "$8,244 — what a half-day actually costs a 20-staff employer, all in" (headline stat card and §3 box) $8,044 R2's computation is $3,843.84 wages+super + $4,400 fee = $8,243.84. The fee input is the superseded price. At the recommended $4,200 the figure is $8,044. A headline statistic on page one is computed from a price the same page rejects.
2 "Our fee is 53% of it" (twice) 52% $4,200 ÷ $8,044 = 52.2%. Stale for the same reason.
3 "3.4× direct cost" 4.8× direct; 3.4× fully loaded Mislabelled in the decision table.
4 "$2,400" community tier R2 recommends $2,800 / $1,800 No source.
5 "Covers cost with a thin margin" $1,172 contribution, 95% over loaded cost Not thin.
6 "$400 minimum … below which it loses money" Loaded cost ~$185 False as stated.

Items 1 and 2 are small in dollars and large in what they signal: the price changed and the downstream numbers were not re-run. If the headline statistic was not recomputed, I have to ask what else was not.

6.2 Claims stronger than their source

Paper says Source says
"a real target for a one-person organisation" (21 sessions) R2: "at or beyond one person's realistic capacity"; "That is not achievable for one person."
"the law … creates a buyer" R1 §1.3: "HONEST ANSWER: not established"; §5.3: "a strong hypothesis, not a proven motivator."
Vistage "operates an open speaker pathway" R1 §9.7: "Hunter may simply not clear that bar in 2026, in which case the Vistage route evaporates." Also: Vistage is "explicitly not a leads group … speakers are there to teach, not sell."
"Expected linkage: 98–100% before-and-after, 90–95% at three weeks" R3 §1.7: "These are linkage rates, not response rates. Response rate at 3 weeks is a completely separate and much larger problem, and is where MFC will actually lose data." The paper prints the flattering rate and omits the one that determines whether we have any three-week data at all. No response-rate assumption appears anywhere in the paper, and the entire differentiator depends on it.
"Perpetual IPAP … The largest realistic solo application" R4: 2026 round closed; reopens ~Oct, closes ~Dec; "funding distributed end June 2027; earliest project start July 2027." Money arrives in eleven months. Against ~$12,000 of runway, presenting it in a funding table without that date is misleading by omission. Also: "Perpetual states next opening 'hasn't been announced.'"
"City of Parramatta — $3,000 — closes 1 September" R4: "Closes 1 Sep 2026 (Small Grants Fund) / 7 Sep 2026 (2027 Community Grants Program) — two dates surfaced, not reconciled." Hedge dropped.
"charities of our size draw about 8% of revenue from government and 39% from donations" R4: correct, but the figures are for extra-small charities (under $50,000 revenue) — fine for us today, and it should say so. What is dropped is the adjacent line: "60% of all charities are small or extra-small … together generate 1.4% of total sector revenue and receive 8.6% of donations and bequests." The 39% is 39% of very little. The paper uses it to argue endurance fundraising is our under-weighted asset without disclosing the denominator.

6.3 Timeline that does not work

R0: draft to Onno and Jake 10 August; final report to the full committee 17 August. R4: FRRR "In a Good Place" Round 12 closes 18 August 2026, 5pm AEST, requires 12–16 hours of application work, and "Do not attempt it without a named site — a vague rural framing will fail." R4 also says the geography decision was needed by 12 August.

Decision 2 asks the full committee to make, on 17 August, a decision that gates a grant closing at 5pm the following day, requiring 12–16 hours of work and a named delivery site we do not have. That is not a decision, it is a formality with a deadline attached. Either the geography question goes to Onno and Jake today with a recommendation and a named site, or the paper should say plainly that FRRR Round 12 is out of reach and the decision is being taken for Round 13 and the council pathways. I would rather be told we missed it than be handed a decision I cannot actually execute.

6.4 Smaller things I would still want fixed

  • "Zero of the eight providers with published in-house pricing use a base fee plus a per-participant charge" — true for in-house pricing, and the paper's own table two rows above prints Lifeline Tasmania at $385/person. The reconciliation (that one is a public course) is not stated, and the paper's next sentence — "Where a per-head element exists it is a $14–$50 materials pass-through" — is contradicted by its own table.
  • "twenty-seven reaches $80,000" — checks out ($80,000 ÷ $2,972 = 26.9). "$3,925 at fifteen and $3,640 at twelve" — both check out. Credit where due.
  • Not disclosed: at a full room of 20, $4,200 flat is $200 less than the current structure ($4,400), and R2 puts break-even at ~18 attendees. The change is a price rise in small rooms and a price cut in full ones. The committee should be told that, not just the headline increase.
  • Pro bono: R2 recommends the entitlement be "explicitly framed as a charitable grant of the full AU$4,200 value on the paperwork, not as 'free,' so it does not corrode the price anchor." Dropped. The accrual structure the paper proposes (one per three paid, capped 3) is better than R2's flat cap of 4 and I would keep it — with the paperwork requirement added.
  • Decision 3 (claims register) has no supporting document in this research pack. "Pending since May" — what is it, who drafted it, and what does adopting it commit us to? I will not vote to adopt a register I have not seen.
  • R5 internal inconsistency, for the record: it states ACNC registration and DGR from 3 April 2025 and then says MFC "has been a registered charity for just over four months" as at 2026-08-10 — which would be sixteen months. One of the two is wrong, and both the paper's credibility with funders and the Sports Fund's "established" test depend on which.

7. What I would need to approve this

Would I approve as written? No. Not decision 1, not decision 2. Decision 3 I cannot vote on at all because the register has not been circulated.

Blockers (must be fixed before approval):

  1. D-0016 becomes decision 1, with a named owner, cost and target date for the clinical, legal and insurance input. No revenue model is approvable while delivery is prohibited.
  2. State the client count behind 21 sessions, and defend it. Four clients × ~6 cohorts, or 21 separate closes? The model works on one and fails on the other.
  3. Route 1 gets an economic mechanism — commission, white-label margin or a named non-cash exchange — or it stops being ranked first.
  4. Regional delivery gets a travel-recovery clause and one worked example before decision 2 is put to a vote.
  5. The Vistage caveat and its fallback go in the paper, with a decision rule for reopening the run club if the application is declined.
  6. Re-run every downstream number against $4,200 and correct the six errors in §6.1.

Would strengthen it considerably:

  1. Segment change to 200+, non-private, out-of-NSW and grant-funded settings, per R6 and R2 §10.
  2. A three-week response-rate assumption, stated, alongside the linkage rate.
  3. Restore SafeWork NSW events (R1 Route 5) and the Black Dog partnership letter (Route 6).
  4. Perpetual's June-2027 disbursement date shown in the funding table.
  5. Founder-hour cost of the endurance-fundraising channel, in the same table as the run club's.

8. The single change that would most improve this paper

Replace the steady-state model with a dated ramp, starting from the D-0016 closure date.

Everything wrong with this paper is downstream of one habit: it describes an equilibrium — 21 sessions, $4,200, six ranked channels, $60,000 — for an organisation that has delivered nothing, is legally blocked from delivering, holds roughly $12,000, and does not know its own monthly burn. A steady state is not a plan; it is a description of a destination.

A ramp forces every honest question into the open at once: when does D-0016 close and who pays for it; what is the burn and the runway date; how many sessions in the twelve months after that date, not in an average year; which four clients; how many founder hours in the first quarter and where do they come from; what happens to price when we have one case study instead of none. The paper's own §9 is close to this and is not carried into the numbers.

Give me year 1, year 2 and year 3 against a dated start, and I will approve the pricing structure in the same meeting.

Challenge issued 2026-08-10. Every quotation above was checked against the file cited. I have not independently re-verified the external sources behind R1–R6; my challenge is to the paper's use of its own research, not to the research itself — which is, with the exceptions noted, considerably more honest than the paper drawn from it.

Original source: 60-projects/committee-pack-v1/C1-challenge-commercial.md

C2 Challenge Evidence

C2 — Evidence and claims challenge

Standing of this review. Adversarial by design. Everything below was checked at primary source or at named secondary source, not against the papers' own working files, except where explicitly stated. Where the papers are right, this record says so — a review that finds only faults is as useless as one that finds none.

Headline. The pack is unusually honest by the standards of this sector, and two of its sections (market paper §7 "What we cannot claim", committee paper §7 "Risks") are better than most charities of any size produce. But the single claim the entire repositioning rests on — that the psychosocial code requires documented review evidence that controls are working — is not what the code says. It is a "should", in a document whose own key-terms page defines "should" as a recommendation and "must" as a legal requirement. And the pack's central competitive claim about Black Dog is factually wrong in a way a board member will find in ninety seconds. Both must be corrected before circulation.

Part 1 — The legal claim

1.1 What checks out, cleanly

Claim in the papers Verdict Source
s26A of the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (NSW) commenced 1 July 2026 Verified Inserted by the Industrial Relations and Other Legislation Amendment (Workplace Protections) Act 2025 (NSW), passed 27 June 2025; commencement 1 July 2026. Confirmed across King & Wood Mallesons, Lockton, Norton Rose Fulbright, Hamilton Locke
Approved codes of practice are no longer guidance alone Verified Applies to all ~30 approved NSW codes, not only the psychosocial code
PCBU must comply with the code, or manage the risk to an equivalent or higher standard Verified This is the operative wording of s26A
A shortfall can be treated as a breach without evidence that harm occurred Verified, with a precision note Consistent across law-firm commentary. Precisely: s26A creates the duty; breach is prosecuted through the Act's existing offence provisions, and can found improvement/prohibition notices. It is not a new standalone offence with its own penalty
$344m NSW workplace mental-health package Verified NSW Government; includes SafeWork NSW as a standalone regulator
20 new psychosocial inspectors Verified, with a date correction 51 additional inspectors, of which 20 psychosocial inspectors and 5 psychosocial investigators, announced/commenced March 2026 — four months before 1 July, not as part of the 1 July change. The papers imply they arrived with the commencement. Minor, but a WHS adviser will notice
Training sits below work redesign in the control order Substantively verified Code §3.4: "Where hazards and risks remain even after the work has been redesigned, then administrative controls, including safe systems of work, and appropriate information, training, instruction and supervision, will also be required. Relying on administrative controls should never be the main risk management approach." Note the phrase "hierarchy of controls" appears once in the whole code, and only in a list of common failures. The papers' wording is a fair paraphrase, not a quotation

Credit where due: the papers get right the thing most organisations get wrong — they refuse to sell the workshop as a psychosocial control, and they say so unprompted. That is the correct call and it should survive everything below.

1.2 The load-bearing claim — it does not hold

The papers say:

"What the code also requires — and what almost nobody supplies — is documented review showing that the controls an employer chose are actually working. That is the evidence layer... it is now a legal expectation rather than a nice-to-have."

I read the code. It does not require this.

Source: Code of Practice — Managing Psychosocial Hazards at Work, SafeWork NSW, May 2021 (gazetted 28 May 2021, approved under s274 WHS Act), retrieved and read in full 2026-08-10 from safework.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0004/983353/Code-of-Practice_Managing-psychosocial-hazards.pdf.

(a) The code's own definition of its verbs. From "How to use this Code of Practice and key terms":

"The words 'must' or 'require' indicates that a legal requirement exists and must be met, 'should' indicates a recommended course of action, and 'may' an optional course of action."

(b) The review section is entirely "should". §3.5 "Step Four: Proactively implement, maintain, monitor and review the effectiveness of controls" reads, in relevant part:

"Clear accountabilities for monitoring, reviewing and maintaining controls should be allocated... Reviews can be used to check whether: ... hazards and risks are being effectively controlled... Reviews should occur: before significant organisational or workplace changes occur... where a new hazard or risk is identified... if a control measure is not adequately minimising the risk... at agreed review dates, such as annually, or where audit results indicate, a review is necessary."

Not one "must". Not one "require". The section contains no obligation to hold evidence that a control is effective — only that reviews can be used to check whether risks are being effectively controlled, and should occur at listed trigger points.

(c) Documentation is explicitly optional, and explicitly substitutable. §4.2 "Keeping a record of the risk management process and outcomes":

"Keeping an organisational risk register... is an optional but helpful way to record psychosocial and physical hazards, risks and incidents... A WHS Inspector may ask to see a copy of any records... If the PCBU does not have a written record, an inspector could, for example, ask for statements from affected workers."

The code anticipates and accepts an employer with no written record at all. The paper's word "documented" is therefore the opposite of what the code says.

(d) The only "review and document" phrase in the code is a planning prompt, not a duty. Under "Adequate planning", among things "it is important to decide on":

"• how and who will review and document the effectiveness of the controls."

One bullet, in a pre-start checklist, introduced by "for example". It is the closest the code comes to the papers' claim, and it is not a requirement.

(e) The code did not change on 1 July 2026. It is still the May 2021 version. What changed is its enforceability, not its content. So the papers' §7 "Established" column — which lists "the legal change and what the code requires" as established — asserts as established the one thing that is not.

1.3 The genuine review duty is real, is older, and is elsewhere

There is a hard legal duty to review control measures — but it sits in the WHS Regulation (NSW), not the code, and it has existed in substantially the same form since 2011 (carried into the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2025 (NSW), which commenced 22 August 2025, alongside the psychosocial-specific control provisions at ss 55C–55D).

Three consequences, all against the paper:

  1. The review obligation is not new, and did not arrive six weeks ago. The papers' entire framing — "what changed six weeks ago" — attaches the review duty to the 1 July commencement. It predates it by roughly fifteen years. Any competent WHS adviser knows this. If a buyer's adviser says "we've had a review duty since 2011", MFC's whole opening collapses in the room.
  2. It is a duty to review and as necessary revise — not to evidence effectiveness. A compliant review can be a documented conversation, a consultation record, or a revised risk register entry. Nothing requires quantitative outcome data, and nothing requires an external supplier.
  3. The duty attaches to the controls the employer chose. Per §3.4 the primary controls should be good work design; training is an administrative control the code says should "never be the main risk management approach". Evidence that staff used a personal procedure MFC taught is effectiveness evidence about an administrative training control — the control type the code deprioritises. The paper's escape hatch ("we don't sell training as a control, we sell the review layer") does not survive contact: you cannot sell review evidence about a control while denying that the thing being reviewed is a control.

1.4 Verdict on the repositioning

The legal facts are right. The commercial inference drawn from them is not.

  • s26A is real, significant, and correctly described.
  • The proposition "the code now creates a legal expectation of documented control-effectiveness evidence, and MFC supplies it" is not supported by the code, and the underlying regulatory review duty is old, lighter, and satisfiable without buying anything.
  • There is no duty anywhere in the WHS Act, Regulation or code that MFC's product discharges.

This is the highest-severity finding in this review, and it is also a legal-exposure finding, not only an accuracy one. If MFC's sales conversations imply that buying its measurement helps discharge a WHS obligation, that is a representation about legal compliance which is not accurate. Australian Consumer Law s18 (misleading or deceptive conduct) applies to a charity acting in trade or commerce. A charity making compliance claims it cannot support, to small businesses, in a regulated area, is the single most reputationally dangerous thing in this pack.

What can honestly be said instead (and it is still a good pitch):

Codes of practice became enforceable in NSW on 1 July 2026, and NSW has put 20 psychosocial inspectors in the field. The code recommends that employers review whether their chosen controls are working, and inspectors can ask how psychosocial risks have been managed. Most employers who run wellbeing training have no way to answer that question about it. We give you one.

That is defensible, it survives a WHS adviser, and it loses almost nothing. Recommendation: rewrite committee §1 and §5 and market §2 and §6 to this standard, and remove "requires", "legal expectation" and "documented review" as descriptions of the code.

Part 2 — The Black Dog claim

2.1 What checks out

Verified at blackdoginstitute.org.au/education-services/workplaces/mental-health-at-work-nsw/ and nsw.gov.au/employment/mental-health-at-work/free-training-and-coaching/training, both retrieved 2026-08-10, full page text read.

  • Free, NSW-Government-funded workplace mental health training. Verified.
  • Delivered by Black Dog Institute psychologists, face-to-face as well as online/Zoom, plus self-paced eLearning. Verified.
  • Funded under SafeWork NSW's Psychological Health and Safety Strategy 2024–2026. Verified — and note the "2024–2026" in the strategy's own name is a stronger signal on the funding-term question than R6's "not established" allows.

2.2 Three errors, one of them serious

Error 1 — there are three programmes, not two, and the third is staff-facing. Both papers say "Two programmes, both aimed at leaders and managers." Black Dog's own page lists three:

Programme Who it's for (Black Dog's own words) Delivery
Leading a Mentally Healthy Workplace Executive leaders, directors, business owners, employers 1 hr, Zoom
Managing for Team Wellbeing Managers, supervisors, people leaders, employers 3 hr face-to-face or online; or 2 hr self-paced
Your Mental Health at Work Employees, sole traders, apprentices, tradespeople, volunteers 2 hr face-to-face or online; or 45 min self-paced

"Your Mental Health at Work" teaches staff to "recognise early warning signs", "have supportive conversations", and "practical self-care strategies and how to support others". Black Dog's FAQ adds that the manager programme contains the employee content: "If you complete the Managing for Team Wellbeing program, you do not need to also complete Your Mental Health at Work, as the employee-focused content is included."

This is not a pedantic correction. It falsifies the pack's central competitive sentence — "Their two programmes train leaders and managers... We do a different job — we teach staff". Black Dog trains staff, free, face-to-face, in NSW, right now.

Error 2 — eligibility is broader than stated, in the direction that flatters MFC. The papers say "any private NSW business with fewer than 200 employees". Black Dog's own eligibility wording:

"A NSW-based business with fewer than 200 employees, or a not-for-profit organisation of any size based in NSW."

MFC's $2,400 "community, not-for-profit, small organisation" tier is priced into a segment that gets Black Dog free regardless of size. That tier's rationale needs rework, not just a footnote.

Error 3 — the room is the same size. Black Dog's private workshops are for 20+ participants, designed for 20–25, and an organisation can book up to three private workshops across the programmes. MFC proposes a 20-cap half-day. The comparison the paper wants to avoid — same audience, same room size, same state, half the duration, $4,200 versus $0 — is available to any committee member with a browser.

2.3 Is the distinction MFC draws accurate, or convenient?

Convenient. As drawn, it is not accurate.

What survives is a narrower and genuinely defensible distinction, and the papers should be rewritten to it:

  • Black Dog's staff programme teaches recognition, supportive conversation and self-care strategies — literacy and support, in Black Dog's own framing.
  • MFC teaches one named procedure, cued to a participant-nominated moment, practised in the room, with a follow-up count of whether it was run.

That is a real difference in kind. It is not the difference the pack asserts (manager-layer vs staff-layer), because the staff layer is occupied. The honest line is "we are the only one at the staff layer measuring whether it got used" — not "we are the only one at the staff layer."

And even that narrower line has a problem, which is Part 3.

2.4 Black Dog publishes an enactment figure — which breaks the market paper's central gap claim

On the same page, Black Dog publishes:

"84% of employees or sole traders report they've used at least one wellbeing strategy from the training."

Also: "93% of managers report increased or high levels of confidence" and "99% of leaders said they plan to apply what they've learned".

The 84% figure is a self-reported post-training enactment measure from a delivered Australian programme in this exact category, published on a public page. The market paper's central gap sentence is:

"no delivered Australian programme in this category can say whether anyone actually used what they were taught."

That is contradicted by the front page of the competitor the paper itself names. MFC's measure is better — it is opportunity-conditional, counted, repeated over time, and reported with nulls, where Black Dog's is a single unanchored post-course item. That is a real and defensible difference of rigour. It is not the difference between "nobody" and "us".

Severity: highest reputational risk in the pack. If circulated as drafted, a funder or journalist who spends ninety seconds on the Black Dog page finds a claim the paper says does not exist, on the site of the organisation the paper names as the market's incumbent. Must be changed before circulation.

Part 3 — Claims-boundary compliance against K-08

3.1 The formal position, stated plainly

Per K-08's control-state warnings, and C-15/C-24: the Claims Register is not adopted. All eight board decisions (BD-01 to BD-08) remain pending, including BD-03 "Approve red-line claims." Every public asset class is Blocked. MFC's publishable claim set is formally empty. MFC has delivered zero sessions. K-08's own status line: "Nothing here is board-approved."

Credit: the committee paper says this out loud, in §8 decision 3 — "Until it is adopted we cannot publish a claim at any level — website, funder and grant language all remain formally blocked." That is exactly right and it is to the pack's credit that it is there.

But the paper then contradicts it. §9 "What happens next" item 6 asks the committee to endorse "Submit the council applications now open, and prepare Perpetual for October", and §8 decision 2 gates the FRRR application closing 18 August. Grant applications require grant language. §8.3 says grant language is formally blocked. The paper asks the committee to approve, in the same document, actions that its own §8.3 says cannot lawfully be taken under the organisation's own controls. Either the register is adopted first (and §8.3 should say the applications are conditional on it), or the paper must state that the applications will be drafted to the Level 1 "Relationship" rung only and held. Internal contradiction; must be resolved before circulation.

3.2 Breach schedule

Severity: A = must change before circulation · B = should change · C = note only.

# Sev Document / location Text Problem under K-08
1 A Market §4 "no delivered Australian programme in this category can say whether anyone actually used what they were taught" Falsified by Black Dog's published 84% figure (Part 2.4). Also relies on an undefined category term doing the load-bearing work
2 A Market §3, Committee §1 "Two programmes, both aimed at leaders and managers" Factually wrong (Part 2.2)
3 A Committee §1, §5; Market §2, §6 "the code... requires documented review showing that the controls an employer chose are actually working"; "a legal expectation rather than a nice-to-have" Not what the code says (Part 1.2). Also an implied compliance claim to buyers — ACL s18 exposure
4 A Committee §4, route 1 "They cannot supply the review evidence it requires. We can." Present-tense capability claim. MFC cannot: the instrument is a draft, no session has been delivered, D-0016 safeguarding matters are open, and the register is unadopted. Must become "we are building the capability to"
5 A Committee §2 table Foundations "delivers... the procedure practised, a personal cue identified, an implementation intention formed, and — at follow-up — self-reported use in a real moment" Stated in the indicative as delivered outcomes for a programme never delivered. K-08 ladder: nothing above Level 1 is even proposed as approved. Must become "is designed to produce"
6 A Committee §5 "Expected linkage: 98–100% before-and-after, 90–95% at three weeks." Drops the qualifier that R3 states explicitly and in bold: "90–95% of those who respond... These are linkage rates, not response rates. Response rate at 3 weeks is a completely separate and much larger problem." As written, a committee member or funder will read 90–95% as three-week retention. It is not
7 B Market §3 Smiling Mind: "Revenue $6.6m (2023) → $4.3m (2025)... Government funding fell to zero. Exited the adult market entirely in 2025... no retention figure ever published" Hard negative assertions about a named charity, single-sourced, not independently verified in this review. Contemporaneous third-party sources still describe a Smiling Mind workplace programme at named corporates. Either cite the audited financials line by line or soften to "we could not find"
8 B Market §3 Gotcha4Life: "Seventeen months later nothing has been published against it" An asserted negative about another charity's research output. Must become "we found no publication"
9 B Committee §5 "This is our differentiator" The differentiator is unbuilt and untested. "This is our intended differentiator"
10 B Committee §1 "It is what we are built to do" Capability claim; nothing is built
11 B Market §3 Commonwealth service described as "non-clinical" The Medicare Mental Health Check In delivers CBT via phone or video by trained professionals (St Vincent's Health Australia). "Free, no referral, no diagnosis" is right; "non-clinical" is a stretch and the wrong word to be loose with in a claims-sensitive charity
12 B Committee §6 "the $20,000-plus the founder has raised... the channel that demonstrably works at our scale" Two events is not a demonstrated channel. Also sits three paragraphs from §7's "$12,000 remaining" — a reader may conflate the two. Standing vault rule: never present $20k as the current position. It isn't here, but the proximity is careless
13 B Committee §6 FRRR: "Our claim boundary is their selection criterion" Rhetorically neat, substantively false. FRRR's criterion is non-clinical, community-driven, rural/regional wellbeing projects. It is not a claim-discipline criterion
14 C Market §1 Spending rose / four indicators worsened / 2017 quote The juxtaposition does causal work the evidence cannot support. The paper does hedge ("Some of the rise likely reflects better recognition... None of this is an argument against treatment") — adequate, but the hedge is placed after the inference has already landed
15 C Market §6 "an active Australian research group... their own published work names this follow-up as the gap" Not verified in this review. Unnamed, so uncheckable by the committee
16 C Committee §3 "Community... $2,400 — covers cost with a thin margin" $2,400 − $1,228 fully-loaded = $1,172, a 49% margin. Not thin. Say "covers cost with a real but reduced margin"

3.3 What the pack does NOT breach — and should be credited for

Checked and clean. Neither document claims treatment, prevention, cure, diagnosis, symptom reduction, clinical validation, guaranteed outcomes, brain rewiring, suicide-risk reduction, or any effect on absenteeism, attrition, productivity, workers' compensation or culture. Market §7 states the causal boundary correctly, including the two corrections this vault has had to make before: "the individual-content model is not demonstrably working" (not "content without environment fails") and "the study most often cited for this is cross-sectional and cannot establish cause". That paragraph is the best-governed writing in the pack. Keep it verbatim.

Committee §5's "We will not be able to say that we caused anything — there is no control group" and the commitment to publish disappointing results with equal prominence are both correct and both rare.

Part 4 — The measurement section

4.1 Is "a measure on which everyone starts high cannot show that anything moved" fair?

Partly. It is over-stated in three ways, and the paper should not put it in front of a committee in this form.

  1. The absolute is wrong. The ANU study's median baseline was 70.8%, not 100%. That leaves ~29% headroom. A ceiling compresses detectable improvement; it does not make movement undetectable. And it does nothing to prevent detection of a decline.
  2. The paper picks one interpretation of a null and presents it as a finding. "[It] returned a null result on the very intervention it was designed to detect" (F₃,₂₁₅.₃₆ = 0.50; P = .68). A null is equally consistent with an ineffective intervention, an underpowered design, or an insensitive instrument. Choosing "insensitive instrument" is the reading most convenient to MFC. It may well be right. It is an inference and must be labelled as one.
  3. The TYDQ objection is stated as a defect of the instrument when it is a mismatch of altitude. The paper says the TYDQ "measures broad daily habits that a half-day workshop has no mechanism to shift in three weeks". That is a correct and honest reason not to use it as a primary. It is not a reason to reject it, and R3 does not reject it — see 4.3.

4.2 The strongest case against MFC building its own instrument

Put at full strength, because the paper does not put it at all.

  1. It is the easiest attack in the pack. An organisation whose stated differentiator is measurement rigour rejects both published, validated Australian instruments and scores itself on a marker it invented. "They wrote their own exam and marked it." That sentence writes itself, and it is the one a hostile reviewer, a rival, or a journalist will reach for. Building bespoke does not merely risk the credibility MFC claims — it attacks it at the exact point MFC has chosen to stand.
  2. A bespoke measure has no psychometrics. No reliability, no validity evidence, no norms, no measurement invariance. A ratio that moves cannot be distinguished from response shift, demand characteristics, item drift, or the participant simply understanding the question better the second time. MFC already knows this — the draft instrument adds a then-test, which is an explicit acknowledgement that the yardstick itself moves. A then-test patches the problem; it does not confer validity.
  3. The opportunity-conditional design trades one bias for a worse one. The ceiling problem is real. But teaching people to notice difficult moments increases the denominator. A participant who learns the procedure notices five moments where they previously noticed two — and the ratio falls while the intervention works. This bias runs against MFC, is invisible in the data, and is not addressed anywhere in the paper. It is a more dangerous failure mode than the ceiling, because a ceiling produces a boring null while this produces an apparent harm.
  4. Small denominators make the ratio unstable. A participant reporting one opportunity produces a ratio of 0.00 or 1.00. At a 20-person cohort, with three-week response loss, the effective sample is tiny and the variance enormous. The first cohort will very likely produce an uninterpretable number — and §9 names "a first cohort showing no movement in the ratio" as a falsifier. MFC has set itself a disconfirmation trigger it may hit for purely statistical reasons.
  5. No external comparability. A bespoke ratio has no benchmark. If the pilot returns 0.38, nobody — MFC, the committee, or a funder — can say whether that is good.
  6. It cannot do the job §4/§6 sells it for. The papers position the measure as review evidence a WHS adviser, insurer or inspector would value. An unvalidated, unpublished, provider-designed marker is precisely what a WHS adviser or insurer will not accept as evidence a control works. The commercial argument and the measurement argument are pulling in opposite directions and the paper does not notice.

4.3 The omission that most damages MFC — and the cheapest fix in the pack

The paper's own research does not recommend building bespoke alone. R3's recommendation, verbatim:

"RECOMMENDATION: build MFC's own primary enactment measure, and adopt TYDQ-15 as a single, clearly-labelled secondary context measure."

R3's reasons for the secondary: "it gives the committee and any funder a validated, Australian, approach-agnostic instrument on the record", and "label it in advance, in the protocol, as a context measure that is not expected to move in three weeks. Writing that down before the pilot is what makes a subsequent null honest rather than embarrassing. Cost: ~2 minutes."

The committee paper drops this entirely and presents the position as "we examined the two published Australian instruments and are not adopting either." Technically true of the primary slot. But it converts a defensible two-instrument design into the indefensible built-our-own-and-marked-it position, and it does so by omission, for no gain.

This is the single highest-value correction available in the whole pack, and it costs two minutes of instrument time. Reinstate TYDQ-15 as a labelled secondary and the "you built your own exam" attack largely evaporates.

Two riders, both from R3 and both absent from the paper: TYDQ licensing was not confirmed (one email to the JMIR corresponding author resolves it), and the actual published item wording must be obtained — a reconstructed TYDQ is not the TYDQ and cannot be compared to its norms.

4.4 Verdict

Building a bespoke primary is defensible, on the specific and narrow ground that no existing instrument measures a cued procedure conditional on opportunity. It is not defensible as presented — as a rejection of the validated field. Present it as primary bespoke + validated secondary + pre-registered protocol + published nulls, and it becomes a strength. Present it as drafted and it is the pack's second-largest vulnerability after the legal claim.

Part 5 — The statistics

Figure Verdict Detail
$14.5bn Australian mental health spend, 2023–24 Verified AIHW: "In 2023–24, national spending on mental health-related services was estimated to be almost $14.5 billion or $537 per capita, up from $466 per capita in 2014–15." Note: it is $14.5bn on mental-health-related services, not total mental health spend. Say "services"
$466 → $537 per person over nine years Verified Same AIHW source. Note it is nominal, not real — real per-capita growth is materially smaller. A funder's analyst will ask

Caution on the comparator — this vault's own second-wave checker (27-checker-findings-second-wave.md) flagged that the "46% fatal across all disease groups" comparator could not be confirmed. That comparator is not in these two papers. Good — keep it out
