Genuinely closed: four and a half of eight.

2 · Runnability — delivering Part B tomorrow, to fifteen strangers, cold

Read as a facilitator, not as a reviewer. Part B is a real improvement: the [SAY] lines carry intent and wording, the stuck points are scripted by name, the minimum-viable pass is stated aloud, the opt-outs are given by default rather than on request, and the online drill variant is specified. C3 §8's items 1–4 are substantially answered. Here is where it still stalls.

2.1 The 0:00 promise is falsified by the 1:21 form

The opening block is marked verbatim in substance and contains:

"Nothing you write today gets collected or read by me or by anyone who booked this session."

At 1:21, participants complete Form 2, which includes P-08 — "Write the one recurring moment you have chosen to work on" and P-11 — "Which of the five does your moment mainly ask for, and why?" Both are collected, both are read, and P-08 is described in the forms draft as "the participant's cue" — the item the entire follow-up depends on. In Foundations, F5's commitment wording and its named owner go onto the facilitator's delivery record.

The 1:21 script then says something narrower and different — "nothing goes to whoever booked this with your name on it" — which is true and is not what was promised at 0:00.

This is the most participant-facing defect in the document. A verbatim safeguarding assurance that the session then breaks is worse than no assurance, and it is the kind of thing that surfaces in the room, from a participant, at 1:22. The 0:00 line needs to become the true one: nothing you write is collected except the anonymous form at the end, which carries a code and not your name, and which nobody who booked this session ever sees.

A second contradiction in the same block. "You will never be asked to say anything personal out loud." At 0:52 the facilitator invites "a time this week you caught something and it still went badly" with "one or two volunteered aloud"; in Foundations, F1 has a participant taken through their own moment out loud by a peer for seven minutes. "Invited" is not "asked" only to a lawyer.

2.2 The self-generated linkage code is never collected

The forms draft is explicit: linkage runs on two keys — the token card and a seven-character self-generated code built from four items (mother's first name, day of birth, month of birth, number of older siblings), and the self-generated code is what "recovers linkage at three weeks and later, when the card may be lost" — the 90–95% match at three weeks depends on it.

Part B's 0:05–0:09 block issues token cards and explains only the card code. The four code items appear nowhere in the script, nowhere in the materials list, and nowhere in §A5's burden arithmetic. Every three-week and durability figure in the chain rests on an item the session never collects.

2.3 Where a first-time facilitator actually stalls

  • 0:05–0:09, four minutes. Issuing shuffled cards to fifteen people, explaining the code, and catching up Form 1 (≈5 min on the forms draft's own estimate) — plus, once fixed, the four code items. C3-10 flagged this; B2 kept the 4 minutes and answered a different question (what to do if Form 1 was never sent). Still underbudgeted.
  • 0:09–0:13. B2 itself calls this "the tightest beat in the format" and instructs "Hold this beat at four minutes — take questions at 1:19." The close is 2 minutes and also has to carry the threshold framing. A room of fifteen strangers that has been told twice to hold its questions will not be emptied in ninety seconds. The instruction is right; the vessel it points at is too small.
  • 0:56–1:08, the moment beat. The private write is 4 minutes and now carries two tasks — narrow a moment to a place and a trigger, and select one of five skills. E8's row claims "60 seconds folded into E1's write", but E1's published split is 2+3+4+3 = 12 with no spare minute. The extra 60 seconds is unfunded; it comes out of the 4-minute write.
  • 1:15–1:16, "say it." "To the person next to you, or under your breath to yourself." With an odd number, or in a room seated in rows, "the person next to you" is not always available. Trivial to fix, and the sort of thing that produces a five-second stall in front of fifteen people.
  • The dominator, the refuser and the silent room. §B5 handles the silent room for three beats and n=1 well. There is no instruction anywhere for the participant who talks over every beat, and none for outright refusal beyond "you can step out." The 0:52 beat, which invites volunteered personal material with no cap and no closing move, is where a dominator will take four minutes out of a format that has two to give.
  • Distress in the room. B2 correctly discloses (§D6) that E6 and F3 raise disclosure exposure and refers both to D-0016 items 1–2. But not one beat in Part B contains a line for what the facilitator says and does if somebody discloses something distressing. The disclosure card is pointed at once, at 0:00. D-0016 gating delivery is the right frame, and it does not remove the need for the plan to say where that content will go when it is written.
  • In-person only, unstated. An online variant is given for the drill and nothing else. The pair beats, the board narrowing, the moment slip, the theme reveal and the full-pass sheet all assume a room. The live build carries online provisions throughout (captions on by default, no registration gate before the privacy notice, 12–25 online). Part B neither carries them nor says it is in-person-only.
  • Room size contradicts itself. Part A sells Essentials to "teams of 1–15." Part B says "Room: 12–20 seated." Both appear in the same document, and a facilitator has to pick one.

2.4 Foundations cannot be run from Part C as written

Part C states: "Not a second plan. Everything in Part B runs as written unless named here." Two consequences its author does not appear to have followed through:

  1. The theme reveal runs twice. Part B's moment beat opens with the 2-minute anonymous theme reveal. In Foundations the reveal has moved into F5 at 1:43–1:49. Part C's "what does not change" list explicitly says the moment beat is "12 minutes, same script." Follow that instruction and the facilitator reveals the same themes at 1:43 and again at 1:49.
  2. The 12-minute moment beat now has 12 minutes for 10 minutes of content (narrow 3 + write 4 + shape check 3), because its 2-minute reveal left. Two minutes are silently unattached — which is the precise flaw C3-11 raised against B1's reconciliation, surviving into B2's.

2.5 The Foundations clock is a delivery hazard

Every time in the Foundations table is a content-clock time, and the 15-minute break sits between 1:05–1:13 and 1:13–1:23 without advancing it. On the wall, the toolkit starts at 1:28, the peer beat at 2:24, and the session ends at 3:15. B2 says "elapsed 3h15" once, in a note. Every operational instruction uses the content clock — including "Foundations' cut-order rule is the same list, checked at 2:09", which on the wall is 2:24. A facilitator with a wall clock and this table is fifteen minutes wrong from the break onward.

2.6 Are the [SAY] lines sayable?

Mostly yes, and this is the biggest single improvement over B1. They use contractions, concrete nouns, and short sentences; 0:09–0:13's four moments, 0:32–0:37's State Check and 1:16–1:19's lapse-and-return are genuinely speakable and would land. Three that are not:

  • 0:00 is ~110 words of dense compliance language delivered standing, cold, marked verbatim. It will be read off a card. That may be acceptable for safeguarding text; it should be designed as a card, not left as prose.
  • 0:13–0:20 (K-E2) is two long paragraphs, and it is the beat B2 itself identifies as the hardest facilitation in the session. A first-timer will read it aloud, which defeats a beat whose whole purpose is that the room recognises itself in it.
  • 0:47–0:52 (Shift menu) instructs "the menu names aloud, never the bare category words" — and the script then leads each item with the bare category word ("Move it — feet on the floor…"). The script contradicts its own instruction one line above it.

3 · The clocks — every number added independently

Essentials. 5+4+4+7+5+7+5+10+5+4+12+8+3+2+9 = 90 ✓. All fifteen clock boundaries reconcile (0:00 → 1:30) ✓. Protected measurement 4+9 = 13 = 14.4% ✓. Internal splits check: E1 2+3+4+3=12 ✓; E7 2+5+1=8 ✓; E4 3.5+1.5=5 ✓; E3 7+10 ✓.

Foundations. First block 8+4+10+4+7+5+7+5+10+5+8 = 73 ✓ (0:00–1:13). Second block 10+15+5+6+12+8+21+15+3+2+10 = 107 ✓ (1:13–3:00). 73+107 = 180 ✓. All boundaries reconcile ✓. Protected 4+10 = 14 = 7.8% ✓.

The delta. 3+10+5+8+5+15+1+6+21+15+1 = 90 ✓, and 90+90 = 180 ✓. I also rebuilt it independently from the two clocks beat by beat, and it holds — with the one qualification in §2.4: the "+6 Our moments" line silently absorbs a +2 expansion of the Foundations moment beat.

Burden. 480 − 120 + 140 = 500 s ≈ 8.3 → 9 ✓, 14 items ✓ (12 − 3 + 5, list verified against the forms draft). Foundations 500 + 45 + 20 = 565 ≈ 9.4 → 10 ✓, 16 items ✓. Form 3: 10 − 1 = 9 ✓.

The arithmetic is clean. B2 has earned that. Two qualifications: the burden figures exclude the four linkage-code items (§2.2), and they exclude Form 2's linkage block entirely.

Against a real room, four beats are underbudgeted even though the sums hold — 0:05–0:09 (cards + Form 1 catch-up + uncollected code items), 0:56–1:08's 4-minute write now carrying two tasks, 1:19–1:21's 2-minute close carrying every held question from a room told twice to hold them, and 0:09–0:13, which B2 correctly identifies as the tightest beat and then protects only by instruction. B2's honesty about arrival ("book the room for 1h45, doors open fifteen minutes early") is the right answer to C3-10's last bullet and should stay.

4 · Decision-record compliance — B2's central compliance claim is wrong

B2's crosswalk: "No D-0018 record is drafted because none is needed — nothing is being removed." That is true of the five skills and false of the document. D-0014 §1 names the essential functions in terms:

"The taxonomy protects, at the design-requirement level: Stage 7's approved outcomes and essential content; Decision 1's five-phase session architecture and the intended function of each phase; Decision 2's explanatory feedback and recall-based retrieval; … Decision 5's approved Radar structure (three personally meaningful moments…)." "These requirements may not be removed, contradicted, or materially weakened."

And D-0018: "a change to an 'essential function' requires a new decision record"; "essential-element changes require Hunter's approval."

B2 alters three of those named essential functions and drafts zero decision records.

  1. The Mechanism phase is removed from Essentials. B2 declares it as Deviation 2 and hedges: "if Hunter reads the five phases as essential functions rather than structure, a decision record is owed." The reading is not open. D-0014 §1 already names the five-phase architecture and each phase's intended function as an essential function, and §6 defines material deviation to include "materially change session sequence or phase function." A record is owed now.
  2. Three Radar moments → one, in both formats. D-0014 §1 names Decision 5's structure verbatim, three moments included. B2's defence is that the live 1-hour already carries this deviation. Precedent in a build is not authority; it is the same deviation twice.
  3. D-0004's recall-based retrieval element is moved out of its approved phase, undeclared. D-0004 approves "one recall-based retrieval element… operating in the Revisiting/Connecting phase." B2's own phase mapping puts the drill inside Skills (0:37, within 0:20–0:52) and says so in a parenthesis: "the recall-based retrieval element sits in the drill at 0:37." The same is true of Foundations (drill 0:50–1:00, inside Skills 0:38–1:05). In both formats, Revisiting/Connecting now contains no retrieval element at all — Essentials' is four minutes on what counts as a rep, which revisits nothing. This is a third deviation, undeclared, to an essential function D-0014 names twice.

The deeper error is what D-0014 is being used for. Its deviation mechanism is a light facilitator-side record for departures that arise in delivery — safety, accessibility, a room that needs something different. It is not a design-time licence for the product design of record to ship without an approved essential function. Used B2's way, the approved design becomes non-compliant by construction and every facilitator records the identical "deviation" every time — which is D-0014's own stated trigger for "repeated adaptations that may indicate a workshop-design problem." D-0018, not D-0014, is the right instrument for all three.

Does E8 satisfy D-0003? Yes, genuinely — see §1.5. It is restoration of taught content with a beat, a script, a card, an outcome and an item, not a relabelling. The one open question is the Radar concept as the sixth item.

Does the Essentials Team Pulse variant sit inside D-0014's allowance? No, on two grounds. It is an addition to the short format, not a deviation from it; and D-0091 and the live build both say the short format works this material not at all in the room. It needs a decision record or it needs cutting — see §1.6.

5 · Claims — K-08 line by line

The claim boundaries are the strongest part of B2's chain, and several are better than the builds they replace. E7's "One rehearsed pass in a supported room is not one pass in a real moment, and the two must never be reported in the same number" is the best claim sentence in this project. E4's narrowing, F3's refusal of any organisational claim, and F5's "the room agreed one shared commitment" as a facilitator record rather than a norms claim are all correct. K-08 rules 6, 7, 9 and 10 are honoured in the room, not in a footnote.

What would still let a facilitator overclaim, or a participant hear a promise:

  1. K-E2's script makes the mechanism claim its own claim boundary forbids. The boundary says the outcome "does not license any claim about mechanism or brain change." The [SAY] line is: "the response you've done ten thousand times arrives before the one you've thought about twice. The old route is faster because it's been used more." A route that strengthens with use is a neural-pathway claim in plain clothes — K-08's ladder puts mechanism at Level 3, pending, and its prohibition list bars "rewiring the brain." B2 bans the amygdala and the brain diagram and then says the thing they are shorthand for. Reword to experience: "whatever you've done most is what turns up first."
  2. "That's it. That's the whole problem. Knowing the answer was never the missing piece." A sufficiency claim about the cause of the knowing–doing gap, stated flat, in a document that elsewhere disciplines itself carefully. It is also the sentence a committee member will quote.
  3. The 0:00 collection promise (§2.1) — a consent statement the session breaks. This is the one to fix first.
  4. "You will never be asked to say anything personal out loud" against E6's invitation and F1's peer turns (§2.1).
  5. E3's "answering 'red, amber, green' is a fail." Correct as design language; it sits in a document a facilitator will read, next to a script that promises "there is no correct move here, and I'm not going to grade one." Mark it as scoring guidance, not room language.

6 · The measurement spine

Every outcome has an item — this side holds. E1→P-08+B-07; K-E2→B-06+P-01b; E3→P-02+P-02b+F-04; E4→P-03 (with the silent half honestly declared unmeasured); E5→P-05+F-07; E6→P-04+P-04b; E7→P-09; E8→P-11; F1→P-12+F-11; F2→P-05b (gap disclosed); F3→F-12; F5→no item, deliberately and defensibly.

Every item does not have an outcome, and the cut rule is applied inconsistently. B2 cuts B-03, B-05 and P-06 for being "attached to no outcome in either format." By that rule it should also have addressed B-01/F-05 — which the forms draft calls "the single most important matched item" — plus B-02, P-01, P-07, F-06, F-08, F-09, F-10, none of which traces to any outcome in this chain. That is 8–9 surviving items outside the spine against 3 cut for being outside it. The circularity C3-12 identified in B1 is intact.

Is the reverted binary-plus-band D-0017-compliant? Yes. D-0017 approved "'at least one reported attempted application,' with an added opportunity-sensitivity item" and a follow-up asking "whether any of the three Radar moments arose; whether a Mental Rep was attempted in any of them." B2's F-01/F-02 are that, and are more compliant than the live forms draft's cardinal ratio. §D3's drafted-not-adopted record for the cardinal alternative is the right way to keep the choice real. This is well handled.

Two defects in the revised items themselves.

  • The two options collide. F-01 offers "not at all" and F-02 offers "there was no relevant moment." A respondent can answer F-01 "once or twice" and F-02 "there was no relevant moment," and nothing says which governs. F-01's "not sure" has no stated treatment in the denominator either. The primary outcome is defined as "the proportion of participants who had an opportunity and attempted at least once" — with no rule for the cells that make that ambiguous.
  • P-09 contradicts the pass the facilitator has just authorised, and re-imports F-03. At 1:10 the script says, verbatim and before they start: "If you only get two lines down, write the moment and the next move. That is a complete pass." At 1:21, P-09 asks: "Today, did you run all three steps on a moment of your own? Yes / no." A participant who did exactly what the facilitator sanctioned must tick no. Worse: B2 recommends cutting F-03 because "a completion standard applied to a unit defined as outcome-independent" contradicts K-07 — and P-09 is a completion standard, in the room, on the same construct. F-02 carries "even partly, even badly"; P-09 carries no such softener while claiming to match F-02's form. B2 cut F-03 and rebuilt it as P-09 without noticing. Reword to attempt: "Today, did you have a go at running the three steps on a moment of your own — even partly?"
  • B-07 is unfieldable — §1.7.

Does B-07 avoid the leading-question problem? Yes. Asked on Form 1, seven days before the session, before any criterion has been taught, it cannot inherit a target answer. That much works. It just does not measure what it replaced, and as worded it cannot be answered.

7 · What is still missing before real participants

Beyond D-0016, and beyond the five items B2 already discloses in §D6 (materials, script, F2's missing item, no pilot, no approved claim level), all of which are honestly stated:

  1. A working cut-order rule with checkpoints placed before each cuttable beat (§1.4).
  2. The 0:00 consent wording corrected against what the session actually collects (§2.1).
  3. The self-generated linkage code written into the 0:05 block, the materials list and the burden arithmetic (§2.2).
  4. Three decision records — Mechanism-block removal, Radar three→one, retrieval-element relocation — or a founder ruling that D-0014's deviation record covers design-time change, which it does not currently say (§4).
  5. A distress-response line at each raised-exposure beat, written now and reviewed under D-0016 rather than waiting on it.
  6. Facilitation for the room that does not behave — the dominator, the refuser, the question that will not wait until 1:19.
  7. Part C rewritten as an operable delta — the duplicate theme reveal removed, the moment beat's loose 2 minutes assigned, and the Foundations table restated on the wall clock (§2.4, §2.5).
  8. An online variant, or an explicit statement that both formats are in-person only.
  9. Room size reconciled — 1–15 or 12–20, not both.
  10. Facilitator competency and rehearsal, which D-0014 §1 names as an essential function (Decision 6) and which B2 touches once, for the drill.
  11. A stated aggregation lead time for the facilitator prep step — §B6 gives a minimum-n rule (under five, do not reveal) and no deadline.

8 · Better or worse than B1

Materially better, and not yet sufficient. B2 opened the file B1 did not, restored two governed elements B1 removed by assertion, told the truth about E7 where B1 overclaimed, produced the first beat-by-beat script this project has, and kept B1's one genuine strength — arithmetic that survives being added up by someone who wants it to fail. The regressions are narrower and more mechanical than B1's, which is what progress looks like at this stage.

But the document's own headline — built against the live build; every BLOCK resolved — is stronger than what it did. It quotes the live build accurately where C3 pointed at it and repeats design-of-record numbers where C3 did not. Four and a half of eight BLOCKs are genuinely closed. The single most operationally important remedy, the cut-order rule, does not work at the checkpoint it names.

Recommended status: NOT_READY_BELOW_EXPERT_STANDARD, with §7 items 1–4 as the correction pass. None of them requires a redesign; all four are half a day's work on a document that is otherwise the best thing in this pack.

Original source: 60-projects/committee-pack-v1/C4-challenge-rebuilt-plan.md

C5 Premise Audit

C5 — Premise audit

What this is. C1 and C2 audited the papers against their own research. C3 and C4 audited the builds against the decision records. All four were handed the same frame and worked inside it. This document audits the frame.

Standing. The founder has personally caught four things in one day that no reviewer caught — the shared cohort requiring four buyers to coordinate, the cap of 20, the compliance-check in the measurement, and frequency-of-practice being the wrong construct. L-050 records the first and fourth; L-024 named the parent failure a week earlier. Every one of those was a premise, not an execution defect. That is a four-for-four record against a system that ran five adversarial review passes and found none of them. The correct response is not more checking of the artefacts. It is checking what the artefacts were built on.

Discipline applied. Where a premise holds, this document says so and says why. §9 lists the premises that survived. Manufacturing doubt about a sound decision costs the same money as missing an unsound one.

0 · Two live contradictions between documents dated the same day

These are not premise findings on their own. They are put first because each one is the visible edge of a premise the pack holds in two incompatible forms at once, and because both are checkable in under a minute.

0.1 The manager layer is simultaneously conceded and load-bearing

Committee paper §2, "Deliberately not offered yet":

"a manager-facing session — Black Dog gives that away free, and we would lose"

Offerings ladder, same date, "Add-on, any size":

"Leaders' Session · 45 minutes with the managers and the chief executive, before the team session… $350 in person / $250 virtual · Free when bundled with Foundations"

and, in the same document, under the heading "why it is not optional in spirit":

"Transfer of training is greatest when the people above the participants have been trained too, not merely briefed… if the person at the top thinks they are above this and their people connect with it, you get dissonance rather than change."

One document sells the manager session. The other says MFC does not offer it because it would lose. That is not an editing slip; it is two different answers to the question is the manager layer necessary for the product to work.

And the consequence is worse than the contradiction. If the offerings document is right — if transfer requires the people above to have been trained, not briefed — then the manager layer is the mechanism, and MFC has just conceded the mechanism to a free competitor in the segment where that competitor operates. In every NSW private business under 200 staff and every NSW not-for-profit of any size, the manager layer is available free from Black Dog, and MFC's own strategy says do not compete there. Read together, the two documents say: our product needs a layer we have decided not to sell, in the market we are targeting.

There are three coherent positions and the pack holds none of them cleanly: (a) manager involvement is necessary → then MFC must either sell it or partner with Black Dog to supply it, which is R1's Route 6 and has still never been attempted; (b) manager involvement is helpful but not necessary → then the offerings document's "not optional in spirit" and its transfer evidence must be softened; (c) MFC only sells above 200 staff and outside the free programme → then the manager session is sellable and §2 is wrong.

Second problem inside the same paragraph. "Norms shift when network-central people visibly adopt something first" is unsourced in a live document. D-0090 records that the study previously cited for this exact claim (Mas & Moretti) "was a misuse… the mechanism is behavioural spillover under observation, not observational learning from a model, and the line-of-sight direction runs opposite to what leader modelling requires." C3-18 flagged the same sentence in B1. It is still in the offerings document, presented as part of evidence that "points one direction and is unusually consistent."

0.2 There are two strategies, of opposite shape, both live

Committee paper Offerings ladder
Buyer 200+ staff, public sector, outside NSW Local small business, 1–15 people
Unit Half-day Foundations, $4,200 90-minute Essentials, $450–$900
Volume 21 sessions = 3–4 clients, series 100 organisations, year one
Sales motion Peak bodies, WHS referral partners, Vistage "walking into a local business and saying we are a charity"
Why it works Series economics; one relationship sold once Volume produces evidence twice as fast

Both are dated 10 August. Both are described as the answer. They are not compatible — the offerings document's own arithmetic puts 100 Essentials sessions at ten hours a week of delivery, which is the entire delivery budget the committee paper allocates to 21 half-days plus everything else.

And R7, MFC's own research, already adjudicated it, against the offerings document:

"MFC has designed an instrument for institutional buyers and is proposing to sell it to the segment least equipped to use it, at a third of the price, into the teeth of the only free competitor in the country, using the most expensive possible sales channel, with one facilitator and four months of runway."

R7 then names the only defence — that the small-business route is a loss-leading proof-generation exercise, not a revenue line — and says it "is a completely different decision from the one on the table [and] should be costed and time-boxed as a marketing expense rather than priced as a product."

The offerings document is that strategy, and it does not say so. Its own strongest argument ("the real argument for volume is evidence, not revenue") is exactly R7's defence, presented with a price list rather than as a marketing budget. Nobody has decided which strategy MFC is running. A committee cannot approve a price without that decision, and the paper does not put it to them.

1 · P1 — The buyer is an employer

Rank: highest consequence. This is the premise that shapes every other one.

What would have to be true

That the organisation people work for is the party most able and most willing to pay for their capacity to reach a skill under load — more so than the person themselves, a funder, an insurer, a community body, or a government programme.

Is it?

It has never been tested, and it has never been decided. There is no decision record selecting workplaces as MFC's buyer. D-0092, D-0093, D-0094, D-0096 and D-0098 all decide product shape, price and format inside an employer-buyer assumption that none of them states. R1–R7 are seven research files: R1 researches employer demand channels, R2 employer pricing, R3 measurement of employees, R6 and R7 the free employer competitor. R4 is the only file about a non-employer payer, and it treats grants as a subsidy for the employer product, not as a different market.

Searched across R1, R2, R4 and R7 for individuals as buyers, community and sporting settings as buyers, clubs, schools as purchasers, or any consumer route: no assessment exists. The only hits are incidental (a run club described as a marketing venue; a competitor's programme described as running in clubs and schools).

Why this is not a matter of taste

MFC's own governing records do not contain a workplace. K-02 (confirmed): "A world where building mental fitness is a normal part of life for everyone." K-03 (confirmed): "help people understand and strengthen their mental fitness through education and lifelong practice." K-00: "a foundational part of society." K-10's Pillar 4.1 says "phased partner sectors and early proof settings" — plural, unspecified. The workplace is an inference, held so long it stopped looking like one.

The specific damage

Every hard fact this pack discovered is a fact about the employer channel specifically, not about the need:

  • Under 200 staff in NSW, and any NSW not-for-profit of any size: a free, credible, government-funded alternative exists (R6, R7).
  • Above 200 staff: MFC's credibility is thinnest, procurement is slowest, and it has zero delivered sessions.
  • The code puts training near the bottom of the control hierarchy, so a competent WHS adviser has a professional reason not to refer (R1 Part 8, quoted in C1 §1.1).
  • In a business under about twenty people, "the report has no reader" (R7 §9).
  • The employer is also the party the measurement's confidentiality promise must be defended against (R3 §6.7).

That is a channel squeezed at both ends, in which the product's differentiator is the thing the buyer must be protected from, and in which the deliverable has no recipient in most of the segment. Nobody has asked whether the squeeze is a reason to change channel, because the channel was never a variable.

The alternatives nobody assessed, with the one that is most interesting

  1. The payer is not the room. A funder, council, insurer or peak body pays for delivery across many small organisations; the organisation pays nothing. The paper has this as "Funded or subsidised — $0 to participant" and treats it as a grant line rather than as a market structure. Treated as a structure it solves three problems at once: it removes the free-competitor comparison (nothing is being sold against free), it aggregates demand (R7's fatal cost-per-contact problem is a direct sales problem, not a funded-delivery problem), and it puts the buying decision with a party that has a documented reason to want measurement.
  2. The payer buys the evidence, not the session. StateCover — the mutual insuring roughly 94% of NSW councils — appears in the paper only as referral Route 3. An insurer or mutual has the one commercial interest in psychological-claim reduction that makes an enactment evidence layer worth money on its own terms. Nobody has asked what MFC would sell to StateCover rather than through it.
  3. Individuals, communities and clubs. Untested entirely. The relevant question is not "would a person pay $450" — it is whether the setting where a person's difficult moments actually recur is a workplace at all. MFC's own definition (K-04) is about "life's everyday moments," not work.
  4. Existing institutions with a captive, recurring audience — sporting clubs, TAFE, community colleges, apprenticeship schemes — where somebody already convenes the room, so MFC does not pay the acquisition cost.

Falsifier and cheapest test

Falsifier: if, across ten conversations spanning three non-employer payer types, none can articulate a reason to pay and no route to a decision exists — while three employer conversations produce a qualified opportunity — the employer premise is confirmed and this finding is closed.

Cheapest test, this week, before 17 August: three phone calls — StateCover (what would you pay for evidence that a control was used, across your councils?), one council community-development officer (would you fund delivery into local organisations?), one philanthropic contact already known to Hunter. Cost: an afternoon. This test is materially cheaper than the twelve-week partner test the paper already commits to, and it tests a bigger question.

2 · P2 — A facilitated workshop is the vehicle

Rank: second. Wrong here wastes the design, not just the sales effort.

What would have to be true

That a facilitated group session, plus a written client commitment, is the cheapest available way to produce access under load in a real moment — given the vault's own finding that individual-level content delivered into an unchanged environment lacks demonstrated durable effect.

Is the answer real or a reframing?

Partly a reframing, and the load-bearing half is undelivered.

The pack's answer to the graveyard finding is the client commitment: the organisation agrees to voluntary attendance, a named real opportunity to use the skill, and manager check-ins. The committee paper's own description of it:

"Client commitment · Written, not priced · This is the environment layer we can actually deliver"

Test it against the four things that make an environment layer real:

Requirement Status in the pack
Priced, so the buyer has committed something No — explicitly "not priced"
Enforced, so non-compliance has a consequence No — no mechanism anywhere
Measured, so we know whether it happened No — no item in the instrument tests whether the named opportunity was created or the check-ins occurred
Delivered by someone who remains present No — the facilitator leaves; the manager layer is the party who would remain, and §2 declines to train them (§0.1)

An unpriced, unenforced, unmeasured, unstaffed commitment is a document, not a layer. The sentence "this is the environment layer we can actually deliver" is the single strongest unexamined claim in the committee paper: it is what allows the paper to acknowledge the graveyard finding and then proceed unchanged. It should not survive as written. Either the commitment gets a price, an item and an owner, or the paper must say plainly that MFC is shipping the individual-content model the evidence has not supported, and is betting that the measurement layer is worth doing anyway.

What was never considered

The workshop was inherited from before this project began; D-0093 decided not to add sessions, D-0094 decided how long the container is, D-0098 decided how many short formats there are. No record asks whether a taught session is the right delivery mechanism at all. Candidates never assessed:

  • Delivery into a group that already meets. The most expensive line in MFC's model is convening a room. Teams, crews, clubs and shifts already convene. A fifteen-minute segment inside an existing meeting, repeated, is a different product with a fraction of the acquisition cost and a natural home for repetition — which is what the transfer literature MFC cites actually points to.
  • Cue placement in the environment rather than in the person. MFC's construct is retrieval under load. A cue that lives where the moment happens (the door, the vehicle, the handover) is the cheapest known retrieval aid and requires no facilitator.
  • Manager-delivered micro-practice, with MFC supplying the design and the measurement — the model §0.1 shows MFC has already half-adopted and half-refused.
  • Asynchronous or self-paced delivery with a measured follow-up. Correctly unattractive on transfer grounds, but never written down and rejected, so it is not clear it was considered.

Falsifier and cheapest test

Falsifier: if the first cohorts show that access-under-load moves for people whose managers did nothing and whose environment was unchanged, the vehicle is vindicated and the environment argument was over-stated. That is a real, cheap, in-design falsifier — and it requires the client commitment to be measured, which it currently is not.

Cheapest test: add two items to Form 3 — did your organisation create the opportunity it agreed to? and did anyone above you ask you about it? — and report enactment split by the answer. Cost: about thirty seconds of instrument time. It converts the largest untested assumption in the product into a variable in the first pilot.

3 · P3 — Measurement is the differentiator

Rank: third by money, first by strategic confusion.

The question nobody asked: which of three things is it?

Reading Who pays What success looks like What it costs
Product feature The employer, inside $4,200 Buyers choose MFC because of it ~$1,700 of the price; ~4 of 11 hours
Research programme A funder or research partner Publication, a validated instrument, sector credibility A partner, a protocol, ethics, years
Business Someone who buys evidence, not sessions Recurring revenue from measurement itself A different company

The pack treats all three as the same thing. It is priced as a feature, argued as a research asset, and described in §5 as "our differentiator" — a business claim. Each reading implies a different plan and they are mutually constraining.

The evidence that the product-feature reading is the weakest one

  • The committee paper's own "Not proven" column: "that measurement motivates a purchase — no Australian employer survey ranks it as a criterion, and we should not claim otherwise."
  • C2 §4.2(6), never answered anywhere in the pack: "an unvalidated, unpublished, provider-designed marker is precisely what a WHS adviser or insurer will not accept as evidence a control works. The commercial argument and the measurement argument are pulling in opposite directions."
  • R7 §9: the buyers who value measurement "are the ones with 200+ staff, a WHS officer, an insurer asking questions, and a budget" — i.e. exactly the segment where MFC has no credibility and the longest procurement.
  • The paper prices the report at ~$1,700 of a $4,200 fee, and its own §3 concedes: "If the committee's view is that the report is not worth $1,700 to a buyer, the correct price is closer to $2,600." That sentence is the whole premise, asked and left open.

And there is a structural tell. A differentiator that a buyer values is a reason to buy. A differentiator that a buyer must be persuaded to value is a research programme being funded out of sales revenue. MFC currently plans to fund the second out of the first while claiming it is the first.

The reading that is strongest and is not on the table

If measurement is the differentiator, then the party that values evidence should be the party that pays for it — a funder, an insurer, a peak body, a research partner — and delivery to the employer becomes cheap or free. That inverts the business model and resolves P1, P2's acquisition cost, and the Black Dog free-competitor problem simultaneously. It is not in the pack in any form.

Falsifier and cheapest test

Falsifier: the paper already contains the right question in §9 — "one direct question asked of each: is the measurement worth it to you?" Its placement is the defect: it is asked after the strategy has been committed to. If three buyers say the report is not worth $1,700, the price is $2,600, the differentiator is not a product feature, and the plan changes shape.

Cheapest test: ask that question first, of five buyers, before the paper goes to the full committee on 17 August. Additionally: one email to Black Dog and one to the ANU authors (R1 Route 6, R3's TYDQ licensing rider) — both still unsent, both approximately free, and both test the research-partner reading directly.

4 · P4 — Founder-delivered is the model

Rank: fourth by consequence, first by time already sunk.

What would have to be true

That the scarce asset is Hunter's delivery, rather than the design, and that year one is best spent proving the product through founder delivery rather than proving the product is deliverable by someone else.

Is it?

The plan's ceiling is one person's calendar, permanently, and no document says so. C1's arithmetic: ~231 delivery hours plus ~530–620 non-delivery hours against an overhead line that funds 111. The offerings ladder's volume model needs ten hours a week of delivery on top of all of it. D-0016 blocks delivery entirely, from today, with no owner, cost or date.

The committee paper defers facilitator licensing as "premature at zero delivered sessions" and proposes "beginning facilitator work at the third delivered cohort." That is a sequencing assumption presented as prudence. It is defensible — you cannot license what you have never run — but it has never been weighed against its cost, which is that every revenue number in the pack is bounded by one diary for at least two years, in an organisation with roughly $12,000 and a founder who has said directly that he wants his own mid-build involvement reduced.

What was never asked

Is MFC's asset the facilitator or the design? The framework is locked, written and detailed (K-07, 13,000 words); B3 is a beat-by-beat script with [SAY] blocks; the measurement is specified. That is a transferable product. The thing that is not transferable is the founder's credibility in a first sales conversation — which is a sales constraint, not a delivery one, and the two have been treated as one.

If the design is the asset, year one's success criterion is not three to eight sessions delivered — it is one session delivered well by someone who is not Hunter, which is the only evidence that anything here scales, and which the current plan does not attempt until year two.

Falsifier and cheapest test

Falsifier: if a competent non-founder cannot deliver Essentials from B3's script to an acceptable standard, the founder-delivered model is not a constraint, it is the product, and the strategy should say so and price accordingly (much higher, much lower volume, explicitly boutique).

Cheapest test: one rehearsal delivery of Essentials, from the script, by someone other than Hunter, to a friendly non-participant room — which requires no D-0016 closure because nobody is a participant. Cost: half a day. It is the single highest-information test available to this organisation and it is not in the plan.

5 · P5 — Per-session pricing

Rank: fifth. Wrong here is recoverable; the structure question is not.

What holds

The pack's pricing reasoning is the strongest purely commercial work in it. Flat versus base-plus-per-head is correctly argued and correctly evidenced (eight published comparators, zero of which use the structure MFC had). The build-up ($2,500 comparable + $1,870 report component) is a defensible construction and the paper now shows it, along with the market floor and midpoint. C1's six arithmetic defects are corrected in the live file. That work should not be reopened.

What was never on the table

Every structure considered is a fee per delivered event. Never assessed:

  • Subscription or retainer — annual access plus a measurement cycle. This is the structure that matches what MFC actually does (repeated waves over time), and it converts the follow-up burden from a cost into the thing being paid for.
  • Free delivery with a funded evaluation — the funder pays for evidence, the employer pays nothing. See P3. The most natural fit to MFC's own claimed differentiator, and absent.
  • Licensing / train-the-trainer, deferred without costing (P4).
  • Per-person — considered and correctly rejected for in-house delivery, but never considered for public delivery, where every comparator that prices per person (Lifeline Tasmania, $385/head) operates. A public-course model is the one route that does not require an employer buyer at all, and it is not in the ladder.
  • Insurer or mutual-funded, per P1.

The premise inside the price that nobody stated

$4,200 is a price for a buyer with a budget line for training. The offerings ladder's own honest paragraph concedes the flip side: "That approach fails against a $4,200 half-day and works against a $450 ninety-minute session." So the pack contains a direct statement that its recommended price is incompatible with its recommended sales motion, and does not resolve it.

Falsifier / cheapest test: the ten-conversation test the offerings document already proposes ("If none converts at $450, the segment is a mirage and we will know inside a fortnight") is right and should be run — but run it at both price points against both buyer types, or it only tests the strategy that was already chosen.

6 · P6 — Self-report is the measurement

Rank: sixth. This premise is largely defensible and I am not going to manufacture doubt about it.

What holds, and why

R3 §6.6–6.8 genuinely assessed the alternatives and rejected them for stated reasons: full EMA (unrunnable at one person, no budget), manager or peer report (destroys the confidentiality promise, and there is almost nothing observable to rate), with a micro-diary offered as a subsample and an in-room application task partly adopted. That is real consideration, not assumed-away, and the rejection of manager report is not merely defensible — it is the correct call, and the refusal is itself a demonstration of the position MFC needs to hold with participants.

B5a is a further, unusually honest correction: it retires the counted ratio for four reasons beyond the ceiling argument, restores a matched ordinal item as primary, and writes its own disconfirming result down before any data exists. The founder's fourth catch has landed properly.

The two premises inside it that have not been examined

  1. Circularity, which B5a names and does not resolve. The argument that the primary item will not ceiling is "a theoretical argument resting on MFC's own premise, not a finding." The instrument's validity depends on the thesis it exists to test. B5a states this and proposes the right falsifier. It is worth escalating because it is not only a measurement risk — it is the cheapest available test of MFC's entire reason to exist. If MFC's own participants do not report a knowing–doing gap at baseline, the market thesis, not the instrument, is what failed.
  2. "Self-report is a poor measure" and "self-report is not evidence a buyer will pay for" are different claims, and only the first was answered. R3 assessed measurement quality. Nobody assessed whether a single self-rated ordinal item, unvalidated, from a provider, is a thing an employer, WHS adviser, insurer or funder treats as evidence. That is P3's question wearing a measurement hat, and it is where the two arguments collide.

Not considered at all, and cheap: artefact or trace evidence — did the person do the thing that leaves a mark (had the conversation, made the decision, sent the message)? A-06's optional narrative gestures at this and is optional, screened and at follow-up only. One structured version of it would be the only non-self-rating datum in the instrument.

Falsifier / cheapest test: cognitive testing of A-01 on six people who have never met MFC, before the first cohort. If they cannot answer it consistently or read it as a competence judgement, it fails before any session is delivered. Cost: an afternoon.

7 · P7 — Why nobody already does this

Rank: seventh by immediate money, but it is the premise the whole market case rests on.

The claim

The market papers' central move is an absence: no delivered Australian programme in this category publishes whether participants used what they were taught; therefore there is a gap; therefore there is an opportunity.

The unexamined step

An absence is evidence of a gap. It is not evidence of an opportunity. The pack applies this distinction once, correctly, and only to small business — the offerings ladder's honest line:

"an absence can mean the market does not work, not that it is unserved. The honest test is cheap: ten conversations with local businesses."

It is never applied to the measurement gap itself, which is the larger claim. L-034 ("absence claims held to a lower standard") and L-033 ("prior art does not defeat an access claim") are both about this class of reasoning; neither is cited anywhere in the pack.

At least four explanations for the absence compete with "nobody built it," and none has been assessed:

  1. Buyers do not want it. The paper's own "Not proven" column says exactly this.
  2. Measuring enactment reliably produces nulls, and a provider whose evidence is a null does not sell more. MFC has committed in advance to publishing disappointing results — admirable, and it makes this explanation more dangerous, not less.
  3. Providers have measured and not published. Black Dog publishes an 84% "used at least one strategy" figure with no located methodology (R7's not-found register). The absence may be an absence of publication, not of measurement.
  4. The unit economics do not support it for anyone. Four of eleven facilitator hours per session go to reading responses and writing the report. If that is why nobody does it, MFC's plan is to enter a market by adopting the cost structure that kept everyone else out.

The vault has a graveyard file (market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/51-the-graveyard) applied rigorously to individual-content delivery models. The same discipline has never been applied to the measurement thesis. That asymmetry — merciless about the thing MFC inherited, credulous about the thing MFC chose — is the clearest signature of L-024 in this pack.

Falsifier / cheapest test: two emails. One to Black Dog asking for the methodology behind the 84% (also opens R1 Route 6). One to any Australian provider asking whether they measure enactment internally. If the answer is "we measure and do not publish," the gap is a publication gap, MFC's differentiator is narrower than claimed, and the strategy needs restating — for the cost of two emails, before 17 August.

8 · Premises presented in the committee paper as established

Each of these appears in the live HTML in a form a reader will take as settled. Each has been challenged and the challenge has not landed in the file.

# Text, as it stands in the paper Status
1 §7 "Established" column: "The legal change and what the code requires" Internally contradicted by §1 of the same paper, which now correctly says the code's review provisions are "should," not "must." C2's blocking finding was applied to §1 and not to §7. This is live in the file today
2 §5: "This is our differentiator" Present tense for something unbuilt, undelivered and unvalidated. C2 breach #9 asked for "intended differentiator"; not applied
3 §6: "the $20,000-plus the founder has raised… the channel that demonstrably works at our scale" Two events is not a demonstrated channel. C2 breach #12; not applied. It also sits three paragraphs from "$12,000 remaining"
4 §6: FRRR — "Our claim boundary is their selection criterion" FRRR's criterion is non-clinical, community-driven, rural/regional work. It is not a claim-discipline criterion. C2 breach #13; not applied
5 §6: "charities of our size draw about 8% of revenue from government and 39% from donations" True of extra-small charities, whose total sector share is 1.4% of revenue and 8.6% of donations. The denominator is still undisclosed, and the figure is used to argue endurance fundraising is under-weighted
6 §2: "Client commitment… This is the environment layer we can actually deliver" Unpriced, unenforced, unmeasured, unstaffed (P2). The single most load-bearing unchallenged sentence in the paper
7 §3: "$2,400 … Covers cost with a thin margin" $1,172 over fully-loaded cost. C1 and C2 both flagged; not applied
8 Offerings: "Transfer of training is greatest when the people above… have been trained too" and "norms shift when network-central people visibly adopt something" Stated as "unusually consistent" evidence; the second claim is the one D-0090 recorded as a misuse of its source (§0.1)
9 Offerings: "the real cost saving on a repeat cohort is only about $132" Two-significant-figure precision on an unstated derivation, in a buyer-facing document
10 Offerings: "Our research found no Australian provider selling short on-site sessions to businesses under about twenty" Correctly hedged in the next sentence ("an absence we searched for, not a documented fact") — credit; this is the right pattern and items 1–9 should follow it

9 · Premises I cannot fault, and why

Stated because an audit that only subtracts produces a worse strategy.

  1. Refusing to sell the workshop as a psychosocial control. Correct, made unprompted, against commercial interest, and it survives contact with a WHS adviser. Do not reopen.
  2. The claims discipline — K-08's ladder, the market paper's "What we cannot claim," the advance commitment to publish nulls, and "we will not be able to say we caused anything — there is no control group." This is the best-governed material in the vault and it is a genuine asset with funders and researchers, whatever happens commercially.
  3. Price is not the variable to optimise. The buyer's real outlay is dominated by released staff time; a $500 fee move is ~6% of it. Sound, correctly sourced, and it survives the symmetry objection (that it licenses $2,500 too) because the build-up now justifies the point inside the range.
  4. Flat fee over base-plus-per-head. Structurally correct: costs do not shrink with the room. Eight published comparators agree.
  5. Surfacing the free competitor before being asked. The behaviour that makes the rest of the pack believable.
  6. Rejecting manager and peer report as measurement (P6). Correct on both privacy and observability grounds.
  7. The cap coming down from 20 (the founder's second catch). The evidence points smaller and the arithmetic under flat pricing is favourable — a bigger employer becomes more sessions. One rider from R0 that must be stated to the committee: the cap of 20 and the co-facilitator threshold of 30 are the committee's own 20 July judgements, so a recommendation to change it is a recommendation to change their judgement and should say so explicitly.
  8. Half-day as a recognised commercial unit (D-0094), with its own honest disclaimer that the longer day is packaging, not efficacy.
  9. The environment layer matters. The diagnosis is right and the transfer literature supports it. What is faulted in P2 is the remedy, not the diagnosis.

10 · Where the founder is most likely right and the system wrong

He is four for four today. The four catches share one structure, and it is predictive.

Catch What the system tested What he tested
Shared cohort of four businesses Provider economics — a full room Can one buyer say yes alone?
Cap of 20 Facilitator capacity and committee precedent What is it like to be the eleventh person in that room?
Compliance-checking in the instrument Item-to-outcome traceability What does it feel like to be asked that question?
Frequency versus access under load Whether the measure could detect movement What is the thing we actually care about?

In every case the system reasoned from the provider's side — cost, evidence, competitor, instrument — and he reasoned from the position of the person on the other side of the transaction. L-050 found half of this ("provider-side viability was mistaken for sellability"). The full pattern is wider than sellability: it covers the participant and the construct too.

So the premises where he is most likely right next are the ones where the provider view and the person view diverge. Named, in order of my confidence:

  1. The employer-as-buyer premise (P1). The person who needs this is not the person who buys it, and every structural problem in the pack traces to that split.
  2. The written findings report as the value (P3). From the provider side it justifies $1,700. From the buyer side, in most of the target segment, it has no reader — R7 already said this about small business and nobody generalised it. Ask who, by name and job title, reads the report in a 220-person aged-care provider.
  3. The client commitment (P2). From the provider side it is an environment layer. From the participant's side it is their employer having volunteered them and arranged for a manager to ask them about it — which is close to the compliance-checking he has already rejected once, relocated from the form into the workplace.
  4. The $4,200 half-day. His small-business catch was that the binding constraint is time, not fee. That logic does not stop at twenty staff. Releasing twenty people for four hours costs the employer $3,844 and a closed department for a morning. The paper treats that as an argument that the fee doesn't matter; from the buyer's side it is an argument that the format is the obstacle.

And one place where the system is more likely right than he is, stated because this must cut both ways: the founder's instinct toward the small-business volume route (100 organisations, $450, walking into local businesses) is the one place today where his person-side reasoning collides with R7's provider-side analysis and R7 is probably correct on the money. The route is defensible only as a time-boxed, costed proof-generation exercise, not as a revenue line — and it should be put to the committee in that form or not at all.

11 · The three premises most likely to be wrong, and what to do about each

1 · The employer is the buyer (P1)

Why first: it is the premise every other one inherits, it has never been decided or tested, it contradicts nothing in MFC's governing records but is supported by nothing in them either, and every hard commercial fact this pack discovered is a fact about the channel rather than about the need. Wrong here wastes the whole plan, not part of it.

Do this week, before 17 August: three calls — StateCover, one council community-development officer, one philanthropic contact — asking a single question: would you pay for people in organisations you cover to get this, and for evidence that they used it? Then add one line to the committee paper naming employer-as-buyer as a choice with named alternatives and a test running, rather than as the setting the strategy happens in. The committee cannot ratify a premise it has not been shown.

2 · Measurement is a product feature (P3)

Why second: it is where $1,700 of a $4,200 price, four of eleven facilitator hours, the entire follow-up operation and MFC's stated identity all rest on a proposition the paper's own risk table lists as unproven. It is also the premise most likely to be half right — genuinely valuable, to a different payer than the one being asked.

Do: move §9's question — is the measurement worth it to you? — from the twelve-week test to this week, and ask it of five people including at least one non-employer payer. Send the two emails (Black Dog; the ANU authors) that have been recommended twice and never sent. Then make the committee paper state which of the three things measurement is, and who pays for it. If the answer is "research programme," that is not a failure — it is a fundable identity and a completely different plan, and it is probably the honest one for an organisation with zero delivered sessions and the best claims discipline in its sector.

3 · Founder delivery is the shape of year one (P4)

Why third: it is the constraint that caps every number in the pack, it has never been argued against, and the argument for it ("premature at zero delivered sessions") is a sequencing habit rather than a finding. It also runs directly against a standing founder instruction to reduce his own mid-build involvement.

Do: run one rehearsal delivery of Essentials from B3's script by someone who is not Hunter, to a non-participant room — no D-0016 exposure, half a day's cost, and the highest-information test available to this organisation. Reframe year one in §9 from "one to two series clients, three to eight sessions" to a capacity milestone alongside it: one session delivered acceptably by someone else. If the design does not transfer, that is the most important thing MFC could learn in 2026, and the current plan does not schedule learning it until 2028.

Method and limits

Read in full: R0, R5, R6, C1, C2, C3, C4, B5a; the committee and offerings papers as rendered text; K-00–K-05, K-10; L-024, L-048, L-050; D-0092, D-0094, D-0096, D-0098. Read in part: R1, R2, R3, R4, R7 (targeted against the premises audited; C1 and C2's quotations from them were spot-checked, not re-verified end to end). Not read: B1, B2, B3 in full, K-07, D-0016, D-0017 in full — C3 and C4's findings against them are treated as settled and this document does not re-litigate them.

Not done: no external source was independently verified in this pass. This is an audit of what the pack assumes, not of whether its facts are true — C1 and C2 did the latter.

A note on my own frame. This document was commissioned to find unexamined premises, which is an instruction that rewards finding them. §9 exists as the counterweight and is not padding: items 1–6 are places where I looked for a fault, found the reasoning already sound, and stopped. Where I have gone beyond the evidence I have said so — P1's alternative payers and P2's alternative vehicles are candidate structures nobody assessed, not recommendations, and none of them has been costed.

One thing this audit cannot do. Every test it proposes is cheap, and none of them can run inside a week while D-0016 remains open with no owner, cost or date. That gate is the premise underneath all of these: that MFC will be able to deliver at all. The paper makes it decision 3. On the evidence in this pack it is decision 0, and the three tests above are the only work that can legitimately proceed until it moves.

This log records the state as verified and completed, including the edits made directly in this pass (findings 3, 4, 5, the remaining parts of 9, and two internal inconsistencies caught while verifying — see below).

D1 Environment Layer

D1 — The environment layer

What this resolves. The committee paper describes the client commitment as "Written, not priced," and then as "the environment layer we can actually deliver." C5 §2 tested that sentence against the four things that make an environment layer real and found it fails all four — unpriced, unenforced, unmeasured, unstaffed — and named it "the single strongest unexamined claim in the committee paper: it is what allows the paper to acknowledge the graveyard finding and then proceed unchanged" (§2), and separately "the single most load-bearing unchallenged sentence in the paper" (§8 item 6). The instruction was to make it real or withdraw it. Both, in that order — the claim is withdrawn, and the part that can be made real is made real.

1 · The decision

1. The sentence "this is the environment layer we can actually deliver" is withdrawn. MFC does not have an environment layer. It has a set of delivery preconditions and, from this decision, a measurement of whether they held. Saying otherwise is a claim K-08 does not support and the transfer literature does not license.

2. The client commitment becomes a condition of delivery, not a document. It is a schedule to the services agreement, alongside the no-re-identification undertaking R3 §3.8(2) already requires. MFC does not deliver without it signed. That is a price, paid in the only currency a one-facilitator charity actually holds: refusal.

3. Three named obligations replace the current three-clause sentence (§3), each written so that a person can tell whether it happened.

4. Two items enter Form 3, and enactment is reported split by the answers (§4). Cost: about thirty seconds of instrument time. This turns the largest untested assumption in the product into a variable — in the pooled dataset, not in the first cohort. With N ≥ 20 / N ≥ 10 floors and cohorts capped at 15–20, no single early cohort can report the split. The items are laid down now because data not collected in cohort one cannot be recovered in cohort four.

4a. The obligations bind series engagements, not standalone sessions (§3a). D-0090 Proposal 2 prohibits retrofitting a leader requirement onto a one-off workshop.

4b. The funder never receives participant-level findings — programme acquittal only (§4a).

5. The consequence is named and it is small, and the paper says so (§5).

6. The committee paper states plainly what MFC is shipping (§6): an individual-content product with the environment as a measured covariate, not as a delivered layer — and a bet that measuring it is worth doing.

2 · Why "make it real" could not mean "build a real environment layer"

C5's four tests, answered honestly rather than aspirationally:

Requirement Can MFC meet it? Verdict
Priced — the buyer has committed something Not in money. Under D1-who-actually-pays.md the room-holder may pay nothing at all Met differently: made a condition of delivery. Refusal is the price
Enforced — non-compliance has a consequence Not by penalty. A charity with ~$12,000 and no delivered sessions cannot litigate a training clause, and would not Met minimally and honestly: reported as a finding; renegotiated before a second cohort. Stated as small
Measured — we know whether it happened Yes, and cheaply. Two Form 3 items Met properly. This is the substantive change
Staffed — someone remains present No. The facilitator leaves. The only party who remains is the manager layer Not met. This is why the claim is withdrawn rather than restated

The fourth row is the one that decides it. An environment layer, in the transfer literature MFC cites, is a standing feature of the setting — not a promise made before a visitor arrives. MFC cannot staff that at one facilitator, and pretending it can is precisely the credulity C5 §7 identified: merciless about the thing MFC inherited, credulous about the thing MFC chose.

What survives is genuinely worth having, and should not be undersold either. A named, signed, measured precondition is more than every content-delivery model in 51-the-graveyard-what-has-already-failed.md had. It is just not a layer, and it must not be called one.

3 · The three obligations, named

Replacing "voluntary attendance, a named real opportunity to use the skill, and manager check-ins." Each is written so that its absence is detectable.

Obligation A — attendance is genuinely voluntary, and demonstrably so. The organisation confirms in writing that no participant is directed to attend, that a named alternative use of the time exists, and that non-attendance is not recorded against anyone. Detectable because: Form 1 asks whether the participant chose to attend or was told to. Why it is first: K-08 safety rule 4 requires opt-out pathways, and obligation C is coercive if stacked on conscription.

Obligation B — one named real opportunity, named before delivery. Before the session, the organisation names one specific, foreseeable situation in the following three weeks in which the procedure would plausibly be used — a handover, a difficult client call, a shift change, a particular meeting. Not a category; an occasion. It is written into the schedule and read aloud in the room. Detectable because: Form 3 asks whether it happened. Why it matters: it is the cheapest available approximation of the practice environment, and it costs the organisation nothing but attention.

Obligation C — one named manager asks once, and records nothing. Within the three weeks, a named manager asks each participant, once: "was there anything from the session you wanted to use?" Not "did you use it." No answer is recorded, reported, or passed to MFC. The question is an invitation, not an audit. Detectable because: Form 3 asks whether they were asked — not what they said.

This obligation is deliberately weaker than the version it replaces, and the reason is a founder catch already on the record. C5 §10.3: from the participant's side, a manager arranged to ask about their use of a skill is "close to the compliance-checking he has already rejected once, relocated from the form into the workplace." That objection is correct and it is fatal to the original wording. The redesign above answers it in three ways: the question asks about want, not compliance; the answer is never recorded; and Form 3 measures whether the organisation did its part, never whether the participant complied. B5a retired a compliance-check from the instrument for exactly this reason; it must not reappear in the workplace under a different name.

4 · The measurement, specified

Two items at Form 3 (three-week follow-up), before the enactment items:

F3-E1. Before the session, your organisation named one specific situation where you might use this. In the last three weeks, did that situation actually happen? ☐ Yes ☐ No ☐ I was not told what it was ☐ Not sure

F3-E2. In the last three weeks, did anyone above you ask whether there was anything from the session you wanted to use? ☐ Yes ☐ No ☐ Not sure

Reporting rule. Enactment is reported split by F3-E1 and F3-E2, alongside the pooled figure, subject to the existing disclosure floors (R3: N ≥ 20 for any report, N ≥ 10 for any subgroup) — which means in most first cohorts the split will not be reportable and MFC must say so rather than report an under-floor breakdown. The split accumulates across cohorts and becomes reportable there.

What this buys, on an honest clock. C5 §2 named the falsifier precisely: if the first cohorts show that access under load moves for people whose managers did nothing and whose environment was unchanged, the vehicle is vindicated and the environment argument was over-stated. That falsifier was unrunnable because nothing measured whether the environment changed. It becomes runnable across pooled cohorts — realistically in 2027, not in the first room, because the reporting floors forbid it there. An earlier draft of this document claimed both that the split would rarely be reportable and that it made the assumption a first-cohort variable. Those cannot both be true; the second is withdrawn.

One limit on what any split can show, and it is the limit MFC applies to everyone else's evidence. Organisations that name an occasion and follow through are systematically different organisations — better led, more engaged, more likely to have volunteered rather than conscripted. A difference between them and the rest is a signal worth investigating, confounded by organisational self-selection, and a later matched or randomised arm would be needed to test it. It is not evidence the precondition caused anything, and K-08 does not license saying so. This is the same shape as the cross-sectional error the vault has already been burned by, and it must not be repeated in the document written to fix that class of error.

And it cuts both ways, which is why it is worth doing. If enactment is materially higher where B and C happened, MFC has a first signal that the preconditions matter — the strongest thing it could learn, and directly fundable under D1-what-measurement-is-for.md. If there is no difference, MFC's own environment argument is weakened by its own instrument, and it must publish that with the same prominence, per the standing commitment.

5 · The consequence, named and deliberately small

If F3-E1 and F3-E2 show the obligations did not happen:

  1. It is reported at contracting level — never in the site findings report. R3 §4.2 forbids anything that reads as criticism of a named or inferable manager. With one named manager and fifteen participants, "most people said nobody asked them" is a judgement about an identifiable person delivered to their employer. An earlier draft of this document required exactly that, in the same section and with the same prominence as the participant results. That was wrong, it reintroduced B5a's retired compliance-check pointing at the manager with the participants as witnesses, and it is withdrawn.
  2. MFC does not sell or accept a second cohort into that organisation until the commitment is renegotiated, in writing, with a different named manager if necessary.
  3. Nothing else. No refund, no penalty, no clause with teeth.

The paper must say that this is small. A one-facilitator charity's only real enforcement is whether it agrees to come back — which, at zero delivered sessions, is not yet a meaningful threat and should not be dressed as one. It becomes meaningful exactly when MFC has something worth being denied.

6 · What the committee paper must now say

Replacing the current row and its claim:

Client commitment · A condition of delivery, signed before the session · Three named obligations, two of them measured at follow-up. This is not an environment layer. MFC cannot supply one — the facilitator leaves, and the only party who remains is the manager layer. What MFC can do is make the preconditions explicit, refuse to deliver without them, and measure whether they held, then report enactment split by the answer. The transfer evidence says the environment matters; MFC is shipping an individual-content product with the environment as a measured variable rather than a delivered layer, and is betting that measuring it honestly is worth more than claiming it.

This is the paragraph that lets the paper acknowledge the graveyard finding and proceed — honestly this time. The previous version proceeded by asserting a layer it did not have. This version proceeds by naming the gap and putting a number on it in the first cohort.

7 · Independent check

Ledger — verification reviewer. Verified against R3, C5, D-0090, K-08 and B5a. Findings recorded at §7.1 after the review ran.

Obverse — premise auditor. Asked what would have to be true for this resolution to be right. Findings recorded at §7.2 after the review ran.
